Ledgerline handbook

Twelve weeks. Build a small banking backend and the test framework around it, one tested step at a time.

How to use this handbook

Work through it top to bottom. Every step has the same parts: why it matters, what to do, what you should see, and what to do when it breaks. Explanations of the code come right after the code.

Every file and every test in this handbook was run on Ubuntu 24.04 before you got it, starting from an empty folder, and every test passes. A few things can't be run from where I build: Docker itself, GitHub Actions, and your own machine's setup. Steps that depend on them have a Verify on your machine box saying what to run, what a pass looks like, and what a failure looks like. If your version numbers come out slightly higher than the ones shown, that's normal.

A few habits make the whole thing smoother:

  • One place for commands. Unless a step says otherwise, run commands in your terminal (Ubuntu on Windows, Terminal on a Mac), inside ~/code/ledgerline.
  • Copy, don't retype. Every code block has a copy button. When a step says "replace" a file, replace the whole file with what's shown.
  • Commit at the end of every step, with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 4: Postgres". Each commit is an undo point, and git diff shows exactly what changed since the last one.
  • Tick steps off. The Done box next to each step saves your place in this browser.
  • Where things run. The "Where everything runs" section, just before Week 1, explains what runs where on your laptop and how a company runs the same pieces. Steps that introduce a new piece end with a short "In a company" note.
  • What, why and how boxes. Every new tool or idea gets a box explaining what it is, why the project uses it, and how you'll use it, assuming you've never met it before. Tap a box's title to fold it away once you know it.

When you're stuck, come back to the chat with the step number, the command you ran, and the full error text or a screenshot. You don't need to explain your code: it's the code in this handbook, so I can match it line by line.

The road ahead

This page covers all 12 weeks, at about 8 to 10 hours a week.

  • Phase 1, weeks 1–3 (on this page): a TypeScript API with a real ledger, tests at three levels, a test framework, and CI.
  • Phase 2, weeks 4–6: queues, Lambda, a fake partner bank, idempotency and webhooks. All three weeks are on this page.
  • Phase 3, weeks 7–8: risk rules and reconciliation. Both weeks are on this page.
  • Phase 4, weeks 9–10: CI at scale, observability and quality metrics. Both weeks are on this page.
  • Phase 5, weeks 11–12: contract drift, load tests, and packaging it all for interviews. Both weeks are on this page.

Every week was built and run end to end before it went in. Where a step depends on something I couldn't run, like Docker on your machine or GitHub Actions, it has a Verify box saying what a pass and a failure look like.

Where everything runs

Everything in this project runs on your own machine. Nothing talks to the internet except downloads, and nothing costs money. That's normal for a learning project, and it's also exactly how most teams run their automated tests. A company's real system is made of the same pieces, but they live in very different places. This section shows both, piece by piece, so you always know what you're actually running, and how it would work at a company.

On your laptop

Two kinds of things run on your machine:

  • Your code runs as ordinary Node processes: the API, the processor, and the tests. When you run the API tests, Playwright starts its own copies of the API and processor.
  • Everything your code depends on runs in Docker containers: the database, the fake AWS, the fake bank and Redis. Each one makes one port available on your machine.

Your code reaches each dependency at localhost and a port. Every address comes from an environment variable, with a default that points at your laptop:

What Runs as Found through Default on your laptop
Postgres a Docker container DATABASE_URL, in src/db.ts postgres://ledgerline:ledgerline@localhost:5432/ledgerline
AWS: SQS, Lambda, DynamoDB, S3 the MiniStack container AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, in src/aws.ts http://localhost:4566, with the dummy credentials test and test
Redis a Docker container REDIS_URL, in src/risk-check.ts redis://localhost:6379
The partner bank the WireMock container PARTNER_URL, in src/processor/partner.ts http://localhost:8080
The API, for the tests a Node process API_URL, in playwright.config.ts http://localhost:3000

That one pattern, an address read from an environment variable with a local default, is what lets the same code run on your laptop, in CI and at a company without changing a line. Only the variables change.

The database, up close

  • Where it lives. Inside the Postgres container. Its files are stored in the postgres-data volume, which survives stopping and restarting the container.
  • How the API connects. The pg library opens a small pool of connections to localhost:5432, logging in with the username and password in the connection string. Docker forwards that port into the container.
  • How you can look at it. Run docker compose exec postgres psql -U ledgerline -d ledgerline, or point any database app (TablePlus, DBeaver or pgAdmin) at host localhost, port 5432, with user and password ledgerline.
  • At a company. The database is a managed service, like Amazon RDS or Aurora. AWS runs it, backs it up, encrypts it and keeps a standby copy ready. It sits on a private network that only the company's own services can reach, so you usually can't connect to the production database from your laptop at all. The connection details come from a secrets manager, not from a default in the code. Each environment has its own database, and migrations run as a step of the deployment pipeline, not by hand.

AWS, up close

  • Where it lives. MiniStack is a program that imitates AWS, running in a container on your laptop. The queues, the table, the bucket and the Lambda exist only inside it, in memory, which is why npm run aws:setup exists: it rebuilds them whenever MiniStack starts empty.
  • How the code connects. The AWS SDK sends every request to AWS_ENDPOINT_URL instead of to Amazon, signed with dummy credentials that MiniStack accepts.
  • At a company. It's real AWS, usually split into several accounts: one for development, one for staging and one for production, so a mistake in one can't reach another.
    • Resources are defined in code. Nobody runs a setup script by hand. Queues, tables and functions are described as infrastructure as code (Terraform, the AWS CDK or CloudFormation), reviewed like any other code, and created by the pipeline.
    • The endpoint setting is left out, so the SDK talks to Amazon itself.
    • There are no keys in the code. A service running in AWS is given an IAM role, and the SDK picks up short-lived credentials from it automatically. People sign in through single sign-on, with only the permissions their job needs.
  • Where QA tests AWS at a company. Most automated tests still run against an emulator like MiniStack in CI, because it's fast, free and isolated. A smaller set runs against the real development or staging account, to catch what an emulator can't, like a missing permission.

The other pieces

  • Redis. On your laptop, a container. At a company, a managed service such as Amazon ElastiCache, on the private network, usually with a standby copy that takes over if the main one fails.
  • The partner bank. On your laptop, WireMock plays the bank. At a company, WireMock still plays the bank in automated tests. For end-to-end testing, the bank provides a sandbox: a test copy of its system with test account numbers. Production connects to the real bank over an authenticated, encrypted link, and no tests run there.
  • Your code. On your laptop, Node processes you start yourself. At a company, it's packaged into container images and run on a cluster (Amazon ECS or Kubernetes), with several copies behind a load balancer, and the processor is deployed as a real Lambda. Only the pipeline deploys, and only after the tests pass.
  • Secrets. On your laptop, the API key local-dev-key, the webhook secret whsec_local_test and the database password ledgerline sit in the code as defaults. That's fine on a laptop and never acceptable at a company. There, a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Parameter Store or HashiCorp Vault) hands secrets to each service when it starts. They're different in every environment, changed regularly, and every access is logged.
  • CI. On your laptop, npm run check. On GitHub, the same containers start on a fresh machine for every push. At a company, the pipeline also deploys: it builds an image, deploys it to development, runs tests against it, then promotes it to staging and production, often with an approval step before production.
  • Logs and monitoring. On your laptop, files in logs/. At a company, every service sends its logs to a central tool such as Datadog or CloudWatch, where people search them by correlation id, build dashboards, and set alerts that wake up whoever is on call.
  • Test data. On your laptop, throwaway: npm run db:reset any time you like. At a company, test environments hold made-up or masked data. Real customer data stays in production, and testers normally can't see it.
  • Environments. You have one, your laptop, plus CI. A company has several: local, CI, development, staging and production. Each is a separate copy of everything, with its own database, AWS account and secrets.

A company, drawn

Everything in the account sits on a private network, called a VPC. Services get credentials from IAM roles, and nobody's laptop connects to production directly.

What this means for you as a QA engineer

  • Your framework already follows the company pattern. Every address and secret comes from an environment variable. Pointing the API tests at a staging environment would mean setting API_URL and API_KEY, not changing code.
  • Some helpers only work where you own everything. The database helper, queue helper and settlement-file helper reach behind the API, which is fine on your laptop and in CI. Against a shared staging environment, you'd normally run the tests that only use the API.
  • It's a common interview follow-up. "How would this run at a real company?" You can now answer it: managed databases, infrastructure as code, IAM roles instead of keys, a secrets manager, separate environments, and deployment only through the pipeline.

Week 1: Foundations

By the end of this week you'll have a TypeScript API talking to Postgres in Docker, unit tests, API tests, and a GitHub pipeline that runs all of them on every push.

Step 1: Set up your machine

About an hour, mostly downloads.

What, why and how: The terminal

What it is. The terminal is a window where you control the computer by typing commands instead of clicking. Each command is a program name followed by options and arguments. In git commit -m "Step 2", git is the program, commit says what to do, -m is an option, and "Step 2" is that option's value. On Windows you'll use Ubuntu's terminal through WSL, which is a real Linux running inside Windows. On a Mac, you'll use the built-in Terminal app.

Why we use it. Every tool in this project, from Git to Docker to the test runner, is driven by commands. Commands can be copied, repeated, saved in scripts and run by CI. Clicks can't.

How we use it. Paste commands from the copy buttons and press Enter. A few you'll use constantly:

  • pwd prints the folder you're in, ls lists what's in it, and cd folder moves into a folder. cd .. goes up one level.
  • ~ means your home folder, so ~/code/ledgerline is the project.
  • Ctrl+C stops whatever is running in that terminal, like a server.
  • The up arrow brings back your previous commands.
  • A command that prints nothing usually worked.

How it works inside. The terminal window only displays text. The program you're typing into is a shell: bash on Ubuntu, zsh on a Mac. When you press Enter, the shell splits the line into words, looks for the program in each folder listed in the PATH environment variable (which node shows where it found Node), and starts it as a new process with your words as its arguments. Every new process gets a copy of the shell's environment variables, which is how PORT=3001 npm run dev hands a setting to your API. When a program ends, it returns an exit code: 0 means success, anything else means failure. && only runs the next command if the previous one returned 0, and CI treats any non-zero code as a failed step. Ctrl+C sends the running process a signal asking it to stop.

What, why and how: Node.js, npm and nvm

What it is. JavaScript was born in web browsers. Node.js runs JavaScript everywhere else, like on a server or in your terminal. npm comes with Node and installs packages: code other people have published, like Fastify or Playwright. nvm installs Node itself, and lets you switch between versions.

Why we use it. Ledgerline's API, its tests, and nearly every tool in the project are JavaScript packages. Node is also what Relay's backend runs on.

How we use it.

  • package.json lists the project's packages and its scripts, and package-lock.json pins the exact versions installed.
  • npm install fastify adds a package. Adding -D marks it as a development tool, like a test runner, that production doesn't need.
  • Installed packages live in the node_modules folder. Git ignores it, because npm install can always recreate it.
  • npm run test:unit runs a script defined in package.json, and npx runs a tool installed in the project, as in npx playwright test.

How it works inside. Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread, with an event loop around it. When your code starts something slow, like a database query, Node hands the waiting to the operating system and moves on to other work. When the answer arrives, the rest of the async function after its await is queued, and runs as soon as the thread is free. That's how one API process serves many requests at once, and why code must never block the thread, for example with a long loop, because nothing else can run until it ends.

npm installs each package into node_modules, along with whatever that package needs itself, and records the exact versions in package-lock.json. A range like ^5.12.5 in package.json means "5.12.5 or any newer 5.x", so npm install can pick up newer versions over time, while npm ci installs exactly what the lock file says. Step through two requests sharing one thread:

What, why and how: Git and GitHub

What it is. Git records snapshots of your project, called commits, so you can see what changed, when and why, and return to any earlier state. GitHub hosts Git repositories online.

Why we use it. Commits are your undo button. GitHub is where your portfolio lives, what hiring managers will open, and what starts the CI pipeline on every push.

How we use it.

  • git add -A stages every change, git commit -m "message" saves a snapshot, and git push sends your commits to GitHub.
  • git status shows what's changed, and git diff shows exactly how.
  • gh is GitHub's own command-line tool. You'll use it to log in, create the repository, and watch CI runs.
  • Everything happens on one branch, main, to keep things simple.

How it works inside. Each commit is a complete snapshot of your files, plus a pointer to the commit before it, named by a hash of its contents: the long id git log shows. Changing anything in the past, even a message, changes every hash after it, which is why history can be trusted. The staging area sits between your files and the next commit: git add copies changes into it, and git commit saves exactly what's staged, nothing more. A branch like main is just a name pointing at one commit, and it moves forward each time you commit. git push copies your new commits to GitHub, and their arrival is what starts the CI workflow.

What, why and how: Docker and containers

What it is. Docker runs programs in containers: isolated boxes holding a program and everything it needs. An image is the recipe, like postgres:17, downloaded once from Docker Hub. A container is a running copy of an image. Docker Desktop is the app that runs Docker on Windows and Mac.

Why we use it. Installing a database, an AWS emulator and a fake bank directly on your machine would be slow, messy and hard to undo. Containers start in seconds, behave the same on every machine and in CI, and disappear without a trace when you're done. It's how most teams, Relay included, run the things their tests depend on.

How we use it. You won't build images yourself. You'll start ready-made ones: Postgres in Week 1, MiniStack in Week 4 and WireMock in Week 5, all listed in one docker-compose.yml file that you'll meet in Step 4. Chapter 3 of the field guide has a demo of port mapping, the one Docker idea you'll need most.

How it works inside. A container isn't a virtual machine. It's an ordinary process that the Linux kernel isolates: it gets its own view of the files, the network and the list of processes (these views are called namespaces), plus limits on CPU and memory (cgroups), so it behaves as if it had the machine to itself. An image is a stack of read-only layers, each one a set of file changes, which is why updating an image often downloads only a few layers. A running container adds one writable layer on top. Delete the container and that layer goes with it, which is why data that must survive lives in a volume instead.

Containers need a Linux kernel, so Docker Desktop on a Mac or Windows quietly runs a small Linux virtual machine and runs every container inside it. Publishing a port, like 5432:5432, forwards traffic from that port on your machine into the container's own network.

You'll run Linux inside Windows with WSL2. The servers you'll test and GitHub's CI machines run Linux, Docker works best there, and nearly every backend tutorial assumes Linux commands. Everything you build lives inside it.

On a Mac, skip the Windows sections and follow On a Mac further down this step. Everything after Step 1 works the same on both, and the few small differences are marked where they come up.

Install WSL2 and Ubuntu

Open PowerShell as administrator: Start, type PowerShell, right-click it, then choose Run as administrator. 

wsl --install

This switches on Windows' built-in Linux support and installs Ubuntu. Restart when it asks. After the restart, an Ubuntu window opens and asks you to create a Linux username and password. The password doesn't show while you type; that's normal. If the window doesn't appear, open Ubuntu from the Start menu.

Update Ubuntu

In the Ubuntu window:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

sudo runs a command as administrator. apt is Ubuntu's package manager, an app store you drive by typing. update refreshes the list of available software, and upgrade -y installs the updates without asking about each one.

Install Docker Desktop

Download Docker Desktop for Windows from docker.com and install it, leaving "Use WSL 2" checked. Open it, go to Settings, then Resources, then WSL integration, and switch Ubuntu on.

Docker runs programs in isolated boxes called containers. Instead of installing Postgres on your machine, you'll run it in a container you can throw away and recreate in seconds. Later phases do the same with fake AWS and a fake bank. Docker Desktop is free for personal projects. 

docker run hello-world

Connect VS Code to Linux

Install VS Code on Windows if you don't have it, then install the extension called WSL, published by Microsoft. Then, in Ubuntu: 

mkdir -p ~/code && cd ~/code
code .

mkdir -p ~/code makes a folder called code in your Linux home folder, cd moves into it, and code . opens VS Code there. The bottom-left corner of VS Code should say WSL: Ubuntu. From now on you can use VS Code's own terminal (Terminal, then New Terminal): it's already an Ubuntu terminal.

Keep projects in ~/code, never under /mnt/c/. That path is your Windows drive, and working across that boundary is much slower and causes strange file-watching bugs.

Install Node with nvm

The Node you installed on Windows doesn't count here; Linux needs its own. nvm, the Node Version Manager, installs Node and lets you switch versions later. 

curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.8/install.sh | bash

curl downloads the install script and | bash runs it. Close the terminal, open a new one, then: 

nvm install 24
node -v
npm -v

Node 24 is the long-term support version, and it's what the CI pipeline in Step 7 uses. Matching them avoids "works on my machine" problems.

Git and GitHub

Use the email address on your GitHub account:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
sudo apt install gh -y
gh auth login

The config lines label your commits and make new repositories start on a branch called main, which is the branch the pipeline watches. gh is GitHub's command-line tool. When gh auth login asks, choose GitHub.com, then HTTPS, then yes to authenticating Git, then log in with a web browser. If no browser opens, copy the one-time code it shows, go to github.com/login/device in Windows, and paste it there.

On a Mac

macOS already has a Unix terminal, so there's no WSL. Open Terminal and install Homebrew, the Mac package manager: 

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

When it finishes, it prints a few commands under "Next steps". Run them: they put brew on your path. Then install the GitHub CLI, and jq for Step 12: 

brew install gh jq

Install Docker Desktop for Mac from docker.com, choosing the build for your chip: Apple silicon or Intel. The Apple menu's About This Mac tells you which you have.

Install VS Code, open the Command Palette with Cmd+Shift+P, and run "Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH" so code . works from the terminal. Then make your projects folder with mkdir -p ~/code.

Install Node with nvm. The Mac terminal uses zsh, and touch makes sure the settings file nvm writes to exists: 

touch ~/.zshrc
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.8/install.sh | bash

Open a new terminal and run nvm install 24. Finish with the Git and GitHub commands from the section above, leaving out the sudo apt install gh -y line, since Homebrew already installed gh.

Verify on your machine

Run these in Ubuntu, or in Terminal on a Mac:

docker run hello-world
node -v
git --version
gh auth status

You should see "Hello from Docker!", a Node version starting with v24, a git version, and "Logged in to github.com". On Windows only, wsl -l -v in PowerShell should list Ubuntu with VERSION 2.

If it breaks

wsl --install mentions virtualization. It has to be switched on in your PC's BIOS. Send me the exact message and I'll walk you through it.

WSL says it's already installed. Run wsl --update, then wsl --install -d Ubuntu.

docker: command not found in Ubuntu. Docker Desktop isn't running, or its WSL integration for Ubuntu is switched off.

nvm: command not found. Open a new terminal after installing nvm. The installer only affects terminals opened afterwards.

Mac: command not found: brew. Run the "Next steps" commands the Homebrew installer printed, then open a new terminal.

Step 2: Create the project and meet TypeScript

About 45 minutes.

What, why and how: TypeScript

What it is. TypeScript is JavaScript plus types: labels saying what shape each value must have. A checker reads your code and refuses anything that breaks those labels, before the code runs. The types are then stripped away, leaving plain JavaScript.

Why we use it. A bank's code passes around amounts, ids and statuses. Types catch "passed text where a number belongs" while you're typing, not in production. They also power your editor's autocomplete, so you can see what an object contains without reading its source. Most professional Node code, Relay's included, is TypeScript.

How we use it. Every file you write ends in .ts. tsx runs those files directly without checking types, and npm run typecheck, which runs tsc --noEmit, checks the types without running anything. The settings live in tsconfig.json. Chapter 2 of the field guide lets you try what the checker accepts.

How it works inside. The checker reads every file and works out a type for every value, including ones you never labelled: const cents = 2500 is known to be a number. That's called inference. Types are structural: any object with the right properties, of the right types, counts as an Account, whatever it's called. After checking, the types are erased. tsx strips them and runs the plain JavaScript that's left, so types have no effect at all while the program runs. That's exactly why data arriving from outside, like the body of an HTTP request, still needs checking at runtime with a JSON Schema: TypeScript never sees it.

Every Node project starts with a package.json: a file listing the project's name, its dependencies, and shortcut commands called scripts. TypeScript is JavaScript plus types. A type says what shape a piece of data must have, and the TypeScript checker refuses code that breaks those promises before it ever runs.

Create the project

mkdir -p ~/code/ledgerline && cd ~/code/ledgerline
git init
npm init -y
npm pkg delete main scripts.test
npm install -D typescript@6 tsx @types/node@24
code .
  • git init turns the folder into a Git repository.
  • npm init -y creates package.json with default values, and npm pkg delete removes two placeholder entries you won't use.
  • npm install -D installs packages as dev dependencies: tools for building and testing, not for running in production. typescript is the type checker, tsx runs TypeScript files directly, and @types/node teaches TypeScript about Node's built-in functions.
  • @6 and @24 pin major versions. TypeScript 7 exists (it's a rewrite), but the linting tools in Step 7 don't support it yet. Pinning a major version while an ecosystem catches up is normal practice.
  • code . opens the project in VS Code.

Configure TypeScript

Create tsconfig.json in the project folder. In VS Code, click the New File icon in the Explorer panel.

tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "Bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "types": ["node"]
  },
  "include": ["src", "scripts", "tests", "*.config.ts", "*.config.mts"]
}
  • strict: true switches on every safety check. Non-negotiable for code that handles money.
  • noEmit: true means TypeScript only checks the code, and tsx does the running. That's why there's no build step.
  • module and moduleResolution tell TypeScript how import statements find files.
  • include lists the folders to check, including ones you'll create later.

Then create .gitignore, the list of things Git should never commit:

.gitignore
node_modules/
.env
playwright-report/
test-results/
coverage/
.DS_Store

node_modules holds installed packages (huge, and recreated by npm install), .env would hold secrets, .DS_Store is a hidden file macOS drops into folders, and the rest are test reports.

The TypeScript you'll use every day

Create src/playground.ts. It's a scratch file; you'll delete it at the end of this step. 

// A type describes the shape of some data.
type Account = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  balanceCents: number;
};

// This function only accepts an Account and always returns a string.
function describeAccount(account: Account): string {
  return `${account.name} has ${account.balanceCents} cents`;
}

const bakery: Account = {
  id: "acc_1",
  name: "Kali's Bakery",
  balanceCents: 2500,
};
console.log(describeAccount(bakery));

// async functions return a Promise: a value that arrives later.
async function fetchBalance(): Promise<number> {
  return 2500;
}

async function main() {
  const balance = await fetchBalance();
  console.log("balance is", balance);
}

main();

Run it:

npx tsx src/playground.ts

Kali's Bakery has 2500 cents
balance is 2500

The ideas in that file carry the whole project:

  • Types describe shapes. Account says an account has an id, a name and a balanceCents, each with a fixed type.
  • Functions declare what goes in and what comes out. describeAccount(account: Account): string only accepts an Account and always returns a string.
  • Template strings use backticks and ${} to put values inside text.
  • Union types like "customer" | "system" mean "exactly one of these values". You'll meet them in Week 2.
  • async and await. Anything slow, like a database query or an HTTP call, returns a Promise: a value that arrives later. await pauses until it arrives. Nearly every function in the API and the tests uses this.

Watch TypeScript catch a mistake

In src/playground.ts, change balanceCents: 2500 to balanceCents: "2500", with quotes, which makes it text. Then run both: 

npx tsx src/playground.ts
npx tsc --noEmit

Kali's Bakery has 2500 cents
balance is 2500
src/playground.ts(16,3): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

tsx ran the broken code without a word of complaint. It strips the types out and runs what's left; it never checks them. That's why the project gets a separate type-check command, and why the pipeline runs it on every push.

Change it back, then delete the playground:

rm src/playground.ts

First commit, and put it on GitHub 

git add -A
git commit -m "Step 2: Create project"
gh repo create ledgerline --public --source=. --push

git add -A stages every change, git commit saves a snapshot with a message, and gh repo create makes a GitHub repository from this folder and pushes to it. Public matters: it's your portfolio, and GitHub Actions is free for public repositories.

Check

Open github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/ledgerline. You should see package.json, package-lock.json, tsconfig.json and .gitignore, and no node_modules folder.

Step 3: Your first API endpoint

About 45 minutes.

What, why and how: APIs, servers and Fastify

What it is. An API is a set of URLs that a program answers, so that other programs can use it. A web server is the program behind an API. It waits on a port, a numbered door on the machine like 3000, for HTTP requests. For each one, it runs some code and sends back a response. Fastify is a Node library that handles all the HTTP plumbing, so you only write what each URL does.

Why we use it. Ledgerline's product is its API. Every account, deposit and transfer goes through it, and your tests use it exactly the way a mobile app or a partner would.

How we use it.

  • A route pairs a method and a path with a function, called a handler: app.get("/health", handler).
  • Whatever the handler returns becomes the JSON response, with status 200 unless you choose another.
  • localhost means "this machine", so http://localhost:3000/health is your own API, on port 3000.
  • Chapter 1 of the field guide walks one request through every layer of the API.

How it works inside. An HTTP request is text sent over a network connection: a first line with the method and path, lines of headers, a blank line, then the body. The response comes back the same way, starting with a status line like HTTP/1.1 201 Created.

Fastify passes every request through a fixed series of stages, called hooks. In order:

  1. onRequest, where Ledgerline checks the API key.
  2. Parsing the body.
  3. preValidation, where webhooks check their signature, from Week 6 on.
  4. Schema validation.
  5. The handler, your route's own code.
  6. Turning the result into JSON.
  7. onSend, where the correlation id header is added, from Week 10.

Any stage can stop the request with an error, which is why a missing API key gets a 401 before validation even runs. Follow one request through them:

An API server is a program that waits for HTTP requests and sends back responses. You've tested plenty of APIs from the outside; this is the inside. Fastify is the Node web framework you'll use: fast, well documented, and built with TypeScript in mind. 

npm install fastify@5

This one has no -D, because the API needs Fastify to run: it's a regular dependency.

Create src/app.ts:

import Fastify from "fastify";

export function buildApp() {
  const app = Fastify({ logger: true });

  app.get("/health", async () => {
    return { status: "ok" };
  });

  return app;
}

Create src/server.ts:

src/server.ts
import { buildApp } from "./app";

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const app = buildApp();

app.listen({ port, host: "0.0.0.0" }).catch((error) => {
  app.log.error(error);
  process.exit(1);
});

Add three scripts to package.json and start the server: 

npm pkg set scripts.dev="tsx watch src/server.ts" scripts.start="tsx src/server.ts" scripts.typecheck="tsc --noEmit"
npm run dev

Open a second terminal (the split icon in VS Code's terminal panel) and call it: 

curl -i http://localhost:3000/health

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
content-length: 15

{"status":"ok"}

You can also open http://localhost:3000/health in your browser. On Windows, WSL forwards localhost for you.

What the code does

buildApp() creates the app and its routes but doesn't start listening. server.ts imports it and starts it. The split is deliberate: tests and scripts can build the app without opening a network port. Designing code so it's easy to test is part of the job now, not only testing it.

  • Fastify({ logger: true }) prints a JSON log line for every request. Look at the first terminal: each curl produced "incoming request" and "request completed" lines with a reqId. You'll debug from logs like these in Week 10.
  • app.get("/health", ...) means: when a GET request arrives for /health, run this function. Whatever object it returns becomes the JSON response, with status 200.
  • process.env.PORT ?? 3000 reads the PORT environment variable and falls back to 3000 when it isn't set. ?? means "if the left side is missing, use the right side".
  • host: "0.0.0.0" accepts connections from outside the machine's own loopback, which is how your Windows browser reaches it, and later how Docker will.
  • .catch(...) handles a failed start, like the port already being taken, by logging it and exiting with code 1. A non-zero exit code is how programs tell CI they failed.

Try this

Leave npm run dev running, change "ok" to "great" in src/app.ts, save, and curl again. tsx watch restarted the server on its own. Change it back.

If it breaks

EADDRINUSE: address already in use. Another copy of the server is running, probably in another terminal. Stop it with Ctrl+C, or run PORT=3001 npm run dev.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 3: First endpoint".

Step 4: Postgres in Docker, and a health check that tells the truth

About an hour.

What, why and how: Databases and PostgreSQL

What it is. A database stores data so it survives restarts, and so that many users can safely read and write it at once. PostgreSQL, usually called Postgres, is a relational database. Data lives in tables with fixed columns, like a set of strict spreadsheets that can point at each other, and you ask for it in a language called SQL.

Why we use it. Money needs guarantees a plain file can't give: several writes that all happen or none do, rules the database enforces itself, and locks when two requests collide. Postgres provides all of that, and it's where most fintechs, Relay included, keep their ledgers.

How we use it.

  • Postgres runs in a Docker container.
  • The API talks to it through the pg library, which keeps a pool of open connections and sends SQL, like SELECT 1.
  • You can talk to it yourself with psql, Postgres's own terminal client, using docker compose exec postgres psql ....
  • Week 2 adds the real tables, with a primer on the SQL you'll need.

How it works inside. Postgres runs as a server. Each client, like your API, opens a network connection, logs in, and sends SQL over it. Opening a connection takes time, so pg keeps a pool: a few connections held open and lent out, one per query, then handed back. A transaction must use one connection from BEGIN to COMMIT, which is why moveMoney borrows its own with pool.connect() and returns it in finally. A connection that's never returned is lost to the pool for good.

Inside, Postgres gives every statement a consistent snapshot of the data, so a reader never sees another transaction's half-finished writes. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes a lock on each row it reads, and any other transaction wanting the same lock waits in line until the first one commits or rolls back. Every change is written to a log on disk, the write-ahead log, before COMMIT returns, which is how committed data survives a crash. Try running out of connections:

What, why and how: Docker Compose

What it is. Docker Compose starts several containers from one file, docker-compose.yml. The file lists each container as a service, with its image, settings, ports and storage.

Why we use it. One command starts everything the project needs, the same way every time, for you and for anyone who clones the repository. By Week 5 that's Postgres, MiniStack and WireMock.

How we use it.

  • docker compose up -d --wait starts everything in the background and waits until it's healthy.
  • docker compose ps shows what's running.
  • docker compose logs postgres shows everything a service has printed.
  • docker compose stop and docker compose start pause and resume services, keeping their data.
  • docker compose down -v removes the containers and deletes their data.

Each setting in the file is explained below.

How it works inside. For each service in docker-compose.yml, docker compose up downloads the image if it's missing, creates a container and starts it. It also creates a private network for the project, on which each container can reach the others by service name, like postgres or wiremock. Your own code runs outside that network, directly on your machine, so it uses the published ports on localhost instead. --wait keeps running each service's healthcheck command until it passes. Volumes are stored by Docker outside any container, so removing a container keeps its data, unless you add -v.

Postgres is the database most fintechs keep their ledgers in, Relay included. You'll run it with Docker Compose, which starts containers described in a YAML file.

A health check that always says "ok" is lying. Load balancers and monitoring tools call /health to decide whether to send traffic to a server, so it should check what the API can't work without. For Ledgerline, that's the database.

Start Postgres

Create docker-compose.yml:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ledgerline
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ledgerline
      POSTGRES_DB: ledgerline
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ledgerline -d ledgerline"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  • image: postgres:17 pins Postgres 17, so everyone who runs the project gets the same version.
  • environment creates a user, password and database, all called ledgerline. Fine locally; real passwords never go in files.
  • ports: "5432:5432" connects port 5432 on your machine to port 5432 inside the container. The left side is yours, the right side is the container's.
  • volumes keeps the data in a named volume, so it survives restarting the container.
  • healthcheck lets Docker report when Postgres is actually ready to answer, not just started. 
docker compose up -d --wait
docker compose ps

-d runs it in the background, and --wait returns once the health check passes. docker compose ps should show the postgres service as healthy. Take a look inside: 

docker compose exec postgres psql -U ledgerline -d ledgerline -c "SELECT version();"

Verify on your machine

Pass: docker compose ps lists postgres with a status containing (healthy), and the last command prints a line starting with PostgreSQL 17.

Fail: the status stays at starting for more than a minute. Run docker compose logs postgres and send me the last lines.

Connect the API

npm install pg@8
npm install -D @types/pg@8

Create src/db.ts:

src/db.ts
import { Pool } from "pg";

// Where the database lives. Locally this points at the Docker container;
// in CI or production it comes from the DATABASE_URL environment variable.
export const DATABASE_URL =
  process.env.DATABASE_URL ??
  "postgres://ledgerline:ledgerline@localhost:5432/ledgerline";

// A pool keeps a few database connections open and lends them out per query.
export const pool = new Pool({
  connectionString: DATABASE_URL,
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000,
});

// If the database drops an idle connection (restart, network blip), pg emits an
// "error" event. Without this listener Node treats it as unhandled and crashes.
pool.on("error", (error) => {
  console.error("Idle database connection error:", error.message);
});

Replace src/app.ts:

src/app.ts
import Fastify from "fastify";
import { pool } from "./db";

export function buildApp() {
  const app = Fastify({ logger: true });

  app.get("/health", async (request, reply) => {
    try {
      await pool.query("SELECT 1");
      return { status: "ok", database: "up" };
    } catch (error) {
      request.log.error({ err: error }, "database health check failed");
      return reply.code(503).send({ status: "degraded", database: "down" });
    }
  });

  return app;
}

With npm run dev running (start it again if you stopped it): 

curl -i http://localhost:3000/health

You should get {"status":"ok","database":"up"}.

Test the failure, not just the success 

docker compose stop postgres
curl -i http://localhost:3000/health
docker compose start postgres
curl -i http://localhost:3000/health

The first curl should return:

HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
...
{"status":"degraded","database":"down"}

The second returns 200 again once Postgres is back. Give it a second or two.

What the code does

  • A pool keeps a few database connections open and lends one out for each query, because opening a fresh connection for every request is slow.
  • connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000 gives up after two seconds instead of hanging when the database is unreachable.
  • SELECT 1 is the cheapest possible query. It proves the database answers.
  • reply.code(503).send(...) sets the status code. 503 means Service Unavailable: the server is up, but it can't do its job right now.
  • request.log.error writes an error log line tied to this request's reqId.

Found while testing this guide

The pool.on("error", ...) block wasn't in my first version. When I ran the stop-Postgres test above while testing this guide, the whole API crashed instead of returning 503. When Postgres shuts down, it closes the idle pooled connections; the pg library reports that as an "error" event, and Node treats an error event with nobody listening as fatal. One listener fixes it. That's a real bug found by testing a failure on purpose, and it makes a good interview story: crash bugs hide in the paths nobody exercises.

If it breaks

port is already allocated for 5432. Something else is using the port. On Windows it's usually a Postgres installed outside Docker: open Services, find postgresql, and click Stop. On a Mac it's usually Postgres.app (quit it) or a Homebrew Postgres (run brew services list, then brew services stop followed by its name).

Cannot connect to the Docker daemon. Docker Desktop isn't running. Start it and wait until it says it's running.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 4: Postgres and health check".

In a company

Postgres runs as a managed service, such as Amazon RDS, on a private network your laptop can't reach. The connection details come from a secrets manager, not from a default in the code, and each environment has its own database. There's more in "Where everything runs", before Week 1.

Step 5: Unit tests with Vitest

About an hour.

What, why and how: Unit tests and Vitest

What it is. A unit test checks one small piece of logic on its own: call a function with an input, and assert on its output. No server, no database, no network. Vitest is the tool that finds the test files, runs them and reports the results.

Why we use it. Unit tests run in milliseconds, so you can check dozens of edge cases, like every odd way to write an amount, far faster than through the API. When one fails, it points at exactly one function.

How we use it. Tests live in tests/unit/ and end in .test.ts. describe groups tests, it is one test, and expect(actual).toBe(expected) is an assertion. npm run test:unit runs them all once, and npx vitest keeps watching and reruns them on every save. Chapter 4 of the field guide shows where unit tests fit among the other kinds.

How it works inside. Vitest finds the files matching its include pattern, converts the TypeScript, and runs each file in its own worker, so tests in different files never share memory. Loading a test file first registers every describe and it, without running them. Then Vitest calls each test function in turn. An assertion like expect(x).toBe(y) simply throws an error when the values differ. A test passes if its function finishes without throwing, and fails if anything throws. it.each registers the same function once per row, with a title filled in from that row.

Unit tests check small pieces of logic in isolation: no server, no database, no network. They run in milliseconds, so you can have hundreds. API tests, in Step 6, check the running system over HTTP. A healthy suite has many unit tests and fewer, more valuable API tests.

Banks store money as whole cents because computers can't store most decimals exactly. Try it: 

node -e "console.log(0.1 + 0.2)"

You'll get 0.30000000000000004. Fine for physics, unacceptable for a balance. So Ledgerline stores $25.10 as 2510, and needs two small functions: one to turn text like "25.10" into cents, and one to show cents as dollars. 

npm install -D vitest@5

Create src/domain/money.ts:

src/domain/money.ts
// Money is stored as whole cents (integers), never as dollars with decimals.
// 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in JavaScript, which is fine for physics
// and unacceptable for a bank balance.

const AMOUNT_PATTERN = /^\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$/;

/** Turns "25.10" into 2510. Throws on anything that isn't a plain, positive amount. */
export function parseAmountToCents(input: string): number {
  const trimmed = input.trim();
  if (!AMOUNT_PATTERN.test(trimmed)) {
    throw new Error(`Invalid amount: "${input}"`);
  }
  const [dollars, fraction = ""] = trimmed.split(".");
  const cents = Number(dollars) * 100 + Number(fraction.padEnd(2, "0"));
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(cents)) {
    throw new Error(`Amount too large: "${input}"`);
  }
  return cents;
}

/** Turns 250010 into "$2,500.10" and -500 into "-$5.00". */
export function formatCents(cents: number): string {
  if (!Number.isInteger(cents)) {
    throw new Error(`Cents must be a whole number, got ${cents}`);
  }
  const sign = cents < 0 ? "-" : "";
  const absolute = Math.abs(cents);
  const dollars = Math.floor(absolute / 100).toLocaleString("en-US");
  const remainder = String(absolute % 100).padStart(2, "0");
  return `${sign}$${dollars}.${remainder}`;
}

Create tests/unit/money.test.ts:

tests/unit/money.test.ts
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { formatCents, parseAmountToCents } from "../../src/domain/money";

describe("parseAmountToCents", () => {
  it.each([
    ["25", 2500],
    ["25.1", 2510],
    ["25.10", 2510],
    ["0.01", 1],
    ["0", 0],
    ["  7.50  ", 750],
    ["1000000", 100_000_000],
  ])("parses %j as %i cents", (input, expected) => {
    expect(parseAmountToCents(input)).toBe(expected);
  });

  it.each(["", "abc", "-5", "1.234", "1,000", "$5", "1e3", ".5", "5."])(
    "rejects %j",
    (input) => {
      expect(() => parseAmountToCents(input)).toThrow("Invalid amount");
    },
  );
});

describe("formatCents", () => {
  it.each([
    [0, "$0.00"],
    [1, "$0.01"],
    [2510, "$25.10"],
    [250_010, "$2,500.10"],
    [-500, "-$5.00"],
  ])("formats %i as %s", (cents, expected) => {
    expect(formatCents(cents)).toBe(expected);
  });

  it("refuses fractional cents", () => {
    expect(() => formatCents(10.5)).toThrow("whole number");
  });
});

Create vitest.config.mts, which tells Vitest where unit tests live, so it never tries to run the Playwright tests:

vitest.config.mts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    include: ["tests/unit/**/*.test.ts"],
  },
});

Add the script and run it:

npm pkg set scripts.test:unit="vitest run"
npm run test:unit

 ✓ tests/unit/money.test.ts (22 tests) 24ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  22 passed (22)

What the code does

  • describe groups tests, it is a single test, and expect(actual).toBe(expected) is the assertion.
  • it.each([...]) runs the same test once per row, so 7 valid inputs and 9 invalid ones become 16 named tests. This is data-driven testing, and you'll cover boundaries this way all through the project.
  • The rejection list is a tester's list: empty text, letters, a negative, three decimal places, a comma, a currency symbol, scientific notation, and a dot at either end. Each is something a real user or a buggy client could send.
  • toThrow("Invalid amount") checks that the function refuses, and with the right message.
  • AMOUNT_PATTERN is a regular expression: one or more digits, optionally followed by a dot and one or two digits.
  • The config file ends in .mts because it's written as a modern ES module. With .ts, Vitest prints a warning.

Try this

Make a test fail on purpose, so you know what failure looks like. Change ["25.1", 2510] to ["25.1", 251] and run npm run test:unit: 

 FAIL  tests/unit/money.test.ts > parseAmountToCents > parses "25.1" as 251 cents
AssertionError: expected 2510 to be 251 // Object.is equality

Change it back. While writing tests, npx vitest (without run) watches your files and reruns on every save.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 5: Unit tests".

Step 6: API tests with Playwright

About an hour.

What, why and how: API testing with Playwright

What it is. You know Playwright for driving browsers. It also has a request fixture that sends HTTP requests directly, with no browser, using the same test runner, reports, parallel workers and retries.

Why we use it. One familiar tool for every level of testing above unit tests, and it's in Relay's stack. API tests check what clients actually experience: status codes, response bodies, and side effects like balances.

How we use it. Tests live in tests/api/ and end in .spec.ts. playwright.config.ts says where the API is, and starts it before the tests run. A test looks like test("name", async ({ request }) => { ... }), where request.get("/health") sends a request and expect(response.status()).toBe(200) checks the answer. npm run test:api runs them all, and npx playwright show-report opens the HTML report.

How it works inside. The runner starts a few worker processes and hands each one tests to run. Before each test, the worker builds the fixtures that test asks for. The request fixture is an HTTP client with your config's baseURL and headers already set. webServer runs before any worker starts: Playwright launches each command, checks its URL until it answers, and stops them all when the run ends. Workers are separate processes, so tests in different workers really do run at the same time, which is exactly why every test creates its own data.

You know Playwright from UI testing. It also has a request fixture for calling APIs directly, with the same runner, reports, parallel workers and retries. API tests don't open a browser, so you don't need npx playwright install. 

npm install -D @playwright/test@1

Create playwright.config.ts:

playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "@playwright/test";

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const baseURL = process.env.API_URL ?? `http://localhost:${port}`;

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: "tests/api",
  fullyParallel: true,
  forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI,
  retries: 0,
  reporter: [["list"], ["html", { open: "never" }]],
  use: {
    baseURL,
  },
  webServer: {
    command: "npm run start",
    url: `${baseURL}/health`,
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    timeout: 30_000,
  },
});

Create tests/api/health.spec.ts:

tests/api/health.spec.ts
import { expect, test } from "@playwright/test";

test("health check reports everything is up", async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.get("/health");

  expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
  expect(await response.json()).toEqual({ status: "ok", database: "up" });
});

test("unknown routes return 404", async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.get("/does-not-exist");

  expect(response.status()).toBe(404);
});

npm pkg set scripts.test:api="playwright test"
npm run test:api

Running 2 tests using 1 worker

  ✓  1 tests/api/health.spec.ts:3:5 › health check reports everything is up (47ms)
  ✓  2 tests/api/health.spec.ts:10:5 › unknown routes return 404 (33ms)

  2 passed (1.7s)

The worker count depends on your CPU, so you'll probably see more than one. To browse the HTML report, run npx playwright show-report and open the address it prints in your browser.

What the config does

  • webServer starts the API before the tests (with npm run start) and waits until /health answers. You never have to remember to start the server.
  • reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI reuses your npm run dev when it's already running locally, but always starts a fresh server in CI.
  • baseURL lets tests write /health instead of a full address. To point the tests at another environment, run API_URL=https://... npm run test:api.
  • retries: 0. A retry turns a flaky test green and hides the problem. You want to see flakiness, not paper over it; Week 9 covers handling it properly.
  • forbidOnly fails a CI run if someone commits a test.only, which would silently skip every other test.
  • fullyParallel: true runs tests at the same time. That only works because every test will create its own data.

If it breaks

Error: Timed out waiting 30000ms from config.webServer. Postgres isn't running, so /health returns 503 and Playwright never sees the API as ready. Run docker compose up -d --wait and try again.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 6: API tests".

Step 7: Linting, formatting, and CI on GitHub

About an hour.

What, why and how: Linters and formatters

What it is. A linter, ESLint here, reads code and flags patterns that are usually mistakes, like a variable that's never used. A formatter, Prettier here, rewrites code into one consistent style: spacing, quotes and line breaks.

Why we use it. The linter catches bugs before the tests even run. The formatter ends arguments about style, and keeps every change small and readable, because nobody's personal habits creep into the diff.

How we use it. npm run lint checks the code, npm run format rewrites every file, and npm run format:check fails if anything isn't formatted, which is what CI runs. Their settings live in eslint.config.mjs and .prettierrc.json.

How it works inside. Both tools start by parsing your code into a tree of its structure, called an abstract syntax tree: this is a function, this is a variable, this is a call with these arguments. Each ESLint rule visits the parts of the tree it cares about and reports what it finds, and the TypeScript rules also understand types. Prettier throws your layout away completely and prints the tree again in its own style, which is why its output is identical however the input was laid out.

What, why and how: CI and GitHub Actions

What it is. Continuous integration, or CI, means every push is checked automatically on a fresh machine. GitHub Actions is GitHub's CI service: you describe a workflow in a YAML file, and GitHub runs it on its own Linux servers.

Why we use it. "It works on my machine" stops mattering: what counts is the fresh machine. Broken code is caught within minutes, before anyone else pulls it. And building and improving CI is the centre of the Relay role.

How we use it.

  • The workflow lives in .github/workflows/ci.yml.
  • on says when it runs, and each entry under steps is one command.
  • services starts containers, like Postgres, next to the job.
  • Results appear in your repository's Actions tab, or live in your terminal with gh run watch.
  • YAML is indentation-sensitive, so always copy-paste workflow files rather than retyping them.
  • Chapter 5 of the field guide lets you break a pipeline on purpose.

How it works inside. When you push, GitHub reads every file in .github/workflows/ and starts the jobs whose on rules match. Each job gets a brand-new virtual machine, called a runner, which is thrown away afterwards, so nothing carries over from one run to the next. Service containers start first, on the same machine. Then each step runs in order in a shell, and a step that exits with a non-zero code fails the job. Anything worth keeping, like a test report, has to be uploaded as an artifact before the machine disappears. cache: npm saves npm's download cache between runs, keyed on package-lock.json, which speeds up npm ci. Break a pipeline on purpose:

A linter catches patterns that are usually bugs, like unused variables or promises nobody awaited. A formatter makes all code look the same, which ends style debates and keeps changes small and readable. CI (continuous integration) runs every check on GitHub's machines for every push, so broken code can't quietly reach main. Building and improving CI is the centre of the Relay role. 

npm install -D eslint@10 @eslint/js@10 typescript-eslint@8 prettier@3 eslint-config-prettier@10
echo '{}' > .prettierrc.json
npm pkg set scripts.lint="eslint ." scripts.format="prettier --write ." scripts.format:check="prettier --check ."

The {} in .prettierrc.json means "use Prettier's defaults". Create eslint.config.mjs:

eslint.config.mjs
import eslint from "@eslint/js";
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";
import prettier from "eslint-config-prettier";
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";

export default defineConfig(
  { ignores: ["node_modules/", "playwright-report/", "test-results/"] },
  eslint.configs.recommended,
  tseslint.configs.recommended,
  prettier,
);

It turns on ESLint's recommended rules and the TypeScript rules, then applies eslint-config-prettier, which switches off any lint rule that would fight the formatter.

Format everything once, then check that all four checks pass:

npm run format
npm run lint
npm run format:check
npm run typecheck

The pipeline

Create .github/workflows/ci.yml. The folder name starts with a dot:

.github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_DB: ledgerline
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U ledgerline -d ledgerline"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run format:check
      - run: npm run test:unit
      - run: npm run test:api

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 14
  • on runs the workflow on every push to main and on every pull request.
  • services starts a Postgres container next to the job, the same way Docker Compose does on your machine. The options make GitHub wait until it's healthy.
  • npm ci installs exactly what package-lock.json lists. Unlike npm install, it never updates anything, so CI tests the same versions you did.
  • Cheapest checks first, so a formatting slip fails in seconds rather than after the API tests.
  • upload-artifact with if: always() saves the Playwright report even when tests fail, which is exactly when you need it. 
git add -A
git commit -m "Step 7: Linting, formatting and CI"
git push
gh run watch

gh run watch follows the pipeline live in your terminal. You can also watch it in the Actions tab of your repository on GitHub.

Verify on your machine

A green check next to your commit on GitHub. Open the run, scroll to Artifacts, and download playwright-report to make sure it's there.

If it breaks

format:check fails in CI. A file wasn't formatted. Run npm run format, then commit and push.

YAML errors, or the Postgres service never starts. YAML is whitespace-sensitive. Compare your indentation with the file above character for character; copy-paste is safest.

In a company

The same kind of pipeline also deploys. After the tests pass, it builds the app into a container image and rolls it out to a development environment, then staging, then production, usually with an approval before production.

Week 1 wrap-up

You now have a service, a database, unit tests, API tests and a pipeline, all built from zero. Before moving on:

  • Teach it back. Out loud, in two minutes: what happens between typing curl localhost:3000/health and seeing JSON, and why the health check touches the database.
  • Start your dev log. Create docs/dev-log.md and write five lines: what you built, what broke, how you fixed it, what surprised you, and what you'd explain differently. Add to it every week. It becomes your interview stories.
  • Commit and push.

In an interview, this week sounds like: "I set up a TypeScript service with Postgres in Docker, and a CI pipeline with unit and API test stages from day one."

Week 2: Money and the ledger

This week the API starts moving money. You'll learn how banks record money so it can't appear or vanish, then test it the way a fintech QA would: boundaries, bad input, concurrency and data integrity.

Step 8: How banks record money

About an hour of reading and drawing. No code.

Double-entry bookkeeping

Every movement of money is written down twice: once as money leaving an account, and once as money arriving in another. Each transfer's entries add up to zero, so money is never created or destroyed by accident.

Here's a small story. Kali's Bakery deposits $100, then pays the Flour Supplier $25. A deposit needs a "from" side too, so it comes out of a system account called External funding. The ledger ends up with four entries:

Transfer Account Amount in cents
Deposit External funding −10,000
Deposit Kali's Bakery +10,000
Payment Kali's Bakery −2,500
Payment Flour Supplier +2,500

An account's balance is the sum of its entries. The Bakery has 10,000 − 2,500 = 7,500 cents, or $75, and the supplier has 2,500. Add up every entry in the table and you get zero. That's the property you'll test.

Keep the books yourself. Try the bug switch, which forgets the debit, and watch the total.

Three rules follow, and your tests will enforce all of them:

  • Every transfer writes exactly two entries, and they sum to zero.
  • Entries are never edited or deleted. Mistakes are fixed with new entries, so history is never lost.
  • Balances aren't stored anywhere. They're calculated from the entries, so they can't drift out of sync.

Transactions

Moving money takes several database writes: the transfer record, the debit and the credit. If the server crashed between the debit and the credit, money would vanish. A database transaction wraps the writes so they all happen, or none of them do. You start one with BEGIN, make it permanent with COMMIT, and undo everything with ROLLBACK.

Crash the server partway through a transfer, with and without a transaction:

Concurrency

Two $30 payments leave a $50 account at the same instant. Both read the balance, both see $50, both decide there's enough, and the account ends at −$10. This is a race condition, and it's one of the most expensive bug classes in payments. The fix is a row lock: the first transfer locks the account's row, the second waits until the first commits, then reads the new balance and gets refused. Step 14 proves this with a test.

Step through both transfers, then switch the lock on:

Posted versus available

Real bank accounts have two balances. Posted is money that has settled; available also subtracts pending payments and holds. Everything in Ledgerline settles instantly for now, so there's one balance. In Week 4, payments to other banks start taking time, and the difference begins to matter.

Try this

On paper, draw the ledger for one more event: the Bakery tries to pay the supplier another $80. Is there enough money? Which entries get written, if any? Step 13's tests will tell you whether you were right.

Step 9: Create the tables with migrations

About 45 minutes.

What, why and how: The SQL you'll meet

What it is. SQL is the language for talking to a relational database. Each statement is one instruction to the database.

Why we use it. Migrations use it to create the tables, the API uses it to read and write rows, and the integrity tests use it to ask questions no API endpoint answers.

How we use it. These are the statements the handbook uses. Each one is explained again where it first appears:

  • CREATE TABLE defines a table and its columns, and ALTER TABLE changes one later.
  • INSERT INTO ... VALUES adds a row, and RETURNING * hands back the row just written.
  • SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE reads rows. SUM, COUNT and GROUP BY combine them, HAVING filters the combined results, and JOIN links rows across tables.
  • UPDATE ... SET changes existing rows.
  • BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK group statements into a transaction.
  • $1, $2 and so on are placeholders the pg library fills in safely. Never paste values into SQL text yourself: that's how SQL injection happens.

How it works inside. For each statement, Postgres first works out a plan, such as "use the index on account_id, then add up the matching rows", and then runs it. Putting EXPLAIN in front of a query shows the plan it chose. Placeholders like $1 travel separately from the SQL text, so a value can never be read as part of the query itself. That separation is exactly what prevents SQL injection.

A migration is a numbered SQL file that changes the database's structure. Each file runs once, in order, and the database records which ones have run. Everyone who clones the project, and the CI pipeline, gets an identical database by running the same files. Banks do this with tools like Flyway and Liquibase; here you'll write a small runner yourself, so you can see how it works.

Create the folders:

mkdir -p db/migrations scripts

Create db/migrations/001_create_accounts.sql:

db/migrations/001_create_accounts.sql
-- Accounts that can hold money.
-- "customer" accounts belong to businesses using Ledgerline.
-- "system" accounts are Ledgerline's own books, like the source of deposits.
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name text NOT NULL,
  type text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'customer' CHECK (type IN ('customer', 'system')),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Deposits need a "from" side too. In double-entry bookkeeping money never
-- appears from nowhere, so deposits come out of this system account.
INSERT INTO accounts (id, name, type)
VALUES ('00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001', 'External funding', 'system');

Create db/migrations/002_create_transfers_and_ledger.sql:

db/migrations/002_create_transfers_and_ledger.sql 
-- One row per money movement: what moved, between whom, and its status.
CREATE TABLE transfers (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  kind text NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('deposit', 'internal')),
  from_account_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts (id),
  to_account_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts (id),
  amount_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents > 0),
  status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('completed')),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CHECK (from_account_id <> to_account_id)
);

-- The ledger: every transfer writes one negative and one positive entry.
-- An account's balance is the sum of its entries. Entries are never updated
-- or deleted; mistakes are corrected with new entries.
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts (id),
  transfer_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES transfers (id),
  amount_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents <> 0),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX ledger_entries_account_id_idx ON ledger_entries (account_id);
CREATE INDEX ledger_entries_transfer_id_idx ON ledger_entries (transfer_id);

Create the runner, scripts/migrate.ts:

scripts/migrate.ts
import { readdir, readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import path from "node:path";
import { pool } from "../src/db";

const MIGRATIONS_DIR = path.join(__dirname, "..", "db", "migrations");

async function migrate() {
  // Remember which files have already run, so each runs exactly once.
  await pool.query(`
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (
      name text PRIMARY KEY,
      applied_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
    )
  `);

  const { rows } = await pool.query<{ name: string }>(
    "SELECT name FROM schema_migrations",
  );
  const applied = new Set(rows.map((row) => row.name));

  const files = (await readdir(MIGRATIONS_DIR))
    .filter((file) => file.endsWith(".sql"))
    .sort();

  for (const file of files) {
    if (applied.has(file)) continue;

    const sql = await readFile(path.join(MIGRATIONS_DIR, file), "utf8");
    const client = await pool.connect();
    try {
      // All or nothing: a half-applied migration is worse than none.
      await client.query("BEGIN");
      await client.query(sql);
      await client.query("INSERT INTO schema_migrations (name) VALUES ($1)", [
        file,
      ]);
      await client.query("COMMIT");
      console.log(`Applied ${file}`);
    } catch (error) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");
      throw error;
    } finally {
      client.release();
    }
  }

  console.log("Database is up to date.");
}

migrate()
  .catch((error) => {
    console.error("Migration failed:", error);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  })
  .finally(() => pool.end());

Add the scripts, including two shortcuts for the database, and run the migrations: 

npm pkg set scripts.db:migrate="tsx scripts/migrate.ts" scripts.db:up="docker compose up -d --wait" scripts.db:reset="docker compose down -v && docker compose up -d --wait && npm run db:migrate"
npm run db:migrate

Applied 001_create_accounts.sql
Applied 002_create_transfers_and_ledger.sql
Database is up to date.

Run npm run db:migrate again. This time it only prints "Database is up to date." Running something twice with the same result as running it once is called idempotency. Remember the word; it's the heart of Week 6.

Run the migrations twice, add a new one, and make one fail:

Look at what you made:

docker compose exec postgres psql -U ledgerline -d ledgerline -c "\dt" -c "SELECT id, name, type FROM accounts;"

What the SQL does

  • uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() gives every row a random unique id, like 1969e398-ff22-4b41-97dc-206b6a233cc4. Random ids can't be guessed or counted, unlike 1, 2, 3.
  • REFERENCES accounts (id) is a foreign key: Postgres refuses a transfer that points at an account that doesn't exist.
  • CHECK (...) constraints are the last line of defence. Even if the API had a bug, the database would refuse a zero or negative amount, a transfer to the same account, or an unknown status.
  • bigint holds very large whole numbers, so balances can't overflow.
  • The indexes make "all entries for this account" fast, which every balance lookup needs.
  • In the runner, each migration runs between BEGIN and COMMIT, so a failing file leaves nothing half-applied.

Try this

Prove the database defends itself. Insert a bad transfer by hand: 

docker compose exec postgres psql -U ledgerline -d ledgerline -c "INSERT INTO transfers (kind, from_account_id, to_account_id, amount_cents, status) VALUES ('internal', '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001', '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001', -5, 'completed');"

ERROR:  new row for relation "transfers" violates check constraint "transfers_amount_cents_check"

If it breaks

relation "accounts" already exists. The tables were created some other way. Wipe the local database and start clean with npm run db:reset. It deletes all local data, which is fine here.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 9: Migrations".

Step 10: The ledger code

About an hour, most of it reading.

All money movement goes through one function, moveMoney. A single path is easier to reason about, easier to lock correctly, and easier to test than several.

Create src/errors.ts:

src/errors.ts
// An error we throw on purpose, carrying the HTTP status and a stable code
// that API clients (and our tests) can rely on.
export class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(
    public readonly statusCode: number,
    public readonly code: string,
    message: string,
  ) {
    super(message);
  }
}

export function notFound(resource: string, id: string): AppError {
  return new AppError(
    404,
    `${resource}_not_found`,
    `No ${resource} with id ${id}`,
  );
}

Create src/ledger.ts:

src/ledger.ts
import type { PoolClient } from "pg";
import { pool } from "./db";
import { formatCents } from "./domain/money";
import { AppError, notFound } from "./errors";

export const FUNDING_ACCOUNT_ID = "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001";

export type TransferKind = "deposit" | "internal";

// What a transfers row looks like coming out of Postgres.
interface TransferRow {
  id: string;
  kind: TransferKind;
  from_account_id: string;
  to_account_id: string;
  amount_cents: string; // bigint arrives as a string, see toCents()
  status: string;
  created_at: Date;
}

// What we send back to API clients.
export interface Transfer {
  id: string;
  kind: TransferKind;
  fromAccountId: string;
  toAccountId: string;
  amountCents: number;
  status: string;
  createdAt: string;
}

// Postgres bigint can hold numbers JavaScript can't represent exactly, so pg
// returns them as strings. Our amounts are far below that limit, so we convert,
// but refuse loudly if a value ever isn't a safe whole number.
export function toCents(value: string | number): number {
  const cents = Number(value);
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(cents)) {
    throw new Error(`Not a safe whole number of cents: ${value}`);
  }
  return cents;
}

export function toTransfer(row: TransferRow): Transfer {
  return {
    id: row.id,
    kind: row.kind,
    fromAccountId: row.from_account_id,
    toAccountId: row.to_account_id,
    amountCents: toCents(row.amount_cents),
    status: row.status,
    createdAt: row.created_at.toISOString(),
  };
}

type Queryable = Pick<PoolClient, "query">;

export async function getBalance(db: Queryable, accountId: string) {
  const { rows } = await db.query<{ balance: string }>(
    "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_cents), 0) AS balance FROM ledger_entries WHERE account_id = $1",
    [accountId],
  );
  return toCents(rows[0].balance);
}

export async function getTransfer(id: string): Promise<Transfer> {
  const { rows } = await pool.query<TransferRow>(
    "SELECT * FROM transfers WHERE id = $1",
    [id],
  );
  if (rows.length === 0) throw notFound("transfer", id);
  return toTransfer(rows[0]);
}

interface MoveMoneyInput {
  kind: TransferKind;
  fromAccountId: string;
  toAccountId: string;
  amountCents: number;
}

// The one place money moves. Everything happens inside a database transaction:
// either the transfer and both ledger entries are saved, or nothing is.
export async function moveMoney(input: MoveMoneyInput): Promise<Transfer> {
  if (input.fromAccountId === input.toAccountId) {
    throw new AppError(
      422,
      "same_account",
      "Can't transfer to the same account",
    );
  }

  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");

    // Lock both account rows until COMMIT, always in the same order (by id).
    // Two transfers touching the same account now take turns instead of both
    // reading the old balance, and opposite transfers can't deadlock.
    const { rows: accounts } = await client.query<{ id: string; type: string }>(
      "SELECT id, type FROM accounts WHERE id = ANY($1::uuid[]) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE",
      [[input.fromAccountId, input.toAccountId]],
    );
    const from = accounts.find((account) => account.id === input.fromAccountId);
    const to = accounts.find((account) => account.id === input.toAccountId);
    if (!from) throw notFound("account", input.fromAccountId);
    if (!to) throw notFound("account", input.toAccountId);

    // Only deposits may draw on the system funding account.
    if (
      input.kind === "internal" &&
      (from.type !== "customer" || to.type !== "customer")
    ) {
      throw new AppError(
        422,
        "account_not_allowed",
        "Transfers must be between customer accounts",
      );
    }

    if (from.type === "customer") {
      const balance = await getBalance(client, from.id);
      if (balance < input.amountCents) {
        throw new AppError(
          422,
          "insufficient_funds",
          `Balance is ${formatCents(balance)} but the transfer needs ${formatCents(input.amountCents)}`,
        );
      }
    }

    const { rows } = await client.query<TransferRow>(
      `INSERT INTO transfers (kind, from_account_id, to_account_id, amount_cents, status)
       VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, 'completed')
       RETURNING *`,
      [input.kind, input.fromAccountId, input.toAccountId, input.amountCents],
    );
    const transfer = rows[0];

    // Double entry: money leaves one account and arrives in the other.
    await client.query(
      "INSERT INTO ledger_entries (account_id, transfer_id, amount_cents) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
      [input.fromAccountId, transfer.id, -input.amountCents],
    );
    await client.query(
      "INSERT INTO ledger_entries (account_id, transfer_id, amount_cents) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
      [input.toAccountId, transfer.id, input.amountCents],
    );

    await client.query("COMMIT");
    return toTransfer(transfer);
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw error;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

Run npm run typecheck. No output means no type errors.

Reading moveMoney, top to bottom

  1. Same account? Refused straight away with a 422. That status means "I understood the request, but it breaks a rule".
  2. pool.connect() borrows one connection for the whole transaction. Every statement in a transaction has to go through the same connection.
  3. BEGIN starts the transaction.
  4. SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE loads both accounts and locks their rows until COMMIT. A second transfer touching either account waits here. The fixed order matters: if one transfer locked A then B while another locked B then A, each would wait for the other forever. That's a deadlock, and always locking in the same order prevents it.
  5. Missing accounts become 404 errors.
