Step 20: A Bruno collection for exploring by hand

About an hour.

What, why and how: Bruno

What it is. Bruno is an API client like Postman: you build requests, send them and read the responses. Unlike Postman, its collections are plain text files in your repository.

Why we use it. Files in Git can be reviewed, versioned and shared like code, and Bruno's command-line tool runs the same collection in CI. It's in Relay's stack.

How we use it. Each .bru file in bruno/ is one request. environments/local.bru holds variables like baseUrl, and small scripts save values for later requests, like a new account's id. npm run test:bruno runs the whole collection, and the desktop app opens the same folder for exploring by hand.

Bruno is an API client like Postman, except its collections are plain text files that live in your repository, so they're reviewed and versioned like code. Use it for exploring and for sharing requests with developers, while Playwright stays your automated suite. Relay lists Bruno in its stack. 

npm install -D @usebruno/cli@4
mkdir -p bruno/environments
npm pkg set scripts.test:bruno="cd bruno && bru run --env local"

npm may print audit warnings about the Bruno CLI. They're in local development tooling that never runs in production, so it's safe to carry on.

Create these files inside bruno/. First, bruno/bruno.json:

bruno/bruno.json
{
  "version": "1",
  "name": "Ledgerline",
  "type": "collection"
}

bruno/collection.bru sends the API key with every request:

bruno/collection.bru
headers {
  x-api-key: {{apiKey}}
}

bruno/environments/local.bru holds the variables:

bruno/environments/local.bru
vars {
  baseUrl: http://localhost:3000
  apiKey: local-dev-key
}

Then the six requests. They run in the order set by seq:

bruno/health.bru
meta {
  name: Health
  type: http
  seq: 1
}

get {
  url: {{baseUrl}}/health
  body: none
  auth: none
}

tests {
  test("API and database are up", function () {
    expect(res.getStatus()).to.equal(200);
    expect(res.getBody().database).to.equal("up");
  });
}
bruno/create-account.bru
meta {
  name: Create account
  type: http
  seq: 2
}

post {
  url: {{baseUrl}}/accounts
  body: json
  auth: none
}

body:json {
  {
    "name": "Bruno's Bakery"
  }
}

script:post-response {
  bru.setVar("accountId", res.getBody().id);
}

tests {
  test("creates an account with a zero balance", function () {
    expect(res.getStatus()).to.equal(201);
    expect(res.getBody().balanceCents).to.equal(0);
  });
}
bruno/create-second-account.bru
meta {
  name: Create second account
  type: http
  seq: 3
}

post {
  url: {{baseUrl}}/accounts
  body: json
  auth: none
}

body:json {
  {
    "name": "Bruno's Flour Supplier"
  }
}

script:post-response {
  bru.setVar("otherAccountId", res.getBody().id);
}

tests {
  test("creates the second account", function () {
    expect(res.getStatus()).to.equal(201);
  });
}
bruno/deposit.bru
meta {
  name: Deposit $100
  type: http
  seq: 4
}

post {
  url: {{baseUrl}}/accounts/{{accountId}}/deposits
  body: json
  auth: none
}

body:json {
  {
    "amountCents": 10000
  }
}

tests {
  test("records the deposit", function () {
    expect(res.getStatus()).to.equal(201);
    expect(res.getBody().kind).to.equal("deposit");
  });
}
bruno/transfer.bru
meta {
  name: Transfer $25
  type: http
  seq: 5
}

post {
  url: {{baseUrl}}/transfers
  body: json
  auth: none
}

body:json {
  {
    "fromAccountId": "{{accountId}}",
    "toAccountId": "{{otherAccountId}}",
    "amountCents": 2500
  }
}

tests {
  test("completes the transfer", function () {
    expect(res.getStatus()).to.equal(201);
    expect(res.getBody().status).to.equal("completed");
  });
}
bruno/check-balance.bru
meta {
  name: Check balance
  type: http
  seq: 6
}

get {
  url: {{baseUrl}}/accounts/{{accountId}}
  body: none
  auth: none
}

tests {
  test("shows $75 left after the transfer", function () {
    expect(res.getStatus()).to.equal(200);
    expect(res.getBody().balanceCents).to.equal(7500);
  });
}

With npm run dev running in another terminal, run the collection: 

npm run test:bruno

The summary at the end should include:

│ Status        │    ✓ PASS    │
│ Requests      │ 6 (6 Passed) │
│ Tests         │     6/6      │

For exploring by hand, install the Bruno desktop app from usebruno.com, choose Open Collection, and select the bruno folder. On a Mac that's ~/code/ledgerline/bruno; on Windows it's \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\home\YOUR-LINUX-USER\code\ledgerline\bruno. Pick the local environment in the top-right corner, then send requests one at a time.

How a .bru file works

  • meta names the request and sets its position with seq.
  • post or get sets the method and URL. {{baseUrl}} comes from the environment file.
  • body:json is the request body, and {{accountId}} inside it is filled in from a variable.
  • script:post-response runs after the response arrives. bru.setVar("accountId", ...) saves the new account's id for the requests that follow.
  • tests holds assertions, written in JavaScript with Chai's expect.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 20: Bruno collection".

Step 21: CI, README, and ship it

About an hour.

Replace .github/workflows/ci.yml. It adds a step that runs the Bruno collection against a live API:

.github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_DB: ledgerline
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U ledgerline -d ledgerline"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run format:check
      - run: npm run test:unit
      - run: npm run db:migrate
      - run: npm run test:api

      - name: Run the Bruno collection
        run: |
          npm run start &
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -sf http://localhost:3000/health && break; sleep 1; done
          npm run test:bruno

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 14

The Bruno step starts the API in the background (that's the &), checks /health once a second for up to 30 seconds, then runs the collection. It comes after the Playwright step, because Playwright starts its own server on the same port.

Add one script that runs both test suites:

npm pkg set scripts.test="npm run test:unit && npm run test:api"

Create README.md. It's the first thing a hiring manager opens:

README.md
# Ledgerline

A small business-banking backend, and the automated test framework around it.
Built to practise how fintech teams test money movement: ledgers, contracts,
concurrency and CI.

## Run it

You need Docker Desktop and Node 24.

```bash
npm install
npm run db:up        # start Postgres in Docker
npm run db:migrate   # create the tables
npm test             # unit tests, then API tests (the API starts automatically)
```

Run the API on its own with `npm run dev`, then try `curl localhost:3000/health`.

## How the tests are organised

```
tests/
  unit/        Vitest. Pure functions, no network or database.
  api/         Playwright specs. Each file covers one feature.
  framework/   The plumbing specs are built on:
    fixtures.ts           api, newAccount, apiWithKey, db
    ledgerline-client.ts  one method per endpoint
    contract.ts           checks every response against openapi.yaml
    account-builder.ts    newAccount().withBalance(5000).create()
    db-helper.ts          ledger integrity queries
    assertions.ts         expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds")
bruno/         Bruno collection for exploring the API by hand
openapi.yaml   The API contract
```

## Add a test

1. Pick the spec file for the feature, or create `tests/api/<feature>.spec.ts`.
2. Import `{ test, expect }` from `../framework/fixtures`.
3. Set up data with `newAccount()`, act with `api`, assert on the result.

```ts
test("rejects a transfer over the balance", async ({ api, newAccount }) => {
  const from = await newAccount().withBalance(1_000).create();
  const to = await newAccount().create();

  const result = await api.createTransfer({
    fromAccountId: from.id,
    toAccountId: to.id,
    amountCents: 1_001,
  });

  expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds");
});
```

Every test creates its own accounts, so tests run in parallel and in any order.

Run everything the way CI will, then ship it:

npm run format
npm run typecheck && npm run lint && npm run format:check && npm test
git add -A
git commit -m "Step 21: Framework, contract, auth, Bruno and README"
git push
gh run watch

Verify on your machine

A green run on GitHub, with every step passing, including "Run the Bruno collection". Your repository's front page shows the README.

Phase 1 wrap-up

In three weeks, you've built:

  • a TypeScript API with a double-entry ledger in Postgres, running in Docker;
  • 22 unit tests and 36 API tests, covering boundaries, bad input, authentication, concurrency and ledger integrity;
  • a test framework with a client, fixtures, builders and a database helper, with the contract checked on every response;
  • a Bruno collection, and a pipeline that runs all of it on every push.

Before Phase 2:

  • Teach it back. Using only the README, onboard an imaginary developer in two minutes: how to run the tests, and how to add one.
  • Dev log. Write up three stories: the pool crash, the Fastify defaults, and the race condition.
  • Interview lines. "I designed a layered API test framework with contract validation on every call." "I reproduced a race condition in money movement and proved the fix with repeatable tests." "I found real defects by testing failure modes on purpose."

Phase 2 starts right below, with Week 4. If you changed anything from this handbook along the way, mention it when you ask for help, so the answers match your code.

Week 4: Queues and a local AWS

Payments to other banks take days, so the API can't make the customer wait. This week the API learns to answer "accepted" and hand the slow work to a queue. You'll run AWS's queue service on your own machine with MiniStack, send payments through it, and test all of it, including what happens when the queue is down. Chapters 13 and 14 of the field guide cover the ideas; read them first.

Step 22: AWS on your machine with MiniStack

About an hour.

What, why and how: Cloud computing and AWS

What it is. Cloud computing means renting computing instead of owning servers. You ask a provider for a database, a queue or somewhere to run code, you pay for what you use, and the provider looks after the hardware. Amazon Web Services, or AWS, is the largest provider. It offers more than 200 services, each one a building block with its own name. This project uses four of them: SQS for queues (this week), Lambda for running code (Week 5), and DynamoDB for fast key-value storage and S3 for files (later weeks).

Why we use it. Most fintechs, Relay included, build their backends out of AWS services. A QA engineer there tests systems where money moves through queues and functions, not just one API and one database. You need to know what those pieces are, how they fail, and how to run them in tests.

How we use it. You won't need an AWS account or a credit card. MiniStack, which you'll set up in this step, answers exactly like AWS but runs on your own machine. Your code talks to it the same way it would talk to real AWS. The only difference is one setting: where to send the requests.

How it works inside. Every AWS service is a web API. Sending a message to SQS, reading a file from S3, or creating a Lambda is an HTTPS request to an address like sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, signed to prove who sent it. The AWS website you click around in and the SDK in your code both make exactly those requests. That's the whole reason an emulator like MiniStack can work: it answers the same requests at a different address.

What, why and how: Regions, credentials and permissions

What it is. Every AWS call involves three ideas:

  • A region is a place where AWS runs its services, like us-east-1 in Virginia. Each region's resources are separate from every other region's.
  • Credentials are an access key id and a secret key that prove who's calling.
  • IAM, Identity and Access Management, decides what each identity is allowed to do.

Why we use it. Every AWS request is signed with credentials and sent to a region, and IAM checks it. Getting one of these wrong is the most common reason AWS code works in one place and fails in another.

How we use it. With MiniStack, the region is us-east-1, the credentials are the dummy values test and test, and IAM isn't enforced, so you can focus on behaviour. The code reads each value from an environment variable first (AWS_REGION, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY), so real values can be swapped in without changing code. With real AWS, never put credentials in files or in Git.

How it works inside. The SDK signs every request with your secret key, using a scheme called Signature Version 4. It computes a fingerprint, an HMAC (the same technique as Week 6's webhooks), from the request's method, path, headers and body, plus the date, region and service, and sends it along. AWS recomputes the fingerprint with its own copy of your secret, and a changed request or a wrong key doesn't match.

Then IAM checks the request against every policy that applies to whoever sent it. An explicit deny always wins; otherwise it needs an explicit allow; anything not allowed is denied. An IAM role hands out temporary credentials that expire on their own, which is why services running in AWS don't need keys in their code.

What, why and how: Amazon SQS

What it is. Simple Queue Service, or SQS, holds messages until a program takes them. One side sends messages, and the other receives, processes and deletes them. Messages wait safely in between, even while the receiving side is down.

Why we use it. Paying another bank takes seconds to days, far too long to keep a customer's request waiting. The API drops a message on the queue and answers straight away, and a separate processor does the slow work at its own pace. If the processor crashes, the messages wait for it instead of being lost.

How we use it. The API sends one message per payment to a queue called ledgerline-transfers, and in Week 5 the processor receives them. Three words you'll meet:

  • Visibility timeout: a received message is hidden, not deleted, until the receiver deletes it. If the receiver never does, the message reappears for another try.
  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ): where a message goes after too many failed tries.
  • At-least-once delivery: occasionally the same message arrives twice, so receivers must be safe to run twice.

Chapter 13 of the field guide has a queue you can work by hand.

How it works inside. SQS stores every message on several servers, so it survives any one of them failing. That same redundancy is why a message is occasionally delivered twice. Receiving works like this:

  1. ReceiveMessage waits up to WaitTimeSeconds for messages (this is long polling), then returns up to 10 of them.
  2. Each returned message becomes invisible for the visibility timeout, and comes with a receipt handle: a ticket for deleting it.
  3. The receiver does its work, then calls DeleteMessage with that handle. Until then, the message still exists.
  4. If the timeout runs out first, the message becomes visible again, and its receive count goes up by one.
  5. Once the receive count passes the queue's maxReceiveCount, SQS moves the message to the dead-letter queue instead.

ChangeMessageVisibility resets a message's timer, which is how the processor retries after 2 or 4 seconds rather than 30. Work the queue yourself:

What, why and how: MiniStack

What it is. MiniStack is an emulator: a program that pretends to be AWS. It runs on your machine, answers on port 4566, and speaks the same language as real AWS for dozens of services.

Why we use it. Tests against it are free, fast, work offline, and can't be disturbed by anyone else, and they behave the same on your laptop and in CI. Relay's QA team is moving to MiniStack for exactly these reasons.

How we use it. It runs as a container in docker-compose.yml. The code points at it with the endpoint setting, http://localhost:4566, instead of at real AWS. npm run aws:setup creates the queues, because MiniStack starts empty and can forget everything when it restarts. When something behaves oddly, docker compose logs ministack shows what it received.

How it works inside. MiniStack is a single program listening on port 4566 that speaks each service's API. It reads which action a request wants, like SendMessage or PutItem, from the request itself, and carries it out with data it keeps in memory. It accepts any credentials and doesn't enforce IAM permissions. That's what makes it fast and free, and also why it can't catch a permission mistake: nothing in it ever says no.

What, why and how: The AWS SDK for JavaScript

What it is. The SDK, short for software development kit, is Amazon's library for calling AWS from code. Each service has its own package, like @aws-sdk/client-sqs.

Why we use it. It signs each request with your credentials, retries network hiccups, and turns AWS's responses into ordinary JavaScript objects.

How we use it. Every call follows the same pattern: create a client once, then send it commands. 

const sqs = new SQSClient({ region, endpoint, credentials });
await sqs.send(new SendMessageCommand({ QueueUrl, MessageBody }));

Every AWS action has a matching command, like CreateQueueCommand, ReceiveMessageCommand or DeleteMessageCommand. You'll see exactly the same pattern with Lambda in Week 5.

How it works inside. sqs.send(command) passes the command through a pipeline of steps, called middleware. It turns your input into the HTTP request the service expects, signs it, sends it, and turns the response back into a JavaScript object. When a request fails in a way worth retrying, like a network blip or AWS asking you to slow down, the SDK retries by itself, waiting a little longer each time. That's why an unreachable MiniStack can take a few seconds to produce an error.

SQS is Amazon's queue service. Your code talks to it through the AWS SDK, which needs three things: a region, credentials, and an endpoint (the address to send requests to). MiniStack pretends to be AWS on port 4566 of your machine and accepts any credentials, so you can build and test against "AWS" for free, offline. Point the same code at real AWS later by leaving the endpoint unset. Relay's QA team is moving to MiniStack for exactly this.

Run MiniStack

Replace docker-compose.yml:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ledgerline
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ledgerline
      POSTGRES_DB: ledgerline
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ledgerline -d ledgerline"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10

  # Pretends to be AWS (SQS now; Lambda, DynamoDB and S3 later) on port 4566.
  ministack:
    image: ministackorg/ministack:latest
    ports:
      - "4566:4566"

volumes:
  postgres-data:

docker compose up -d --wait
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:4566/

The curl should print 200: MiniStack is answering. The image uses the latest tag to keep things simple while MiniStack moves quickly. On a team, you'd pin an exact version once you'd picked one, the same way the Postgres image is pinned.

Verify on your machine

I ran MiniStack installed directly on the machine for this handbook, so this is the first time its Docker image meets your setup.

Pass: docker compose ps lists ministack as running, and the curl prints 200.

Fail: the container keeps restarting, or the curl prints 000. Run docker compose logs ministack and send me the last lines.

Talk to it from code

npm install @aws-sdk/client-sqs@3

Create src/queue.ts:

src/queue.ts
import {
  GetQueueUrlCommand,
  SendMessageCommand,
  SQSClient,
} from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";

// Locally and in CI this points at MiniStack, which pretends to be AWS on port
// 4566 and accepts any credentials. In real AWS you'd leave the endpoint unset.
export const sqs = new SQSClient({
  region: process.env.AWS_REGION ?? "us-east-1",
  endpoint: process.env.AWS_ENDPOINT_URL ?? "http://localhost:4566",
  credentials: {
    accessKeyId: process.env.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID ?? "test",
    secretAccessKey: process.env.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY ?? "test",
  },
});

export const TRANSFERS_QUEUE =
  process.env.TRANSFERS_QUEUE_NAME ?? "ledgerline-transfers";

// The message the API sends when a customer pays another bank. The "version"
// field lets the format change later without breaking older processors.
export interface TransferRequestedMessage {
  version: 1;
  type: "transfer.requested";
  transferId: string;
  correlationId: string;
  amountCents: number;
  counterparty: { name: string; routingNumber: string; accountNumber: string };
}

let queueUrl: string | undefined;

async function transfersQueueUrl(): Promise<string> {
  if (!queueUrl) {
    const result = await sqs.send(
      new GetQueueUrlCommand({ QueueName: TRANSFERS_QUEUE }),
    );
    if (!result.QueueUrl) throw new Error(`No URL for ${TRANSFERS_QUEUE}`);
    queueUrl = result.QueueUrl;
  }
  return queueUrl;
}

export async function publishTransferRequested(
  message: TransferRequestedMessage,
): Promise<void> {
  await sqs.send(
    new SendMessageCommand({
      QueueUrl: await transfersQueueUrl(),
      MessageBody: JSON.stringify(message),
      MessageAttributes: {
        correlationId: {
          DataType: "String",
          StringValue: message.correlationId,
        },
      },
    }),
  );
}

Create scripts/aws-setup.ts, which creates the queues:

scripts/aws-setup.ts
import {
  CreateQueueCommand,
  GetQueueAttributesCommand,
  ListQueuesCommand,
} from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";
import { sqs, TRANSFERS_QUEUE } from "../src/queue";

const DEAD_LETTER_QUEUE = `${TRANSFERS_QUEUE}-dlq`;

// MiniStack can take a few seconds to start, especially in CI.
async function waitForMiniStack() {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 30; attempt++) {
    try {
      await sqs.send(new ListQueuesCommand({}));
      return;
    } catch {
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1000));
    }
  }
  throw new Error("MiniStack didn't answer on port 4566. Is it running?");
}

async function setup() {
  await waitForMiniStack();

  // The dead-letter queue first, because the main queue points at it.
  const dlq = await sqs.send(
    new CreateQueueCommand({ QueueName: DEAD_LETTER_QUEUE }),
  );
  const { Attributes } = await sqs.send(
    new GetQueueAttributesCommand({
      QueueUrl: dlq.QueueUrl,
      AttributeNames: ["QueueArn"],
    }),
  );

  // After 3 failed receives, SQS moves a message to the dead-letter queue.
  await sqs.send(
    new CreateQueueCommand({
      QueueName: TRANSFERS_QUEUE,
      Attributes: {
        VisibilityTimeout: "30",
        RedrivePolicy: JSON.stringify({
          deadLetterTargetArn: Attributes?.QueueArn,
          maxReceiveCount: 3,
        }),
      },
    }),
  );

  console.log(`Queues ready: ${TRANSFERS_QUEUE} and ${DEAD_LETTER_QUEUE}`);
}

setup().catch((error) => {
  console.error("AWS setup failed:", error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Add a script for it, and make db:reset recreate the queues too: 

npm pkg set scripts.aws:setup="tsx scripts/aws-setup.ts" scripts.db:reset="docker compose down -v && docker compose up -d --wait && npm run db:migrate && npm run aws:setup"
npm run aws:setup

Queues ready: ledgerline-transfers and ledgerline-transfers-dlq

What the code does

  • new SQSClient({...}) creates the connection. Each setting reads an environment variable first and falls back to MiniStack's values, so CI or a real AWS account can override them without code changes.
  • TransferRequestedMessage is the message format, with a version field so the format can change later without breaking older processors.
  • GetQueueUrlCommand looks up the queue's address once and remembers it.
  • MessageAttributes carries the correlation ID alongside the message, where tools can read it without parsing the body.
  • The setup script creates the dead-letter queue first, because the main queue's RedrivePolicy points at it: after 3 failed receives, a message moves there. VisibilityTimeout: "30" hides a taken message for 30 seconds.
  • waitForMiniStack retries for up to 30 seconds. Containers take a moment to start, and a setup script that gives up instantly is a classic source of "fails the first time, passes on rerun" CI runs.

If it breaks

port is already allocated for 4566. Something else is on that port, often a LocalStack container. Stop it with docker ps and docker stop followed by its name.

MiniStack didn't answer on port 4566. Run docker compose ps to check it's running, and docker compose logs ministack to see why not.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 22: MiniStack".

In a company

The same code talks to real AWS, with AWS_ENDPOINT_URL left unset. Queues and tables are created by infrastructure as code (Terraform or the AWS CDK) in the deployment pipeline rather than by a setup script, and services get their credentials from IAM roles instead of keys. MiniStack still earns its place: it's what the CI tests run against.

Step 23: Payments to other banks

About two hours.

A payment to another bank works differently from a transfer between two Ledgerline accounts:

  • The money leaves straight away. It moves from the customer's account into a system account called Outgoing payments clearing, where it waits until the partner bank confirms. That's still double entry: minus the customer, plus clearing. If the payment comes back later, the money moves back.
  • The API answers 202 Accepted, not 201 Created. The payment has been accepted, not finished.
  • The slow work goes on a queue. The API saves the transfer as pending and publishes a message. In Week 5, a processor picks it up and talks to the bank.
  • The dual-write problem. Saving to the database and publishing to a queue can't happen as one atomic step. Ledgerline publishes just before COMMIT: if the queue is down, the whole transfer rolls back and the customer gets a 503, so there's never a pending payment nobody will process. The rare opposite case, a message sent but then the commit fails, means the processor must ignore messages about transfers that don't exist. The industry-standard fix for both is called the outbox pattern. Know the name; Phase 5 comes back to it.

The database

Create db/migrations/003_external_transfers.sql:

db/migrations/003_external_transfers.sql
-- Payments to other banks. The money leaves the customer's account as soon as
-- the payment is accepted, and waits in a clearing account until the partner
-- bank confirms it. Double entry still holds: minus the customer, plus clearing.
INSERT INTO accounts (id, name, type)
VALUES ('00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002', 'Outgoing payments clearing', 'system');

ALTER TABLE transfers DROP CONSTRAINT transfers_kind_check;
ALTER TABLE transfers ADD CONSTRAINT transfers_kind_check
  CHECK (kind IN ('deposit', 'internal', 'external'));

ALTER TABLE transfers DROP CONSTRAINT transfers_status_check;
ALTER TABLE transfers ADD CONSTRAINT transfers_status_check
  CHECK (status IN ('completed', 'pending'));

-- Where an external payment is going. Only external transfers have one.
ALTER TABLE transfers
  ADD COLUMN counterparty_name text,
  ADD COLUMN counterparty_routing text,
  ADD COLUMN counterparty_account text,
  ADD CONSTRAINT transfers_counterparty_check
    CHECK ((kind = 'external') = (counterparty_account IS NOT NULL));

npm run db:migrate

Applied 003_external_transfers.sql
Database is up to date.

The code

Replace src/ledger.ts:

src/ledger.ts
import type { PoolClient } from "pg";
import { pool } from "./db";
import { formatCents } from "./domain/money";
import { AppError, notFound } from "./errors";

export const FUNDING_ACCOUNT_ID = "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001";
export const CLEARING_ACCOUNT_ID = "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002";

export type TransferKind = "deposit" | "internal" | "external";
export type TransferStatus = "completed" | "pending";

// Where a payment to another bank is going.
export interface Counterparty {
  name: string;
  routingNumber: string;
  accountNumber: string;
}

// What a transfers row looks like coming out of Postgres.
interface TransferRow {
  id: string;
  kind: TransferKind;
  from_account_id: string;
  to_account_id: string;
  amount_cents: string; // bigint arrives as a string, see toCents()
  status: TransferStatus;
  counterparty_name: string | null;
  counterparty_routing: string | null;
  counterparty_account: string | null;
  created_at: Date;
}

// What we send back to API clients.
export interface Transfer {
  id: string;
  kind: TransferKind;
  fromAccountId: string;
  toAccountId: string;
  amountCents: number;
  status: TransferStatus;
  createdAt: string;
  // Only the last four digits ever leave the API.
  counterparty?: { name: string; routingNumber: string; accountLast4: string };
}

// Postgres bigint can hold numbers JavaScript can't represent exactly, so pg
// returns them as strings. Our amounts are far below that limit, so we convert,
// but refuse loudly if a value ever isn't a safe whole number.
export function toCents(value: string | number): number {
  const cents = Number(value);
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(cents)) {
    throw new Error(`Not a safe whole number of cents: ${value}`);
  }
  return cents;
}

export function toTransfer(row: TransferRow): Transfer {
  const transfer: Transfer = {
    id: row.id,
    kind: row.kind,
    fromAccountId: row.from_account_id,
    toAccountId: row.to_account_id,
    amountCents: toCents(row.amount_cents),
    status: row.status,
    createdAt: row.created_at.toISOString(),
  };
  if (row.counterparty_account) {
    transfer.counterparty = {
      name: row.counterparty_name ?? "",
      routingNumber: row.counterparty_routing ?? "",
      accountLast4: row.counterparty_account.slice(-4),
    };
  }
  return transfer;
}

type Queryable = Pick<PoolClient, "query">;

export async function getBalance(db: Queryable, accountId: string) {
  const { rows } = await db.query<{ balance: string }>(
    "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_cents), 0) AS balance FROM ledger_entries WHERE account_id = $1",
    [accountId],
  );
  return toCents(rows[0].balance);
}

export async function getTransfer(id: string): Promise<Transfer> {
  const { rows } = await pool.query<TransferRow>(
    "SELECT * FROM transfers WHERE id = $1",
    [id],
  );
  if (rows.length === 0) throw notFound("transfer", id);
  return toTransfer(rows[0]);
}

interface MoveMoneyInput {
  kind: TransferKind;
  fromAccountId: string;
  toAccountId: string;
  amountCents: number;
  status?: TransferStatus;
  counterparty?: Counterparty;
  // Runs inside the transaction, after everything is written but before
  // COMMIT. If it throws, the whole transfer is rolled back.
  beforeCommit?: (transfer: Transfer) => Promise<void>;
}

// The one place money moves. Everything happens inside a database transaction:
// either the transfer and both ledger entries are saved, or nothing is.
export async function moveMoney(input: MoveMoneyInput): Promise<Transfer> {
  if (input.fromAccountId === input.toAccountId) {
    throw new AppError(
      422,
      "same_account",
      "Can't transfer to the same account",
    );
  }

  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");

    // Lock both account rows until COMMIT, always in the same order (by id).
    // Two transfers touching the same account now take turns instead of both
    // reading the old balance, and opposite transfers can't deadlock.
    const { rows: accounts } = await client.query<{ id: string; type: string }>(
      "SELECT id, type FROM accounts WHERE id = ANY($1::uuid[]) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE",
      [[input.fromAccountId, input.toAccountId]],
    );
    const from = accounts.find((account) => account.id === input.fromAccountId);
    const to = accounts.find((account) => account.id === input.toAccountId);
    if (!from) throw notFound("account", input.fromAccountId);
    if (!to) throw notFound("account", input.toAccountId);

    // Only deposits may draw on a system account.
    if (
      input.kind === "internal" &&
      (from.type !== "customer" || to.type !== "customer")
    ) {
      throw new AppError(
        422,
        "account_not_allowed",
        "Transfers must be between customer accounts",
      );
    }
    if (input.kind === "external" && from.type !== "customer") {
      throw new AppError(
        422,
        "account_not_allowed",
        "Only customer accounts can pay other banks",
      );
    }

    if (from.type === "customer") {
      const balance = await getBalance(client, from.id);
      if (balance < input.amountCents) {
        throw new AppError(
          422,
          "insufficient_funds",
          `Balance is ${formatCents(balance)} but the transfer needs ${formatCents(input.amountCents)}`,
        );
      }
    }

    const { rows } = await client.query<TransferRow>(
      `INSERT INTO transfers (kind, from_account_id, to_account_id, amount_cents, status,
         counterparty_name, counterparty_routing, counterparty_account)
       VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7, $8)
       RETURNING *`,
      [
        input.kind,
        input.fromAccountId,
        input.toAccountId,
        input.amountCents,
        input.status ?? "completed",
        input.counterparty?.name ?? null,
        input.counterparty?.routingNumber ?? null,
        input.counterparty?.accountNumber ?? null,
      ],
    );
    const transfer = toTransfer(rows[0]);

    // Double entry: money leaves one account and arrives in the other.
    await client.query(
      "INSERT INTO ledger_entries (account_id, transfer_id, amount_cents) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
      [input.fromAccountId, transfer.id, -input.amountCents],
    );
    await client.query(
      "INSERT INTO ledger_entries (account_id, transfer_id, amount_cents) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
      [input.toAccountId, transfer.id, input.amountCents],
    );

    if (input.beforeCommit) await input.beforeCommit(transfer);

    await client.query("COMMIT");
    return transfer;
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw error;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

Create src/routes/external-transfers.ts:

src/routes/external-transfers.ts
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import type { FastifyInstance } from "fastify";
import { AppError } from "../errors";
import { CLEARING_ACCOUNT_ID, moveMoney, type Counterparty } from "../ledger";
import { publishTransferRequested } from "../queue";
import { amountCents } from "./schemas";

interface ExternalTransferBody {
  fromAccountId: string;
  amountCents: number;
  counterparty: Counterparty;
}

export async function externalTransferRoutes(app: FastifyInstance) {
  app.post<{ Body: ExternalTransferBody }>(
    "/transfers/external",
    {
      schema: {
        body: {
          type: "object",
          required: ["fromAccountId", "amountCents", "counterparty"],
          additionalProperties: false,
          properties: {
            fromAccountId: { type: "string", format: "uuid" },
            amountCents,
            counterparty: {
              type: "object",
              required: ["name", "routingNumber", "accountNumber"],
              additionalProperties: false,
              properties: {
                name: { type: "string", minLength: 1, maxLength: 100 },
                routingNumber: { type: "string", pattern: "^[0-9]{9}$" },
                accountNumber: { type: "string", pattern: "^[0-9]{4,17}$" },
              },
            },
          },
        },
      },
    },
    async (request, reply) => {
      // One id that follows this payment through every log and message.
      const correlationId = randomUUID();
      const { fromAccountId, counterparty } = request.body;

      const transfer = await moveMoney({
        kind: "external",
        fromAccountId,
        toAccountId: CLEARING_ACCOUNT_ID,
        amountCents: request.body.amountCents,
        status: "pending",
        counterparty,
        // Publish before COMMIT. If the queue is down, the transfer rolls back,
        // so there's never a pending payment that nobody will ever process.
        beforeCommit: async (saved) => {
          try {
            await publishTransferRequested({
              version: 1,
              type: "transfer.requested",
              transferId: saved.id,
              correlationId,
              amountCents: saved.amountCents,
              counterparty,
            });
          } catch (error) {
            request.log.error(
              { err: error, correlationId },
              "could not publish the transfer message",
            );
            throw new AppError(
              503,
              "queue_unavailable",
              "Payments to other banks are unavailable right now. Nothing was sent.",
            );
          }
        },
      });

      request.log.info(
        { transferId: transfer.id, correlationId },
        "external transfer accepted",
      );
      return reply
        .code(202)
        .header("x-correlation-id", correlationId)
        .send(transfer);
    },
  );
}

Replace src/app.ts to register the new route:

src/app.ts
import Fastify, { type FastifyError } from "fastify";
import { pool } from "./db";
import { AppError } from "./errors";
import { accountRoutes } from "./routes/accounts";
import { externalTransferRoutes } from "./routes/external-transfers";
import { transferRoutes } from "./routes/transfers";

const API_KEY = process.env.API_KEY ?? "local-dev-key";

export function buildApp() {
  const app = Fastify({
    logger: true,
    ajv: {
      customOptions: {
        // Fastify's defaults quietly turn "2500" into 2500 and drop unknown
        // fields. For money we want strict: wrong types and extra fields fail.
        coerceTypes: false,
        removeAdditional: false,
      },
    },
  });

  // Every route except the health check needs the right x-api-key header.
  app.addHook("onRequest", async (request, reply) => {
    if (request.routeOptions.url === "/health") return;
    if (request.headers["x-api-key"] !== API_KEY) {
      return reply
        .code(401)
        .send({ error: "unauthorized", message: "Missing or invalid API key" });
    }
  });

  app.get("/health", async (request, reply) => {
    try {
      await pool.query("SELECT 1");
      return { status: "ok", database: "up" };
    } catch (error) {
      request.log.error({ err: error }, "database health check failed");
      return reply.code(503).send({ status: "degraded", database: "down" });
    }
  });

  app.register(accountRoutes);
  app.register(transferRoutes);
  app.register(externalTransferRoutes);

  // Every error leaves the API in the same shape: { error, message }.
  app.setErrorHandler<FastifyError>((error, request, reply) => {
    if (error instanceof AppError) {
      return reply
        .code(error.statusCode)
        .send({ error: error.code, message: error.message });
    }
    if (error.validation) {
      return reply
        .code(400)
        .send({ error: "validation_error", message: error.message });
    }
    if (error.statusCode && error.statusCode < 500) {
      // Things like malformed JSON, which Fastify rejects before our code runs.
      return reply
        .code(error.statusCode)
        .send({ error: "bad_request", message: error.message });
    }
    request.log.error({ err: error }, "unhandled error");
    return reply
      .code(500)
      .send({ error: "internal_error", message: "Something went wrong" });
  });

  app.setNotFoundHandler((request, reply) => {
    reply.code(404).send({
      error: "route_not_found",
      message: `No route for ${request.method} ${request.url}`,
    });
  });

  return app;
}

What changed

  • moveMoney now takes a status, optional counterparty details, and a beforeCommit function that runs inside the transaction after everything is written. If it throws, everything rolls back. External payments must come from a customer account.
  • Only the last four digits leave the API. The full account number is stored because the bank needs it, but responses show accountLast4. Leaking account numbers in API responses is a classic finding in fintech security reviews.
  • The route's schema requires a 9-digit routing number and a 4 to 17-digit account number, using pattern.
  • correlationId is a fresh id for this payment. It goes in the message, in the logs, and in the x-correlation-id response header, so one search finds the payment's whole journey.
  • The contract now includes TransferRequestedMessage. Messages have contracts too: the processor in Week 5 depends on this format as much as a mobile app depends on the API's.

Try it by hand

With npm run dev running, create and fund an account as in Step 12 (with the API key header), then send a payment: 

curl -s -i -X POST localhost:3000/transfers/external -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'x-api-key: local-dev-key' -d "{\"fromAccountId\":\"$A\",\"amountCents\":2500,\"counterparty\":{\"name\":\"Flour Supplier Ltd\",\"routingNumber\":\"021000021\",\"accountNumber\":\"123456789\"}}"
curl -s -H 'x-api-key: local-dev-key' localhost:3000/accounts/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002 | jq .balanceCents

You should see HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted, an x-correlation-id header, a transfer with "status":"pending" and "accountLast4":"6789", and the clearing account holding the $25.00.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 23: Payments to other banks".

Step 24: Test the queue

About two hours.

Three new testing ideas this step. Tests that read a shared queue have to take turns. The framework needs a way to read the queue. And the most important test proves what happens when the queue is down, without adding any test-only code to the API: Playwright starts a second copy of the API configured with a queue name that doesn't exist. That's fault injection by configuration.

Replace tests/framework/contract.ts:

tests/framework/contract.ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";
import Ajv2020 from "ajv/dist/2020";
import addFormats from "ajv-formats";
import { parse } from "yaml";

// Load openapi.yaml once and teach Ajv (a JSON Schema validator) about it.
const specPath = path.join(__dirname, "..", "..", "openapi.yaml");
const spec = parse(readFileSync(specPath, "utf8"));

// strict: false lets Ajv ignore OpenAPI-only keys like "paths" and "info".
const ajv = new Ajv2020({ allErrors: true, strict: false });
addFormats(ajv);
ajv.addSchema(spec, "openapi");

export type SchemaName =
  | "Account"
  | "Transfer"
  | "Error"
  | "HealthStatus"
  | "TransferRequestedMessage";

/** Throws a readable error if body doesn't match the named schema. */
export function assertMatchesContract(
  schemaName: SchemaName,
  body: unknown,
  context: string,
): void {
  const validate = ajv.getSchema(`openapi#/components/schemas/${schemaName}`);
  if (!validate) {
    throw new Error(`openapi.yaml has no schema called ${schemaName}`);
  }
  if (!validate(body)) {
    throw new Error(
      [
        `Contract violation: ${context}`,
        `Expected ${schemaName}: ${ajv.errorsText(validate.errors)}`,
        `Body: ${JSON.stringify(body, null, 2)}`,
      ].join("\n"),
    );
  }
}

Replace tests/framework/ledgerline-client.ts:

tests/framework/ledgerline-client.ts
import type { APIRequestContext, APIResponse } from "@playwright/test";
import { assertMatchesContract, type SchemaName } from "./contract";
import type { Account, HealthStatus, Transfer } from "./types";

export interface ApiResult<T> {
  status: number;
  body: T;
}

// One method per endpoint. Tests talk to this class, never to raw URLs, so
// when an endpoint changes you fix it here once instead of in every test.
export class LedgerlineClient {
  constructor(private readonly request: APIRequestContext) {}

  health() {
    return this.send<HealthStatus>(
      this.request.get("/health"),
      "HealthStatus",
      "HealthStatus",
    );
  }

  createAccount(name: string) {
    return this.send<Account>(
      this.request.post("/accounts", { data: { name } }),
      "Account",
    );
  }

  getAccount(id: string) {
    return this.send<Account>(this.request.get(`/accounts/${id}`), "Account");
  }

  deposit(accountId: string, amountCents: unknown) {
    return this.send<Transfer>(
      this.request.post(`/accounts/${accountId}/deposits`, {
        data: { amountCents },
      }),
      "Transfer",
    );
  }

  // Takes a loose object on purpose, so negative tests can send bad input.
  createTransfer(data: Record<string, unknown>) {
    return this.send<Transfer>(
      this.request.post("/transfers", { data }),
      "Transfer",
    );
  }

  // Pays a business at another bank. Answers 202: accepted, not finished.
  createExternalTransfer(data: Record<string, unknown>) {
    return this.send<Transfer>(
      this.request.post("/transfers/external", { data }),
      "Transfer",
    );
  }

  getTransfer(id: string) {
    return this.send<Transfer>(
      this.request.get(`/transfers/${id}`),
      "Transfer",
    );
  }

  async balanceOf(accountId: string): Promise<number> {
    const { status, body } = await this.getAccount(accountId);
    if (status !== 200) {
      throw new Error(`Couldn't read balance of ${accountId}: HTTP ${status}`);
    }
    return body.balanceCents;
  }

  // Every response is checked against openapi.yaml before a test sees it:
  // successes against their resource schema, failures against Error.
  private async send<T>(
    pending: Promise<APIResponse>,
    successSchema: SchemaName,
    errorSchema: SchemaName = "Error",
  ): Promise<ApiResult<T>> {
    const response = await pending;
    const status = response.status();
    const body = await response.json();
    const context = `${response.url()} returned ${status}`;
    assertMatchesContract(
      response.ok() ? successSchema : errorSchema,
      body,
      context,
    );
    return { status, body };
  }
}

Replace tests/framework/db-helper.ts:

tests/framework/db-helper.ts
import { Pool } from "pg";

// Read-only questions tests ask the database directly. One instance per
// Playwright worker (see fixtures.ts), closed when the worker finishes.
export class DbHelper {
  private readonly pool = new Pool({
    connectionString:
      process.env.DATABASE_URL ??
      "postgres://ledgerline:ledgerline@localhost:5432/ledgerline",
    max: 2,
  });

  /** Transfers that don't have exactly two ledger entries summing to zero. */
  async unbalancedTransfers() {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(`
      SELECT t.id, COUNT(e.id) AS entries, COALESCE(SUM(e.amount_cents), 0) AS total
      FROM transfers t
      LEFT JOIN ledger_entries e ON e.transfer_id = t.id
      GROUP BY t.id
      HAVING COUNT(e.id) <> 2 OR COALESCE(SUM(e.amount_cents), 0) <> 0
    `);
    return rows;
  }

  /** Sum of every ledger entry ever written. Should always be "0". */
  async ledgerTotal(): Promise<string> {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(
      "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_cents), 0)::text AS total FROM ledger_entries",
    );
    return rows[0].total;
  }

  /** Customer accounts whose balance has gone below zero. */
  async negativeCustomerBalances() {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(`
      SELECT a.id, SUM(e.amount_cents) AS balance
      FROM accounts a
      JOIN ledger_entries e ON e.account_id = a.id
      WHERE a.type = 'customer'
      GROUP BY a.id
      HAVING SUM(e.amount_cents) < 0
    `);
    return rows;
  }

  async countAccountsNamed(name: string): Promise<number> {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(
      "SELECT COUNT(*)::int AS count FROM accounts WHERE name = $1",
      [name],
    );
    return rows[0].count;
  }

  async countTransfersFrom(accountId: string): Promise<number> {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(
      "SELECT COUNT(*)::int AS count FROM transfers WHERE from_account_id = $1",
      [accountId],
    );
    return rows[0].count;
  }

  async close() {
    await this.pool.end();
  }
}

Create tests/framework/queue-helper.ts:

tests/framework/queue-helper.ts
import {
  DeleteMessageCommand,
  GetQueueUrlCommand,
  ReceiveMessageCommand,
  SQSClient,
  type Message,
} from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";

export interface ReceivedMessage {
  body: Record<string, unknown>;
  correlationId: string | undefined;
}

// Reads the transfers queue directly, the way the processor will in Week 5.
export class QueueHelper {
  private readonly sqs = new SQSClient({
    region: process.env.AWS_REGION ?? "us-east-1",
    endpoint: process.env.AWS_ENDPOINT_URL ?? "http://localhost:4566",
    credentials: { accessKeyId: "test", secretAccessKey: "test" },
  });
  private url: string | undefined;

  constructor(
    private readonly queueName = process.env.TRANSFERS_QUEUE_NAME ??
      "ledgerline-transfers",
  ) {}

  /** Deletes every message waiting on the queue, so a test starts clean. */
  async drain(): Promise<void> {
    for (;;) {
      const messages = await this.receive(0);
      if (messages.length === 0) return;
      await Promise.all(messages.map((message) => this.delete(message)));
    }
  }

  /** Waits for the message about one transfer, deletes it, and returns it. */
  async takeMessageFor(
    transferId: string,
    timeoutMs = 5_000,
  ): Promise<ReceivedMessage> {
    const deadline = Date.now() + timeoutMs;
    while (Date.now() < deadline) {
      for (const message of await this.receive(1)) {
        const body = JSON.parse(message.Body ?? "{}");
        if (body.transferId === transferId) {
          await this.delete(message);
          return {
            body,
            correlationId:
              message.MessageAttributes?.correlationId?.StringValue,
          };
        }
      }
    }
    throw new Error(
      `No message for transfer ${transferId} within ${timeoutMs} ms`,
    );
  }

  /** True when nothing is waiting. Looks without hiding anything. */
  async isEmpty(): Promise<boolean> {
    const messages = await this.receive(1, 0);
    return messages.length === 0;
  }

  private async receive(waitSeconds: number, visibilityTimeout = 30) {
    const result = await this.sqs.send(
      new ReceiveMessageCommand({
        QueueUrl: await this.queueUrl(),
        MaxNumberOfMessages: 10,
        WaitTimeSeconds: waitSeconds,
        VisibilityTimeout: visibilityTimeout,
        MessageAttributeNames: ["All"],
      }),
    );
    return result.Messages ?? [];
  }

  private async delete(message: Message) {
    await this.sqs.send(
      new DeleteMessageCommand({
        QueueUrl: await this.queueUrl(),
        ReceiptHandle: message.ReceiptHandle,
      }),
    );
  }

  private async queueUrl(): Promise<string> {
    if (!this.url) {
      const result = await this.sqs.send(
        new GetQueueUrlCommand({ QueueName: this.queueName }),
      );
      if (!result.QueueUrl) throw new Error(`No queue ${this.queueName}`);
      this.url = result.QueueUrl;
    }
    return this.url;
  }
}

    await use(() => new AccountBuilder(api));
  },

  // A client with a different API key, or none, for authentication tests.
  apiWithKey: async ({ playwright, baseURL }, use) => {
    const contexts: APIRequestContext[] = [];
    await use(async (apiKey) => {
      const context = await playwright.request.newContext({
        baseURL,
        extraHTTPHeaders: apiKey ? { "x-api-key": apiKey } : {},
      });
      contexts.push(context);
      return new LedgerlineClient(context);
    });
    // Everything after use() runs when the test finishes: clean up.
    for (const context of contexts) await context.dispose();
  },

  // A client for the second API, the one whose queue doesn't exist.
  brokenQueueApi: async ({ playwright }, use) => {
    const context = await playwright.request.newContext({
      baseURL: BROKEN_QUEUE_API_URL,
      extraHTTPHeaders: { "x-api-key": API_KEY },
    });
    await use(new LedgerlineClient(context));
    await context.dispose();
  },

  // Reads the transfers queue in MiniStack. One per worker.
  queue: [
    // eslint-disable-next-line no-empty-pattern
    async ({}, use) => {
      await use(new QueueHelper());
    },
    { scope: "worker" },
  ],

  db: [
    // Playwright requires the {} here even though this fixture needs nothing.
    // eslint-disable-next-line no-empty-pattern
    async ({}, use) => {
      const db = new DbHelper();
      await use(db);
      await db.close();
    },
    { scope: "worker" },
  ],
});

Create tests/api/external-transfers.spec.ts:

tests/api/external-transfers.spec.ts
import { expectApiError } from "../framework/assertions";
import { assertMatchesContract } from "../framework/contract";
import { expect, test } from "../framework/fixtures";
import { CLEARING_ACCOUNT_ID, SUPPLIER_BANK } from "../framework/test-data";

// These tests read one shared queue, so they take turns instead of running in
// parallel, and each one starts by emptying it.
test.describe.configure({ mode: "serial" });

test.describe("payments to other banks", () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ queue }) => {
    await queue.drain();
  });

  test("are accepted with 202 and wait as pending", async ({
    api,
    newAccount,
  }) => {
    const from = await newAccount().withBalance(10_000).create();

    const { status, body } = await api.createExternalTransfer({
      fromAccountId: from.id,
      amountCents: 2_500,
      counterparty: SUPPLIER_BANK,
    });

    expect(status).toBe(202);
    expect(body).toMatchObject({
      kind: "external",
      status: "pending",
      amountCents: 2_500,
      toAccountId: CLEARING_ACCOUNT_ID,
      counterparty: {
        name: SUPPLIER_BANK.name,
        routingNumber: SUPPLIER_BANK.routingNumber,
        accountLast4: "6789",
      },
    });
    expect(await api.balanceOf(from.id)).toBe(7_500);
  });

  test("put a message on the queue that matches the contract", async ({
    api,
    newAccount,
    queue,
  }) => {
    const from = await newAccount().withBalance(10_000).create();
    const { body: transfer } = await api.createExternalTransfer({
      fromAccountId: from.id,
      amountCents: 2_500,
      counterparty: SUPPLIER_BANK,
    });

    const message = await queue.takeMessageFor(transfer.id);

    assertMatchesContract(
      "TransferRequestedMessage",
      message.body,
      "the transfers queue",
    );
    expect(message.body).toMatchObject({
      transferId: transfer.id,
      amountCents: 2_500,
      counterparty: SUPPLIER_BANK,
    });
    expect(message.correlationId).toBe(message.body.correlationId);
  });

  test("never return the full account number", async ({ api, newAccount }) => {
    const from = await newAccount().withBalance(10_000).create();

    const { body } = await api.createExternalTransfer({
      fromAccountId: from.id,
      amountCents: 100,
      counterparty: SUPPLIER_BANK,
    });

    expect(JSON.stringify(body)).not.toContain(SUPPLIER_BANK.accountNumber);
  });

  test("refuse a payment over the balance and send nothing", async ({
    api,
    newAccount,
    queue,
  }) => {
    const from = await newAccount().withBalance(1_000).create();

    const result = await api.createExternalTransfer({
      fromAccountId: from.id,
      amountCents: 1_001,
      counterparty: SUPPLIER_BANK,
    });

    expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds");
    expect(await queue.isEmpty()).toBe(true);
  });

  const badDetails = [
    {
      label: "an 8-digit routing number",
      change: { routingNumber: "02100002" },
    },
    {
      label: "letters in the account number",
      change: { accountNumber: "12AB5678" },
    },
    { label: "an empty name", change: { name: "" } },
  ];

  for (const { label, change } of badDetails) {
    test(`reject ${label}`, async ({ api, newAccount }) => {
      const from = await newAccount().withBalance(1_000).create();

      const result = await api.createExternalTransfer({
        fromAccountId: from.id,
        amountCents: 100,
        counterparty: { ...SUPPLIER_BANK, ...change },
      });

      expectApiError(result, 400, "validation_error");
    });
  }

  test("roll back completely when the queue is down", async ({
    api,
    brokenQueueApi,
    newAccount,
    db,
  }) => {
    const from = await newAccount().withBalance(10_000).create();

    const result = await brokenQueueApi.createExternalTransfer({
      fromAccountId: from.id,
      amountCents: 2_500,
      counterparty: SUPPLIER_BANK,
    });

    expectApiError(result, 503, "queue_unavailable");
    expect(await api.balanceOf(from.id)).toBe(10_000);
    expect(await db.countTransfersFrom(from.id)).toBe(0);
  });
});

44 passed: the 36 from Week 3 and 8 new ones.

What the tests do

  • test.describe.configure({ mode: "serial" }) makes this file's tests run one at a time. They share one queue, and parallel tests would read each other's messages.
  • queue.drain() in beforeEach empties the queue, so each test starts clean and only sees its own message.
  • takeMessageFor polls the queue until it finds the message for one transfer, or gives up after five seconds with a clear error. Polling with a deadline, never a fixed sleep, is how you test anything asynchronous.
  • isEmpty looks at the queue with a visibility timeout of 0, so it doesn't hide anything while checking.
  • The contract check on the message proves the processor will get exactly the format it expects.
  • "Never return the full account number" searches the whole response for it. A data-exposure test is cheap, and fintech interviewers love it.
  • "Roll back completely when the queue is down" uses brokenQueueApi, the client for the second API on port 3001. It checks the 503, then proves nothing leaked: the balance is untouched and no transfer row exists.
  • Two webServers in playwright.config.ts: the second sets env to change the port and the queue name. Same code, broken configuration.

Replace README.md, which now mentions MiniStack and the queue helper:

README.md
# Ledgerline

A small business-banking backend, and the automated test framework around it.
Built to practise how fintech teams test money movement: ledgers, contracts,
concurrency and CI.

## Run it

You need Docker Desktop and Node 24.

```bash
npm install
npm run db:up        # start Postgres and MiniStack in Docker
npm run db:migrate   # create the tables
npm run aws:setup    # create the queues in MiniStack
npm test             # unit tests, then API tests (the API starts automatically)
```

Run the API on its own with `npm run dev`, then try `curl localhost:3000/health`.

## How the tests are organised

```
tests/
  unit/        Vitest. Pure functions, no network or database.
  api/         Playwright specs. Each file covers one feature.
  framework/   The plumbing specs are built on:
    fixtures.ts           api, newAccount, apiWithKey, db
    ledgerline-client.ts  one method per endpoint
    contract.ts           checks every response against openapi.yaml
    account-builder.ts    newAccount().withBalance(5000).create()
    db-helper.ts          ledger integrity queries
    queue-helper.ts       reads the transfers queue in MiniStack
    assertions.ts         expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds")
bruno/         Bruno collection for exploring the API by hand
openapi.yaml   The API contract
```

## Add a test

1. Pick the spec file for the feature, or create `tests/api/<feature>.spec.ts`.
2. Import `{ test, expect }` from `../framework/fixtures`.
3. Set up data with `newAccount()`, act with `api`, assert on the result.

```ts
test("rejects a transfer over the balance", async ({ api, newAccount }) => {
  const from = await newAccount().withBalance(1_000).create();
  const to = await newAccount().create();

  const result = await api.createTransfer({
    fromAccountId: from.id,
    toAccountId: to.id,
    amountCents: 1_001,
  });

  expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds");
});
```

Every test creates its own accounts, so tests run in parallel and in any order.

Week 5 adds the processor: a Lambda that takes messages off the queue and calls a fake partner bank built with WireMock.

Week 5: The processor and a fake bank

Week 4 put payments on a queue. This week, something takes them off. You'll build the processor, the code that sends each payment to the partner bank, as a Lambda handler. You'll give it a fake bank to talk to with WireMock, then prove how it behaves when the bank accepts, refuses, breaks, or receives the same payment twice. Chapters 14, 15 and 18 of the field guide cover the ideas.

Step 26: A fake partner bank with WireMock

About 45 minutes.

What, why and how: WireMock

What it is. WireMock is a fake HTTP server you program. You give it stubs, each saying "when a request looks like this, answer like that", and it records every request it receives.

Why we use it. You can't make a real bank fail on demand, and tests shouldn't depend on someone else's system being up. With WireMock, you choose the bank's behaviour for each test: accept, refuse, break, stall, or fail once and then work. Afterwards you can check exactly what your code sent. It's in Relay's stack.

How we use it.

  • Default stubs are JSON files in infra/wiremock/mappings, loaded when the container starts.
  • Tests add their own stubs, and read what arrived, through WireMock's admin API at http://localhost:8080/__admin.
  • The framework wraps all of that in a FakePartner class, so a test just says partner.rejects() or partner.requests().
  • Chapter 18 of the field guide lets you program a fake bank by hand.

How it works inside. WireMock keeps a list of stubs. For each request it receives, it checks the stubs in priority order, lowest number first, and sends back the response of the first one whose pattern matches: the method, the path, the headers or the body. It also records every request in a journal, which its admin API lets you search. That's how partner.requests() counts what the processor sent. A scenario is a small state machine: a stub can require the scenario to be in a given state, and move it to a new state when it matches, which is how "fails once, then works" is built. Program the fake bank:

You can't make a real bank return an error on demand, and tests shouldn't depend on one anyway. WireMock is a fake HTTP server you program with stubs: when a request matches, send this response. You'll give it one default stub, a bank that accepts every payment. Tests then add their own stubs on top, like "reject this one" or "fail once, then work".

What the files do

  • request is what a call must look like to match: a POST to /ach/originate.
  • response is what WireMock sends back.
  • priority: 10 makes this the fallback. Lower numbers win, and the stubs tests add use priority 1, so they always take precedence.
  • The volume mounts infra/wiremock into the container, where WireMock loads every file in mappings when it starts.
  • The admin API lives under /__admin. Try curl -s localhost:8080/__admin/mappings to list every stub.

Step 27: The processor

About two hours.

What, why and how: AWS Lambda

What it is. Lambda runs your code without you managing a server. You upload a function and tell AWS what should trigger it, like messages arriving on a queue. AWS then runs the function for each event, starting copies when there's work and none when there isn't.

Why we use it. Relay's backend is built from Lambdas and microservices, and their QA posting mentions testing Lambdas specifically. A Lambda is a natural fit for the processor, which sits idle until a payment arrives.

How we use it. Words you'll meet:

  • Handler: the exported function AWS calls. Here, handler(event) in src/processor/handler.ts.
  • Event: whatever triggered the run. From SQS, it's a batch of messages under event.Records.
  • Runtime: the language and version the function runs on. Here, nodejs22.x.
  • Event source mapping: the connection that makes a queue trigger a function.
  • Limits: one run can last up to 15 minutes, and remembers nothing from earlier runs.
  • Cold start: the extra delay the first time a new copy starts.

You'll run the handler in two ways. For the tests, a local runner script imitates the queue trigger, which is fast and predictable. In Step 29, you'll deploy it into MiniStack as a real Lambda. Chapter 14 of the field guide covers batches and partial failures.

How it works inside. For an SQS trigger, AWS runs a poller on your behalf, called an event source mapping. It long-polls the queue, gathers messages into a batch, calls your function with the batch, and waits for it to finish:

  • If the function returns normally, the poller deletes every message in the batch.
  • If it returns batchItemFailures, only those messages stay on the queue, and the rest are deleted.
  • If it throws an error, nothing is deleted, and every message comes back after its visibility timeout.

Each call runs in an execution environment: a small, isolated container with your code loaded. The first call has to create one, which is the cold start. After that, AWS keeps it warm and reuses it, so anything created outside the handler, like a database pool, survives from one call to the next. When messages pile up, AWS starts more environments side by side, which is how Lambda scales. Ledgerline's local runner imitates exactly this loop. See what happens when one message in a batch fails:

What, why and how: Retries, backoff and dead-letter queues

What it is. A retry repeats an operation that failed for a temporary reason. Backoff waits longer before each new try: here, 2 seconds, then 4. A dead-letter queue catches whatever still fails after the last try.

Why we use it. Networks blip and partners have bad minutes, and most of those failures fix themselves if you wait. Some failures never will, like a wrong account number or a garbled message, and retrying those forever wastes effort and hides the problem.

How we use it. The processor sorts every failure first. Server errors, timeouts and 429 "slow down" answers are retryable. Any other 4xx is final, and the payment is marked rejected at once. A retryable failure gets up to three tries. After the third, the payment is marked failed, the money goes back to the customer, and the message moves to the dead-letter queue for a person to look at.

How it works inside. Exponential backoff doubles the wait after each failure, so a struggling partner gets breathing room instead of a flood of retries. Real systems also add jitter, a small random amount on each wait, so a thousand clients that failed at the same moment don't all retry at the same moment too. Ledgerline's waits are 2 seconds, then 4, set with ChangeMessageVisibility, and the third failure is final.

What, why and how: Idempotency

What it is. An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. "Set the status to submitted" is idempotent. "Pay $25" is not.

Why we use it. Queues deliver at least once, clients retry after timeouts, and partners resend webhooks. In payments, every one of those duplicates is a chance to move money twice, which is the most expensive bug there is.

How we use it. The processor has three defences against paying twice:

  • it skips any transfer that's no longer pending;
  • recordPartnerOutcome locks the transfer's row and only ever changes a pending transfer;
  • every call to the bank carries an idempotency-key header, so the bank can spot a repeat.

Week 6 adds idempotency keys to Ledgerline's own API. Chapter 15 of the field guide has a demo.

How it works inside. Every idempotency scheme has the same three parts: a key naming the operation, somewhere to remember the keys already seen, and an atomic check-and-claim, so two copies arriving together can't both look new. Ledgerline has two such schemes. The API's keys live in DynamoDB, claimed with a conditional write. The processor's duplicates are caught by the payment's status, checked under a row lock in Postgres. The time window matters too: a key is remembered for 24 hours, and after that the same key would be treated as new. Retry a payment after a timeout:

The processor handles one message at a time:

  1. Read the message. If it isn't a valid transfer message, it never will be. It fails until SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue, where a person can look at it.
  2. Check the transfer is still pending. Delivery is at least once, so the same message can arrive twice. Anything already handled is skipped.
  3. Call the partner bank, with an idempotency-key header so the bank can spot a payment it has already seen.
  4. Record the outcome in one transaction. Accepted becomes submitted. A refusal becomes rejected. A bank that keeps failing becomes failed after three tries. Rejected and failed payments send the money back with a reversal: a new transfer from clearing to the customer, never an edit.
  5. Tell SQS what failed. Failed messages go back on the queue for another try, after a short delay: 2 seconds, then 4.

In AWS, this code runs as a Lambda that SQS triggers. On your machine, a small runner script does the same job: it fetches messages, calls the handler, and deletes the ones that succeeded. Step 29 deploys the same code as a real Lambda.

db/migrations/004_payment_outcomes.sql
-- What can happen to a payment after the API accepts it:
-- submitted (the partner bank took it), rejected (the partner refused it),
-- or failed (the partner never answered, even after retries).
ALTER TABLE transfers DROP CONSTRAINT transfers_status_check;
ALTER TABLE transfers ADD CONSTRAINT transfers_status_check
  CHECK (status IN ('completed', 'pending', 'submitted', 'rejected', 'failed'));

-- A reversal sends the money back when a payment can't go through.
-- It's a new transfer, never an edit to the old one.
ALTER TABLE transfers DROP CONSTRAINT transfers_kind_check;
ALTER TABLE transfers ADD CONSTRAINT transfers_kind_check
  CHECK (kind IN ('deposit', 'internal', 'external', 'reversal'));

ALTER TABLE transfers
  ADD COLUMN reverses_transfer_id uuid REFERENCES transfers (id),
  ADD COLUMN partner_reference text,
  ADD COLUMN status_reason text;
