import type { FastifyInstance } from "fastify";
import { runReconciliation } from "../reconciliation";

export async function reconciliationRoutes(app: FastifyInstance) {
  app.post<{ Body: { date: string } }>(
    "/reconciliations",
    {
      schema: {
        body: {
          type: "object",
          required: ["date"],
          additionalProperties: false,
          properties: { date: { type: "string", format: "date" } },
        },
      },
    },
    async (request) => runReconciliation(request.body.date),
  );
}

Replace src/app.ts:

src/app.ts
import Fastify, { type FastifyError } from "fastify";
import { pool } from "./db";
import { AppError } from "./errors";
import { accountRoutes } from "./routes/accounts";
import {
  externalTransferRoutes,
  reviewRoutes,
} from "./routes/external-transfers";
import { transferRoutes } from "./routes/transfers";
import { reconciliationRoutes } from "./routes/reconciliations";
import { webhookRoutes } from "./routes/webhooks";

const API_KEY = process.env.API_KEY ?? "local-dev-key";

export function buildApp() {
  const app = Fastify({
    logger: true,
    ajv: {
      customOptions: {
        // Fastify's defaults quietly turn "2500" into 2500 and drop unknown
        // fields. For money we want strict: wrong types and extra fields fail.
        coerceTypes: false,
        removeAdditional: false,
      },
    },
  });

  // Every route needs the right x-api-key header, except the health check and
  // the partner's webhooks, which prove who sent them with a signature instead.
  app.addHook("onRequest", async (request, reply) => {
    const url = request.routeOptions.url;
    if (url === "/health" || url === "/webhooks/partner") return;
    if (request.headers["x-api-key"] !== API_KEY) {
      return reply
        .code(401)
        .send({ error: "unauthorized", message: "Missing or invalid API key" });
    }
  });

  app.get("/health", async (request, reply) => {
    try {
      await pool.query("SELECT 1");
      return { status: "ok", database: "up" };
    } catch (error) {
      request.log.error({ err: error }, "database health check failed");
      return reply.code(503).send({ status: "degraded", database: "down" });
    }
  });

  app.register(accountRoutes);
  app.register(transferRoutes);
  app.register(externalTransferRoutes);
  app.register(webhookRoutes);
  app.register(reviewRoutes);
  app.register(reconciliationRoutes);

  // Every error leaves the API in the same shape: { error, message }.
  app.setErrorHandler<FastifyError>((error, request, reply) => {
    if (error instanceof AppError) {
      return reply
        .code(error.statusCode)
        .send({ error: error.code, message: error.message });
    }
    if (error.validation) {
      return reply
        .code(400)
        .send({ error: "validation_error", message: error.message });
    }
    if (error.statusCode && error.statusCode < 500) {
      // Things like malformed JSON, which Fastify rejects before our code runs.
      return reply
        .code(error.statusCode)
        .send({ error: "bad_request", message: error.message });
    }
    request.log.error({ err: error }, "unhandled error");
    return reply
      .code(500)
      .send({ error: "internal_error", message: "Something went wrong" });
  });

  app.setNotFoundHandler((request, reply) => {
    reply.code(404).send({
      error: "route_not_found",
      message: `No route for ${request.method} ${request.url}`,
    });
  });

  return app;
}

Create src/reconciler/handler.ts, the same reconciliation as a Lambda:

src/reconciler/handler.ts
import type { S3Event } from "aws-lambda";
import { runReconciliation } from "../reconciliation";

// The same reconciliation, as a Lambda. With a bucket notification set up,
// S3 calls this whenever the bank drops settlements/<date>.csv in the bucket.
export async function handler(event: S3Event): Promise<void> {
  for (const record of event.Records) {
    const key = decodeURIComponent(record.s3.object.key.replace(/\+/g, " "));
    const match = /^settlements\/(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})\.csv$/.exec(key);
    if (match) await runReconciliation(match[1]);
  }
}

Queues ready: ledgerline-transfers, ledgerline-transfers-dlq and ledgerline-transfers-inspect
Table ready: ledgerline-idempotency-keys
Bucket ready: ledgerline-settlements

What the code does

  • settledPaymentsOn joins each payment to its settlement movement and picks the ones settled on that day, in UTC.
  • A missing file is a 404 and an unreadable one is a 422, so whoever runs the reconciliation knows which problem they have.
  • The report goes back to S3, next to the file it came from, where a finance team or another job can pick it up.
  • The Lambda handler runs the same function when S3 reports a new file. In a real deployment, a bucket notification would call it the moment the bank's file lands. The tests use the endpoint instead, which is faster and gives each test a direct answer. Wiring the notification up with the deploy pattern from Step 29 is a good stretch exercise.

Fail: the bucket step errors. MiniStack's S3 in Docker may answer differently from the one I ran. Send me the error.

Step 40: Test reconciliation

About two hours.

The tests need payments that have really settled, so each one creates payments, has the fake bank accept them, and sends settled webhooks. Then comes a problem: reconciliation covers a whole day, and every test runs today, in parallel. Each test would see everyone else's payments as missing from its file.

The fix is another test data shortcut. Each test picks its own made-up day, somewhere between the years 2100 and 2899, and moves its payments' settlement to that day in the database. With about 290,000 possible days, two tests almost never pick the same one.

Replace tests/framework/contract.ts:

tests/framework/contract.ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";
import Ajv2020 from "ajv/dist/2020";
import addFormats from "ajv-formats";
import { parse } from "yaml";

// Load openapi.yaml once and teach Ajv (a JSON Schema validator) about it.
const specPath = path.join(__dirname, "..", "..", "openapi.yaml");
const spec = parse(readFileSync(specPath, "utf8"));

// strict: false lets Ajv ignore OpenAPI-only keys like "paths" and "info".
const ajv = new Ajv2020({ allErrors: true, strict: false });
addFormats(ajv);
ajv.addSchema(spec, "openapi");

export type SchemaName =
  | "Account"
  | "Transfer"
  | "Error"
  | "HealthStatus"
  | "TransferRequestedMessage"
  | "WebhookResult"
  | "ReconciliationReport";

/** Throws a readable error if body doesn't match the named schema. */
export function assertMatchesContract(
  schemaName: SchemaName,
  body: unknown,
  context: string,
): void {
  const validate = ajv.getSchema(`openapi#/components/schemas/${schemaName}`);
  if (!validate) {
    throw new Error(`openapi.yaml has no schema called ${schemaName}`);
  }
  if (!validate(body)) {
    throw new Error(
      [
        `Contract violation: ${context}`,
        `Expected ${schemaName}: ${ajv.errorsText(validate.errors)}`,
        `Body: ${JSON.stringify(body, null, 2)}`,
      ].join("\n"),
    );
  }
}

Replace tests/framework/ledgerline-client.ts:

tests/framework/ledgerline-client.ts
import type { APIRequestContext, APIResponse } from "@playwright/test";
import { assertMatchesContract, type SchemaName } from "./contract";
import type {
  Account,
  HealthStatus,
  ReconciliationReport,
  Transfer,
  WebhookResult,
} from "./types";

export interface ApiResult<T> {
  status: number;
  body: T;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
}

export interface RequestOptions {
  idempotencyKey?: string;
}

function headersFor(options: RequestOptions): Record<string, string> {
  return options.idempotencyKey
    ? { "idempotency-key": options.idempotencyKey }
    : {};
}

// One method per endpoint. Tests talk to this class, never to raw URLs, so
// when an endpoint changes you fix it here once instead of in every test.
export class LedgerlineClient {
  constructor(private readonly request: APIRequestContext) {}

  health() {
    return this.send<HealthStatus>(
      this.request.get("/health"),
      "HealthStatus",
      "HealthStatus",
    );
  }

  createAccount(name: string) {
    return this.send<Account>(
      this.request.post("/accounts", { data: { name } }),
      "Account",
    );
  }

  getAccount(id: string) {
    return this.send<Account>(this.request.get(`/accounts/${id}`), "Account");
  }

  deposit(accountId: string, amountCents: unknown) {
    return this.send<Transfer>(
      this.request.post(`/accounts/${accountId}/deposits`, {
        data: { amountCents },
      }),
      "Transfer",
    );
  }

  // Takes a loose object on purpose, so negative tests can send bad input.
  createTransfer(data: Record<string, unknown>, options: RequestOptions = {}) {
    return this.send<Transfer>(
      this.request.post("/transfers", { data, headers: headersFor(options) }),
      "Transfer",
    );
  }

  // Pays a business at another bank. Answers 202: accepted, not finished.
  createExternalTransfer(
    data: Record<string, unknown>,
    options: RequestOptions = {},
  ) {
    return this.send<Transfer>(
      this.request.post("/transfers/external", {
        data,
        headers: headersFor(options),
      }),
      "Transfer",
    );
  }

  // Sends a webhook body exactly as given. It's a Buffer so Playwright doesn't
  // re-encode it: the signature covers these exact bytes.
  postPartnerEvent(rawBody: string, headers: Record<string, string>) {
    return this.send<WebhookResult>(
      this.request.post("/webhooks/partner", {
        data: Buffer.from(rawBody),
        headers: { "content-type": "application/json", ...headers },
      }),
      "WebhookResult",
    );
  }

  reviewTransfer(id: string, decision: "approve" | "decline") {
    return this.send<Transfer>(
      this.request.post(`/transfers/${id}/review`, { data: { decision } }),
      "Transfer",
    );
  }

  reconcile(date: string) {
    return this.send<ReconciliationReport>(
      this.request.post("/reconciliations", { data: { date } }),
      "ReconciliationReport",
    );
  }

  getTransfer(id: string) {
    return this.send<Transfer>(
      this.request.get(`/transfers/${id}`),
      "Transfer",
    );
  }

  async balanceOf(accountId: string): Promise<number> {
    const { status, body } = await this.getAccount(accountId);
    if (status !== 200) {
      throw new Error(`Couldn't read balance of ${accountId}: HTTP ${status}`);
    }
    return body.balanceCents;
  }

  // Every response is checked against openapi.yaml before a test sees it:
  // successes against their resource schema, failures against Error.
  private async send<T>(
    pending: Promise<APIResponse>,
    successSchema: SchemaName,
    errorSchema: SchemaName = "Error",
  ): Promise<ApiResult<T>> {
    const response = await pending;
    const status = response.status();
    const body = await response.json();
    const context = `${response.url()} returned ${status}`;
    assertMatchesContract(
      response.ok() ? successSchema : errorSchema,
      body,
      context,
    );
    return { status, body, headers: response.headers() };
  }
}

Replace tests/framework/db-helper.ts:

tests/framework/db-helper.ts
import { Pool } from "pg";

// Read-only questions tests ask the database directly. One instance per
// Playwright worker (see fixtures.ts), closed when the worker finishes.
export class DbHelper {
  private readonly pool = new Pool({
    connectionString:
      process.env.DATABASE_URL ??
      "postgres://ledgerline:ledgerline@localhost:5432/ledgerline",
    max: 2,
  });

  /** Transfers that don't have exactly two ledger entries summing to zero. */
  async unbalancedTransfers() {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(`
      SELECT t.id, COUNT(e.id) AS entries, COALESCE(SUM(e.amount_cents), 0) AS total
      FROM transfers t
      LEFT JOIN ledger_entries e ON e.transfer_id = t.id
      GROUP BY t.id
      HAVING COUNT(e.id) <> 2 OR COALESCE(SUM(e.amount_cents), 0) <> 0
    `);
    return rows;
  }

  /** Sum of every ledger entry ever written. Should always be "0". */
  async ledgerTotal(): Promise<string> {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(
      "SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_cents), 0)::text AS total FROM ledger_entries",
    );
    return rows[0].total;
  }

  /** Customer accounts whose balance has gone below zero. */
  async negativeCustomerBalances() {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(`
      SELECT a.id, SUM(e.amount_cents) AS balance
      FROM accounts a
      JOIN ledger_entries e ON e.account_id = a.id
      WHERE a.type = 'customer'
      GROUP BY a.id
      HAVING SUM(e.amount_cents) < 0
    `);
    return rows;
  }

  async countAccountsNamed(name: string): Promise<number> {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(
      "SELECT COUNT(*)::int AS count FROM accounts WHERE name = $1",
      [name],
    );
    return rows[0].count;
  }

  async countTransfersFrom(accountId: string): Promise<number> {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(
      "SELECT COUNT(*)::int AS count FROM transfers WHERE from_account_id = $1",
      [accountId],
    );
    return rows[0].count;
  }

  /** The kinds of money movement that followed a payment, oldest first. */
  async followUps(transferId: string): Promise<string[]> {
    const { rows } = await this.pool.query(
      "SELECT kind FROM transfers WHERE reverses_transfer_id = $1 OR settles_transfer_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at",
      [transferId],
    );
    return rows.map((row) => row.kind);
  }

  /** Makes an account look as if it was opened some days ago. */
  async backdateAccount(accountId: string, days: number): Promise<void> {
    await this.pool.query(
      "UPDATE accounts SET created_at = now() - make_interval(days => $2) WHERE id = $1",
      [accountId, days],
    );
  }

  /** Moves the settlement of these payments to midday UTC on a given date. */
  async settleOnDate(transferIds: string[], date: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.pool.query(
      `UPDATE transfers SET created_at = $2::date + interval '12 hours'
       WHERE kind = 'settlement' AND settles_transfer_id = ANY($1::uuid[])`,
      [transferIds, date],
    );
  }

  async close() {
    await this.pool.end();
  }
}

Create tests/framework/settlement-files.ts:

tests/framework/settlement-files.ts
import {
  GetObjectCommand,
  PutObjectCommand,
  S3Client,
} from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";

const BUCKET = process.env.SETTLEMENT_BUCKET ?? "ledgerline-settlements";

export interface FileLine {
  transferId: string;
  amountCents: number;
}

// Plays the bank's side of reconciliation: writes settlement files into the
// bucket, and reads back the reports Ledgerline writes.
export class SettlementFiles {
  private readonly s3 = new S3Client({
    region: process.env.AWS_REGION ?? "us-east-1",
    endpoint: process.env.AWS_ENDPOINT_URL ?? "http://localhost:4566",
    credentials: { accessKeyId: "test", secretAccessKey: "test" },
    forcePathStyle: true,
  });

  /** Uploads a settlement file, with amounts written in dollars, as banks do. */
  async upload(
    date: string,
    lines: FileLine[],
    header = "transfer_id,amount,settled_on",
  ) {
    const rows = lines.map(
      (line) =>
        `${line.transferId},${(line.amountCents / 100).toFixed(2)},${date}`,
    );
    await this.uploadRaw(date, [header, ...rows].join("\n"));
  }

  async uploadRaw(date: string, body: string) {
    await this.s3.send(
      new PutObjectCommand({
        Bucket: BUCKET,
        Key: `settlements/${date}.csv`,
        Body: body,
        ContentType: "text/csv",
      }),
    );
  }

  async readReport(date: string): Promise<Record<string, unknown>> {
    const result = await this.s3.send(
      new GetObjectCommand({ Bucket: BUCKET, Key: `reports/${date}.json` }),
    );
    return JSON.parse((await result.Body?.transformToString()) ?? "{}");
  }
}

Create tests/api/reconciliation.spec.ts:

tests/api/reconciliation.spec.ts
import { randomInt, randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { expectApiError } from "../framework/assertions";
import type { AccountBuilder } from "../framework/account-builder";
import type { DbHelper } from "../framework/db-helper";
import type { FakePartner } from "../framework/fake-partner";
import { expect, test } from "../framework/fixtures";
import type { LedgerlineClient } from "../framework/ledgerline-client";
import type { PartnerWebhooks } from "../framework/partner-webhooks";
import { SettlementFiles } from "../framework/settlement-files";

const files = new SettlementFiles();

// Each test reconciles its own made-up day, far in the future, so parallel
// tests never see each other's payments.
function uniqueDate(): string {
  const year = 2100 + randomInt(800);
  const month = String(1 + randomInt(12)).padStart(2, "0");
  const day = String(1 + randomInt(28)).padStart(2, "0");
  return `${year}-${month}-${day}`;
}

// Makes payments, has the bank accept and settle them, then files their
// settlement under the test's own day.
async function settledPayments(
  amounts: number[],
  date: string,
  deps: {
    api: LedgerlineClient;
    newAccount: () => AccountBuilder;
    partner: FakePartner;
    webhooks: PartnerWebhooks;
    db: DbHelper;
  },
) {
  const { api, newAccount, partner, webhooks, db } = deps;
  await partner.accepts();
  const from = await newAccount().withBalance(100_000).create();
  const ids: string[] = [];
  for (const amountCents of amounts) {
    const { body } = await api.createExternalTransfer({
      fromAccountId: from.id,
      amountCents,
      counterparty: partner.counterparty,
    });
    ids.push(body.id);
  }
  for (const id of ids) {
    await expect
      .poll(async () => (await api.getTransfer(id)).body.status)
      .toBe("submitted");
    await webhooks.send(webhooks.settled(id));
  }
  await db.settleOnDate(ids, date);
  return ids;
}

test.describe("reconciliation", () => {
  test("a file that matches the ledger has no breaks", async ({
    api,
    newAccount,
    partner,
    webhooks,
    db,
  }) => {
    const deps = { api, newAccount, partner, webhooks, db };
    const date = uniqueDate();
    const [a, b, c] = await settledPayments([2_500, 100, 9_999], date, deps);
    await files.upload(date, [
      { transferId: a, amountCents: 2_500 },
      { transferId: b, amountCents: 100 },
      { transferId: c, amountCents: 9_999 },
    ]);

    const { status, body } = await api.reconcile(date);

    expect(status).toBe(200);
    expect(body).toMatchObject({ date, matched: 3, breaks: [] });
  });

  test("every kind of break is found", async ({
    api,
    newAccount,
    partner,
    webhooks,
    db,
  }) => {
    const deps = { api, newAccount, partner, webhooks, db };
    const date = uniqueDate();
    const [ok, wrong, twice, missing] = await settledPayments(
      [100, 7_550, 1_999, 30_000],
      date,
      deps,
    );
    const stranger = randomUUID();
    await files.upload(date, [
      { transferId: ok, amountCents: 100 },
      { transferId: wrong, amountCents: 7_505 },
      { transferId: twice, amountCents: 1_999 },
      { transferId: twice, amountCents: 1_999 },
      { transferId: stranger, amountCents: 50_000 },
    ]);

    const { body } = await api.reconcile(date);

    expect(body.matched).toBe(2);
    expect(body.breaks.map((b) => [b.type, b.transferId]).sort()).toEqual(
      [
        ["amount_mismatch", wrong],
        ["duplicate_at_bank", twice],
        ["missing_at_bank", missing],
        ["unknown_to_ledger", stranger],
      ].sort(),
    );
    const mismatch = body.breaks.find((b) => b.type === "amount_mismatch");
    expect(mismatch).toMatchObject({
      ledgerAmountCents: 7_550,
      bankAmountCents: 7_505,
    });
  });

  test("the report is written back to the bucket", async ({
    api,
    newAccount,
    partner,
    webhooks,
    db,
  }) => {
    const deps = { api, newAccount, partner, webhooks, db };
    const date = uniqueDate();
    const [a] = await settledPayments([2_500], date, deps);
    await files.upload(date, [{ transferId: a, amountCents: 2_500 }]);

    const { body } = await api.reconcile(date);

    expect(await files.readReport(date)).toEqual(body);
  });

  test("a day with no file returns 404", async ({ api }) => {
    expectApiError(await api.reconcile(uniqueDate()), 404, "file_not_found");
  });

  test("a file with the wrong header is refused", async ({ api }) => {
    const date = uniqueDate();
    await files.uploadRaw(date, "id,amount\nabc,1.00");

    expectApiError(await api.reconcile(date), 422, "invalid_settlement_file");
  });
});

81 passed.

What the tests prove

  • A clean file has no breaks.
  • Every kind of break is found at once: a wrong amount, a duplicate, a payment missing from the file, and one the ledger never heard of. The unit tests prove the logic; this test proves the whole path: S3, Postgres, the endpoint and the report.
  • The report written to S3 is exactly the response, read back from the bucket.
  • A missing file and a malformed file each get their own clear error.

Found while testing this guide

Two things broke the first time I ran these tests.

My first version passed the fixtures as one object, async (deps) => ..., and every test failed with Cannot read properties of undefined. Playwright reads the names inside the braces, async ({ api, partner }) => ..., to decide which fixtures to build. Without the braces, it builds none.

The second was sneakier: an old webhook test failed, waiting for a payment to become submitted. With these tests adding more payments, the processor's queue was busier, and expect.poll's default of 5 seconds wasn't enough. The fix is the expect: { timeout: 15_000 } line in the config. A timeout that's fine for one test can be too tight for a busy suite. That's the most common cause of flaky tests, and Week 9 is about exactly that.

Step 41: README and CI

About 20 minutes.

CI needs no changes: S3 runs inside MiniStack, and npm run aws:setup creates the bucket. Replace README.md:

README.md
# Ledgerline

A small business-banking backend, and the automated test framework around it.
Built to practise how fintech teams test money movement: ledgers, contracts,
concurrency and CI.

## Run it

You need Docker Desktop and Node 24.

```bash
npm install
npm run db:up        # start Postgres, MiniStack, WireMock and Redis in Docker
npm run db:migrate   # create the tables
npm run aws:setup    # create the queues in MiniStack
npm test             # unit tests, then API tests (the API starts automatically)
```

Run the API on its own with `npm run dev`, then try `curl localhost:3000/health`.

## How the tests are organised

```
tests/
  unit/        Vitest. Pure functions, no network or database.
  api/         Playwright specs. Each file covers one feature.
  framework/   The plumbing specs are built on:
    fixtures.ts           api, newAccount, apiWithKey, db
    ledgerline-client.ts  one method per endpoint
    contract.ts           checks every response against openapi.yaml
    account-builder.ts    newAccount().withBalance(5000).create()
    db-helper.ts          ledger integrity queries
    queue-helper.ts       reads and writes queues in MiniStack
    fake-partner.ts       programs WireMock to act as the partner bank
    partner-webhooks.ts   sends signed webhooks, as the partner bank would
    settlement-files.ts   drops the bank's settlement files into S3
    assertions.ts         expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds")
bruno/         Bruno collection for exploring the API by hand
infra/wiremock/  the fake partner bank's default stubs
src/processor/   the Lambda that sends payments to the partner bank
openapi.yaml   The API contract
```

## Add a test

1. Pick the spec file for the feature, or create `tests/api/<feature>.spec.ts`.
2. Import `{ test, expect }` from `../framework/fixtures`.
3. Set up data with `newAccount()`, act with `api`, assert on the result.

```ts
test("rejects a transfer over the balance", async ({ api, newAccount }) => {
  const from = await newAccount().withBalance(1_000).create();
  const to = await newAccount().create();

  const result = await api.createTransfer({
    fromAccountId: from.id,
    toAccountId: to.id,
    amountCents: 1_001,
  });

  expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds");
});
```

Every test creates its own accounts, so tests run in parallel and in any order.

Week 8 wrap-up

  • Teach it back. Explain the four kinds of break, and what a finance team does about each one.
  • Dev log. Write up how each test got its own day, and why reconciliation over "today" couldn't work for parallel tests.
  • The interview line. "I built daily reconciliation between the ledger and the bank's settlement files in S3, as a pure matching function tested at 100,000 rows, with end-to-end tests that seed every kind of break."

Phase 4 starts with Week 9: making CI fast, parallel and trustworthy.

Week 9: CI people trust

Phase 4 is about trust: a pipeline that's fast, that people believe, and that makes writing tests easy. You'll add one-command setup and a test generator, write a flaky-test policy, split the suite across two machines with a merged report and a summary on every run, and add a nightly job that hunts flaky tests. Building and improving CI is the centre of the Relay role, so this week is the one to talk about in interviews. Chapter 5 of the field guide covers pipeline basics.

Step 42: One command to set up, one to check, one to start a test

About 45 minutes.

A test framework people actually use is one where the right thing is the easy thing. Three new scripts make that true: npm run setup starts everything and prepares it, npm run check runs everything CI checks, and npm run new:test creates a new spec file already wired to the framework.

Create scripts/new-test.ts:

scripts/new-test.ts
import { existsSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";

// Creates a new API spec, already wired to the framework, so starting a test
// takes one command. Usage: npm run new:test -- "monthly statements"
const title = process.argv.slice(2).join(" ").trim();
if (!title) {
  console.error('Name the feature: npm run new:test -- "monthly statements"');
  process.exit(1);
}

const slug = title
  .toLowerCase()
  .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-")
  .replace(/^-|-$/g, "");
const file = path.join("tests", "api", `${slug}.spec.ts`);
if (existsSync(file)) {
  console.error(`${file} already exists`);
  process.exit(1);
}

writeFileSync(
  file,
  `import { expect, test } from "../framework/fixtures";

test.describe(${JSON.stringify(title)}, () => {
  // fixme: listed in the report as a test to write, but skipped for now.
  test.fixme("describe the behaviour", async ({ api, newAccount }) => {
    const account = await newAccount().withBalance(10_000).create();

    const result = await api.getAccount(account.id);

    expect(result.status).toBe(200);
  });
});
`,
);
console.log(`Created ${file}`);

npm pkg set scripts.setup="docker compose up -d --wait && npm run db:migrate && npm run aws:setup" scripts.check="npm run typecheck && npm run lint && npm run format:check && npm test" scripts.new:test="tsx scripts/new-test.ts"
npm run new:test -- "Monthly statements"
npx playwright test tests/api/monthly-statements.spec.ts

Created tests/api/monthly-statements.spec.ts
  1 skipped

The new file is already formatted, lints cleanly, and imports the framework's fixtures. test.fixme means the test shows up in the report as one to write, but is skipped, so the suite stays green until someone fills it in. Delete the example when you've looked at it: rm tests/api/monthly-statements.spec.ts.

What the code does

  • The slug turns "Monthly statements" into monthly-statements.spec.ts, so file names stay consistent.
  • The script refuses to overwrite an existing file, and explains itself when you forget the name.
  • setup and check mean a new developer runs two commands instead of reading a page of instructions. That's what "improving developer experience" means in a QA job description.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 42: Setup, check and new:test".

Step 43: A policy for flaky tests

About 30 minutes.

What, why and how: Flaky tests

What it is. A flaky test passes and fails without any change to the code. Run it ten times and it fails once or twice, for reasons that have nothing to do with a bug in the product.

Why we use it. Flaky tests destroy trust. Once people expect random red runs, they stop reading failures, and real bugs get through alongside the noise. Relay measures test flakiness directly, as one of the numbers its QA engineers are judged on.

How we use it. Retries stay off, so flakes are visible instead of hidden. A nightly workflow runs the whole suite three times to catch the rare ones. A short written policy says what the team does when one appears: report it, quarantine it with test.fixme (never delete it), fix the cause, and prove the fix with --repeat-each 20.

How it works inside. Almost every flaky test comes down to one of three causes: timing (a wait that's usually, but not always, long enough), shared state (tests touching the same data, queue or counter), or order (a test relying on another having run first). Each has a matching cure: poll for conditions instead of waiting a fixed time, give every test its own data, and make every test set up everything it needs.

A flaky-test policy is a short agreement a team makes before the first flake, so nobody argues in the middle of a red build. Create docs/flaky-tests.md:

docs/flaky-tests.md
# Flaky tests

A flaky test passes and fails without any change to the code. It's worse than
no test at all: people learn to ignore red runs, and real failures slip
through with them.

## How we find them

- The nightly workflow runs the whole API suite three times over.
- Retries are off (`retries: 0`), so a flaky test fails where everyone can see
  it instead of quietly passing on a second try.

## What we do when one flakes

1. Open an issue with a link to the failing run and the test's name.
2. If it's blocking other people, mark it `test.fixme` with the issue link in a
   comment. Never delete it.
3. Fix the cause, not the symptom. Most flakes come from one of these:
   - a timeout that's too tight for a busy machine;
   - tests sharing data, or a queue, with each other;
   - waiting with fixed sleeps instead of polling for a condition;
   - depending on the order tests run in.
4. Remove the `fixme` once the test passes 20 repeats in a row:
   `npx playwright test -g "the test's name" --repeat-each 20`.

## What we don't do

- Turn retries on to make the run green. That hides the problem instead of
  fixing it.

Every cause on that list is one you've already met in this project. The tight timeout was Week 8. The shared-data rule is why every test makes its own accounts. The race conditions were Weeks 2 and 7.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 43: Flaky-test policy".

Step 44: A staged, sharded pipeline

About two hours.

What, why and how: Jobs, matrices and sharding

What it is. A GitHub Actions workflow can hold several jobs, each running on its own fresh machine. needs puts them in order, and a matrix runs the same job several times with different values. Sharding splits a test suite into parts that run on different machines at the same time: Playwright's --shard=1/2 runs the first half.

Why we use it. As a suite grows, one machine running everything becomes the bottleneck. Two machines each running half finish in about half the time. And putting cheap checks in their own first job means a simple mistake fails in a minute, before any expensive job starts. Relay measures test duration too.

How we use it. The checks job runs types, lint, formatting and unit tests. api-tests runs twice, as shards 1 and 2, each with its own Postgres, MiniStack, Redis and WireMock. Each shard saves a blob report, Playwright's raw results. The report job downloads both, merges them into one HTML report and one JUnit XML file, and writes a summary onto the run's page.

How it works inside. Playwright shards by splitting the list of tests into equal-sized groups, by count, not by how long each test takes. If the slow tests land together, one shard finishes long after the others. Every shard also pays the full setup cost: a new machine, npm ci, and starting every service, so beyond a point, adding shards saves very little. A blob report is a zip of one shard's raw results, and merge-reports combines them into one report, as if everything had run on one machine. Compare one machine with several:

The pipeline becomes three jobs: - checks runs the cheap checks, with no services, so a formatting slip fails in about a minute. - api-tests runs twice at once, as shards 1 and 2, each on its own machine with its own services. - report merges the two halves into one HTML report and writes a summary onto the run's page.

Create scripts/ci-summary.ts:

scripts/ci-summary.ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

// Turns Playwright's JUnit XML into a short Markdown summary, which CI adds
// to the run's page. Usage: npm run ci:summary -- results.xml
const file = process.argv[2] ?? "results.xml";
const xml = readFileSync(file, "utf8");

const decode = (text: string) =>
  text
    .replace(/&quot;/g, '"')
    .replace(/&apos;|&#39;/g, "'")
    .replace(/&lt;/g, "<")
    .replace(/&gt;/g, ">")
    .replace(/&amp;/g, "&");

const attr = (tag: string, name: string) =>
  decode(new RegExp(`\\b${name}="([^"]*)"`).exec(tag)?.[1] ?? "");

const suites = /<testsuites\b[^>]*>/.exec(xml)?.[0] ?? "";
const total = Number(attr(suites, "tests"));
const failed =
  Number(attr(suites, "failures")) + Number(attr(suites, "errors") || 0);
const skipped = Number(attr(suites, "skipped"));
const seconds = Number(attr(suites, "time"));

const cases = [
  ...xml.matchAll(/<testcase\b([^>]*?)(?:\/>|>([\s\S]*?)<\/testcase>)/g),
].map((match) => ({
  name: attr(match[1], "name"),
  seconds: Number(attr(match[1], "time")),
  failed: /<failure\b/.test(match[2] ?? ""),
}));

const lines = [
  "## API tests",
  "",
  `**${total - failed - skipped} passed**, ${failed} failed, ${skipped} skipped, in ${seconds.toFixed(1)} seconds.`,
  "",
  "### Slowest tests",
  "",
  "| Test | Seconds |",
  "| --- | ---: |",
  ...[...cases]
    .sort((a, b) => b.seconds - a.seconds)
    .slice(0, 5)
    .map((c) => `| ${c.name} | ${c.seconds.toFixed(1)} |`),
];

const failures = cases.filter((c) => c.failed);
if (failures.length > 0) {
  lines.push("", "### Failures", "", ...failures.map((c) => `- ${c.name}`));
}

console.log(lines.join("\n"));

Replace .github/workflows/ci.yml:

.github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  # Fast checks first. No services, so a mistake fails in about a minute.
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run format:check
      - run: npm run test:unit

  # The API suite, split across two machines that each run half of it.
  api-tests:
    needs: checks
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2]

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_DB: ledgerline
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U ledgerline -d ledgerline"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10
      ministack:
        image: ministackorg/ministack:latest
        ports:
          - 4566:4566
      redis:
        image: redis:7
        ports:
          - 6379:6379
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci

      # Started here rather than under services, because it needs the stub
      # files from the checked-out repository.
      - name: Start the fake partner bank
        run: |
          docker run -d --name wiremock -p 8080:8080 -v "$PWD/infra/wiremock:/home/wiremock" wiremock/wiremock:3.13.2
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -sf http://localhost:8080/__admin/mappings > /dev/null && break; sleep 1; done

      - run: npm run db:migrate
      - run: npm run aws:setup

      - name: Run shard ${{ matrix.shard }} of 2
        run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/2 --reporter=blob

      - name: Run the Bruno collection
        if: matrix.shard == 1
        run: |
          npm run start &
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -sf http://localhost:3000/health && break; sleep 1; done
          npm run test:bruno

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: blob-report-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: blob-report/
          retention-days: 3

  # Joins both halves into one HTML report, and writes a summary on the run.
  report:
    needs: api-tests
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci

      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          pattern: blob-report-*
          path: all-blob-reports
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Merge the reports
        run: npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html,junit ./all-blob-reports
        env:
          PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME: results.xml

      - name: Write the summary
        run: npm run --silent ci:summary -- results.xml >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 14

Add the summary script, and keep the new report files out of Git: 

npm pkg set scripts.ci:summary="tsx scripts/ci-summary.ts"
printf "blob-report/\nall-blob-reports/\nresults.xml\n" >> .gitignore

Run the pipeline's test half on your machine

You can do exactly what the two shards and the report job do, one after the other: 

rm -rf blob-report all-blob-reports && mkdir all-blob-reports
CI=true npx playwright test --shard=1/2 --reporter=blob && mv blob-report/*.zip all-blob-reports/
CI=true npx playwright test --shard=2/2 --reporter=blob && mv blob-report/*.zip all-blob-reports/
PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME=results.xml npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html,junit ./all-blob-reports
npm run --silent ci:summary -- results.xml

## API tests

**81 passed**, 0 failed, 0 skipped, in 46.6 seconds.

### Slowest tests

| Test | Seconds |
| --- | ---: |
| the payment processor › parks an unreadable message in the dead-letter queue | 12.2 |
| the payment processor › gives up after three failures, returns the money, and parks the message | 7.0 |

Your times will differ. npx playwright show-report opens the merged HTML report, with both halves in one place.

What the pipeline does

  • needs: checks means the expensive job only starts once the cheap one has passed.
  • matrix: shard: [1, 2] runs api-tests twice, with matrix.shard set to 1, then 2. fail-fast: false lets both halves finish even if one fails, so you see every failure in one run.
  • --shard=1/2 runs the first half of the tests. Playwright splits by test, and keeps serial groups together.
  • --reporter=blob saves raw results instead of a finished report, so the halves can be joined later.
  • The report job runs with if: always(), even when tests fail, which is exactly when you need it. merge-reports builds one HTML report and one JUnit XML file from both halves.
  • $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY is a file GitHub shows on the run's page. The summary script turns the JUnit XML into Markdown: totals, and the five slowest tests, which are where to look first when the suite gets slow.
  • The Bruno collection runs on shard 1 only, because once is enough.

Verify on your machine

Push, and open the run in the Actions tab.

Pass: three jobs, checks, then two api-tests in parallel, then report, all green. The run's page shows the summary table, and the artifacts include one playwright-report with every test in it.

Fail: the report job can't find any blob reports. Check the upload-artifact step in each shard uploaded blob-report-1 and blob-report-2, and that the names match the pattern in the report job.

Fail: one shard fails and the other passes. That's sharding doing its job: the failure is real. Open the merged report to see it.

Step 45: The nightly flaky-test hunt

About 30 minutes.

A test that fails one run in fifty won't show up on a normal push. Running the whole suite three times every night catches those, before they start interrupting people's days.

Create .github/workflows/nightly.yml:

.github/workflows/nightly.yml
name: Nightly flaky-test hunt

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *" # every day at 06:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch: # and whenever you press "Run workflow"

jobs:
  repeat:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_DB: ledgerline
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U ledgerline -d ledgerline"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10
      ministack:
        image: ministackorg/ministack:latest
        ports:
          - 4566:4566
      redis:
        image: redis:7
        ports:
          - 6379:6379

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Start the fake partner bank
        run: |
          docker run -d --name wiremock -p 8080:8080 -v "$PWD/infra/wiremock:/home/wiremock" wiremock/wiremock:3.13.2
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -sf http://localhost:8080/__admin/mappings > /dev/null && break; sleep 1; done
      - run: npm run db:migrate
      - run: npm run aws:setup

      # Every test three times. A test that fails even once here is flaky.
      - name: Run the suite three times
        run: npx playwright test --repeat-each 3 --reporter=list,junit
        env:
          PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME: results.xml

      - name: Write the summary
        if: always()
        run: npm run --silent ci:summary -- results.xml >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

README.md
# Ledgerline

A small business-banking backend, and the automated test framework around it.
Built to practise how fintech teams test money movement: ledgers, contracts,
concurrency and CI.

## Run it

You need Docker Desktop and Node 24.

```bash
npm install
npm run setup        # start Postgres, MiniStack, WireMock and Redis, then create
                     # the tables, queues, table and bucket they need
npm run check        # everything CI checks: types, lint, formatting and tests
```

Start a new test file with `npm run new:test -- "feature name"`. When a test
flakes, follow [docs/flaky-tests.md](docs/flaky-tests.md).

Run the API on its own with `npm run dev`, then try `curl localhost:3000/health`.

## How the tests are organised

```
tests/
  unit/        Vitest. Pure functions, no network or database.
  api/         Playwright specs. Each file covers one feature.
  framework/   The plumbing specs are built on:
    fixtures.ts           api, newAccount, apiWithKey, db
    ledgerline-client.ts  one method per endpoint
    contract.ts           checks every response against openapi.yaml
    account-builder.ts    newAccount().withBalance(5000).create()
    db-helper.ts          ledger integrity queries
    queue-helper.ts       reads and writes queues in MiniStack
    fake-partner.ts       programs WireMock to act as the partner bank
    partner-webhooks.ts   sends signed webhooks, as the partner bank would
    settlement-files.ts   drops the bank's settlement files into S3
    assertions.ts         expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds")
bruno/         Bruno collection for exploring the API by hand
infra/wiremock/  the fake partner bank's default stubs
src/processor/   the Lambda that sends payments to the partner bank
openapi.yaml   The API contract
```

## Add a test

1. Pick the spec file for the feature, or create `tests/api/<feature>.spec.ts`.
2. Import `{ test, expect }` from `../framework/fixtures`.
3. Set up data with `newAccount()`, act with `api`, assert on the result.

```ts
test("rejects a transfer over the balance", async ({ api, newAccount }) => {
  const from = await newAccount().withBalance(1_000).create();
  const to = await newAccount().create();

  const result = await api.createTransfer({
    fromAccountId: from.id,
    toAccountId: to.id,
    amountCents: 1_001,
  });

  expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds");
});
```

Every test creates its own accounts, so tests run in parallel and in any order.

Week 10 is observability: following one payment through every log, and turning test results into a quality dashboard.

Week 10: Observability and the quality story

When a payment test fails, "expected submitted, received pending" tells you what went wrong but not why. This week you'll make every request carry a correlation id, send the logs from every service somewhere a test can read them, and attach the relevant lines to any failing test automatically. Then you'll turn repeated runs into a quality dashboard, and use it to catch a real race condition that had been hiding in the processor since Week 5. Chapter 21 of the field guide covers the ideas.

Step 46: Correlation ids

About an hour.

What, why and how: Logs, traces and correlation ids

What it is. Observability is being able to tell what a running system is doing from the outside. Logs record what happened, one line per event. Metrics count how often and how fast. Traces show where the time went as one request crosses several services. A correlation id is the thread that ties them together: one id attached to a request, and carried everywhere that request goes.

Why we use it. A payment in Ledgerline crosses the API, a queue, the processor and a fake bank. When it fails, the question is always "what happened to this one payment?", and without a shared id the answer is buried among thousands of lines from everything else. Relay's posting asks for engineers who debug from logs and traces.

How we use it. Every request gets a correlation id. It appears in every API log line, comes back in the x-correlation-id response header, and travels in the queue message to the processor, which logs it too. In a company, these logs would flow into a tool like Datadog or Sentry, which search on exactly the same ids. Those tools need accounts, so this project stops at log files, but the idea is identical. Chapter 21 of the field guide lets you filter a log stream by id.

How it works inside. A structured log line is a JSON object rather than a sentence, so tools can filter on any field: correlationId, the level, the route. A trace goes further. Each step of a request becomes a span, with a start time, a duration, and the id of the span that caused it, which lets a tool draw the whole request as a timeline across services. OpenTelemetry is the standard way to create spans, and tools like Datadog display them. Ledgerline builds the part that makes all of that possible: one id, passed along everywhere. Follow one transfer through a shared log stream:

The API now gives every request a correlation id. If the caller sends a safe x-correlation-id header, that's the id; otherwise the API makes a new one. It appears in every log line for the request, comes back in the response's headers, and, for a payment, travels in the queue message to the processor.

Replace src/app.ts:

src/app.ts
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import Fastify, { type FastifyError } from "fastify";
import { pool } from "./db";
import { AppError } from "./errors";
import { accountRoutes } from "./routes/accounts";
import {
  externalTransferRoutes,
  reviewRoutes,
} from "./routes/external-transfers";
import { transferRoutes } from "./routes/transfers";
import { reconciliationRoutes } from "./routes/reconciliations";
import { webhookRoutes } from "./routes/webhooks";

const API_KEY = process.env.API_KEY ?? "local-dev-key";

// Letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores only. Anything else could be
// used to forge extra lines in the logs, so it's replaced.
const SAFE_ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,100}$/;

export function buildApp() {
  const app = Fastify({
    // With LOG_FILE set (the tests set it), logs go to that file.
    logger: process.env.LOG_FILE ? { file: process.env.LOG_FILE } : true,
    // Every request gets a correlation id: the caller's, if it sent a safe
    // one, or a new one. It's the request's id in every log line.
    genReqId: (request) => {
      const sent = request.headers["x-correlation-id"];
      return typeof sent === "string" && SAFE_ID.test(sent)
        ? sent
        : randomUUID();
    },
    requestIdLogLabel: "correlationId",
    ajv: {
      customOptions: {
        // Fastify's defaults quietly turn "2500" into 2500 and drop unknown
        // fields. For money we want strict: wrong types and extra fields fail.
        coerceTypes: false,
        removeAdditional: false,
      },
    },
  });

  // Every route needs the right x-api-key header, except the health check and
  // the partner's webhooks, which prove who sent them with a signature instead.
  app.addHook("onRequest", async (request, reply) => {
    const url = request.routeOptions.url;
    if (url === "/health" || url === "/webhooks/partner") return;
    if (request.headers["x-api-key"] !== API_KEY) {
      return reply
        .code(401)
        .send({ error: "unauthorized", message: "Missing or invalid API key" });
    }
  });

  // Every response says which correlation id to search the logs for.
  app.addHook("onSend", async (request, reply) => {
    reply.header("x-correlation-id", request.id);
  });

  app.get("/health", async (request, reply) => {
    try {
      await pool.query("SELECT 1");
      return { status: "ok", database: "up" };
    } catch (error) {
      request.log.error({ err: error }, "database health check failed");
      return reply.code(503).send({ status: "degraded", database: "down" });
    }
  });

  app.register(accountRoutes);
  app.register(transferRoutes);
  app.register(externalTransferRoutes);
  app.register(webhookRoutes);
  app.register(reviewRoutes);
  app.register(reconciliationRoutes);

  // Every error leaves the API in the same shape: { error, message }.
  app.setErrorHandler<FastifyError>((error, request, reply) => {
    if (error instanceof AppError) {
      return reply
        .code(error.statusCode)
        .send({ error: error.code, message: error.message });
    }
    if (error.validation) {
      return reply
        .code(400)
        .send({ error: "validation_error", message: error.message });
    }
    if (error.statusCode && error.statusCode < 500) {
      // Things like malformed JSON, which Fastify rejects before our code runs.
      return reply
        .code(error.statusCode)
        .send({ error: "bad_request", message: error.message });
    }
    request.log.error({ err: error }, "unhandled error");
    return reply
      .code(500)
      .send({ error: "internal_error", message: "Something went wrong" });
  });

  app.setNotFoundHandler((request, reply) => {
    reply.code(404).send({
      error: "route_not_found",
      message: `No route for ${request.method} ${request.url}`,
    });
  });

  return app;
}

Replace src/routes/external-transfers.ts, where a payment now uses the request's id instead of making its own:

src/routes/external-transfers.ts
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import type { FastifyInstance, FastifyRequest } from "fastify";
import { AppError } from "../errors";
import { idempotent } from "../idempotency";
import {
  accountAgeDays,
  CLEARING_ACCOUNT_ID,
  moveMoney,
  reviewPayment,
  type Counterparty,
  type Transfer,
} from "../ledger";
import { publishTransferRequested } from "../queue";
import { checkPayment, releasePayment } from "../risk-check";
import { amountCents, idParams } from "./schemas";

interface ExternalTransferBody {
  fromAccountId: string;
  amountCents: number;
  counterparty: Counterparty;
}

export async function externalTransferRoutes(app: FastifyInstance) {
  app.post<{ Body: ExternalTransferBody }>(
    "/transfers/external",
    {
      schema: {
        body: {
          type: "object",
          required: ["fromAccountId", "amountCents", "counterparty"],
          additionalProperties: false,
          properties: {
            fromAccountId: { type: "string", format: "uuid" },
            amountCents,
            counterparty: {
              type: "object",
              required: ["name", "routingNumber", "accountNumber"],
              additionalProperties: false,
              properties: {
                name: { type: "string", minLength: 1, maxLength: 100 },
                routingNumber: { type: "string", pattern: "^[0-9]{9}$" },
                accountNumber: { type: "string", pattern: "^[0-9]{4,17}$" },
              },
            },
          },
        },
      },
    },
    async (request, reply) =>
      idempotent(request, reply, async () => {
        // One id that follows this payment through every log and message.
        // The request's own correlation id follows the payment everywhere.
        const correlationId = request.id;
        const { fromAccountId, counterparty } = request.body;

        // Risk first. A held payment still reserves the money, but isn't
        // published, so it can't reach the bank until a person approves it.
        const amount = request.body.amountCents;
        const risk = await checkPayment(
          fromAccountId,
          amount,
          (await accountAgeDays(fromAccountId)) ?? 0,
        );
        const held = risk.decision === "review";

        let transfer;
        try {
          transfer = await moveMoney({
            kind: "external",
            fromAccountId,
            toAccountId: CLEARING_ACCOUNT_ID,
            amountCents: amount,
            status: held ? "in_review" : "pending",
            statusReason: held ? risk.reason : undefined,
            counterparty,
            // Publish before COMMIT. If the queue is down, the transfer rolls
            // back, so there's never a pending payment nobody will process.
            beforeCommit: held
              ? undefined
              : (saved) => publish(saved, counterparty, correlationId, request),
          });
        } catch (error) {
          // It didn't go ahead, so it mustn't count towards today's limit.
          if (!held) await releasePayment(fromAccountId, amount);
          throw error;
        }

        request.log.info(
          { transferId: transfer.id, correlationId },
          "external transfer accepted",
        );
        return { statusCode: 202, body: transfer };
      }),
  );
}

// Puts the payment on the queue for the processor. Used when a payment is
// accepted, and again when a reviewer approves a held one.
async function publish(
  transfer: Transfer,
  counterparty: Counterparty,
  correlationId: string,
  request: FastifyRequest,
) {
  try {
    await publishTransferRequested({
      version: 1,
      type: "transfer.requested",
      transferId: transfer.id,
      correlationId,
      amountCents: transfer.amountCents,
      counterparty,
    });
  } catch (error) {
    request.log.error(
      { err: error, correlationId },
      "could not publish the transfer message",
    );
    throw new AppError(
      503,
      "queue_unavailable",
      "Payments to other banks are unavailable right now. Nothing was sent.",
    );
  }
}

export async function reviewRoutes(app: FastifyInstance) {
  app.post<{
    Params: { id: string };
    Body: { decision: "approve" | "decline" };
  }>(
    "/transfers/:id/review",
    {
      schema: {
        params: idParams,
        body: {
          type: "object",
          required: ["decision"],
          additionalProperties: false,
          properties: { decision: { enum: ["approve", "decline"] } },
        },
      },
    },
    async (request) =>
      reviewPayment(
        request.params.id,
        request.body.decision,
        (transfer, counterparty) =>
          publish(transfer, counterparty, randomUUID(), request),
      ),
  );
}

npm run typecheck

With npm run dev running, send your own id and a hostile one: 

curl -s -o /dev/null -D - -H 'x-correlation-id: my-first-id' localhost:3000/health | grep -i correlation
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - -H 'x-correlation-id: fake" level="error' localhost:3000/health | grep -i correlation

The first answers with my-first-id. The second gets a fresh UUID, because its id contains characters that could forge extra fields in a log line.

What the code does

  • genReqId decides each request's id. Fastify then puts it in every log line, under the label set by requestIdLogLabel.
  • SAFE_ID allows only letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores. Accepting anything a caller sends and writing it into logs is called log injection, and it's a real security finding.
  • The onSend hook adds the id to every response, errors included, so whoever called can quote it in a bug report.
  • logger: { file } writes logs to a file instead of the terminal when LOG_FILE is set. The tests set it in the next step.

Step 47: Logs every test can find

About two hours.

Every test's requests now carry the test's own correlation id. The API and the processor write their logs to files when Playwright starts them. And when a test fails, a fixture collects every log line carrying that test's id, from both services, and attaches it to the report, right next to the failure.

Replace src/processor/handler.ts, whose log function can now write to a file. It also has a fix you'll meet in Step 48:

src/processor/handler.ts
import { appendFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs";
import type { SQSBatchResponse, SQSEvent, SQSRecord } from "aws-lambda";
import { findTransferStatus, recordPartnerOutcome } from "../ledger";
import { sqs, TRANSFERS_QUEUE, type TransferRequestedMessage } from "../queue";
import { originatePayment } from "./partner";

// Must match maxReceiveCount in scripts/aws-setup.ts.
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = Number(process.env.MAX_ATTEMPTS ?? 3);
const RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS = Number(process.env.RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS ?? 2);

// One JSON line per event. With LOG_FILE set (the tests set it), lines go to
// that file, so a test can find every line about its own payment.
function log(level: string, msg: string, fields: Record<string, unknown>) {
  const line = JSON.stringify({
    level,
    time: new Date().toISOString(),
    msg,
    ...fields,
  });
  if (process.env.LOG_FILE) appendFileSync(process.env.LOG_FILE, `${line}\n`);
  else console.log(line);
}

// The Lambda entry point. AWS calls it with a batch of SQS messages and reads
// back which ones failed, so only those are retried.
export async function handler(event: SQSEvent): Promise<SQSBatchResponse> {
  const batchItemFailures: { itemIdentifier: string }[] = [];
  for (const record of event.Records) {
    const succeeded = await processRecord(record);
    if (!succeeded)
      batchItemFailures.push({ itemIdentifier: record.messageId });
  }
  return { batchItemFailures };
}

function parse(body: string): TransferRequestedMessage | null {
  try {
    const message = JSON.parse(body);
    const valid =
      message?.version === 1 &&
      message.type === "transfer.requested" &&
      typeof message.transferId === "string" &&
      Number.isInteger(message.amountCents) &&
      typeof message.counterparty?.accountNumber === "string";
    return valid ? message : null;
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

async function processRecord(record: SQSRecord): Promise<boolean> {
  const attempt = Number(record.attributes.ApproximateReceiveCount ?? "1");
  const message = parse(record.body);
  if (!message) {
    // It will never parse, however often it's retried. Let it fail its way
    // to the dead-letter queue, where a person can look at it.
    log("error", "unreadable message", {
      messageId: record.messageId,
      attempt,
    });
    await retryLater(record, attempt);
    return false;
  }

  const context = {
    transferId: message.transferId,
    correlationId: message.correlationId,
    attempt,
  };

  // The API publishes just before it commits, so a fast processor can see
  // the message before the payment exists, or while an approval is still
  // committing. That's "not yet", not "never": try again shortly. A payment
  // that truly never arrives fails its way to the dead-letter queue.
  const status = await findTransferStatus(message.transferId);
  if (status === null || status === "in_review") {
    log("info", "payment not ready yet, will retry", { ...context, status });
    await retryLater(record, attempt);
    return false;
  }

  // At-least-once delivery means duplicates. Only pending payments are sent.
  if (status !== "pending") {
    log("info", "nothing to do", { ...context, status });
    return true;
  }

  const result = await originatePayment(message);

  if (result.kind === "accepted") {
    await recordPartnerOutcome(message.transferId, {
      status: "submitted",
      partnerReference: result.reference,
    });
    log("info", "payment submitted", {
      ...context,
      reference: result.reference,
    });
    return true;
  }

  if (result.kind === "rejected") {
    await recordPartnerOutcome(message.transferId, {
      status: "rejected",
      reason: result.reason,
    });
    log("warn", "payment rejected, money returned", {
      ...context,
      reason: result.reason,
    });
    return true;
  }

  if (attempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
    await recordPartnerOutcome(message.transferId, {
      status: "failed",
      reason: result.reason,
    });
    log("error", "payment failed, money returned", {
      ...context,
      reason: result.reason,
    });
    // Fail once more with no delay, so SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue.
    await retryLater(record, 0);
    return false;
  }

  log("warn", "partner problem, will retry", {
    ...context,
    reason: result.reason,
  });
  await retryLater(record, attempt);
  return false;
}

// Hide the message for a while before its next try: 2s, then 4s.
async function retryLater(record: SQSRecord, attempt: number) {
  const queueUrl = record.eventSourceARN
    ? await queueUrlFromArn(record.eventSourceARN)
    : undefined;
  if (!queueUrl) return;
  await sqs.send(
    new ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand({
      QueueUrl: queueUrl,
      ReceiptHandle: record.receiptHandle,
      VisibilityTimeout: RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS * attempt,
    }),
  );
}

async function queueUrlFromArn(arn: string): Promise<string> {
  // arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:ledgerline-transfers
  const [, , , region, account, name] = arn.split(":");
  const endpoint =
    process.env.AWS_ENDPOINT_URL ?? `https://sqs.${region}.amazonaws.com`;
  return `${endpoint}/${account}/${name ?? TRANSFERS_QUEUE}`;
}

Create tests/framework/service-logs.ts:

tests/framework/service-logs.ts
import { existsSync, readFileSync } from "node:fs";

// Where playwright.config.ts tells the API and the processor to write logs.
export const LOG_FILES = ["logs/api.log", "logs/processor.log"];

/** The correlation id a test's requests carry. */
export function correlationIdFor(testId: string): string {
  return `test-${testId}`;
}

/** Every log line, from every service, that mentions a correlation id. */
export function logsFor(correlationId: string): string[] {
  return LOG_FILES.filter((file) => existsSync(file)).flatMap((file) =>
    readFileSync(file, "utf8")
      .split("\n")
      .filter((line) => line.includes(correlationId)),
  );
}

/** True when the services were started with log files, as in CI. */
export function logFilesExist(): boolean {
  return LOG_FILES.every((file) => existsSync(file));
}

Replace tests/framework/fixtures.ts:

tests/framework/fixtures.ts
import { test as base, type APIRequestContext } from "@playwright/test";
import { AccountBuilder } from "./account-builder";
import { DbHelper } from "./db-helper";
import { LedgerlineClient } from "./ledgerline-client";
import { PartnerWebhooks } from "./partner-webhooks";
import { FakePartner } from "./fake-partner";
import { QueueHelper } from "./queue-helper";
import { correlationIdFor, logsFor } from "./service-logs";
import {
  API_KEY,
  BROKEN_QUEUE_API_URL,
  BROKEN_RISK_API_URL,
  DEAD_LETTER_QUEUE,
  INSPECT_API_URL,
  INSPECT_QUEUE,
  TRANSFERS_QUEUE,
} from "./test-data";

interface TestFixtures {
  api: LedgerlineClient;
  newAccount: () => AccountBuilder;
  apiWithKey: (apiKey?: string) => Promise<LedgerlineClient>;
  brokenQueueApi: LedgerlineClient;
  brokenRiskApi: LedgerlineClient;
  inspectApi: LedgerlineClient;
  partner: FakePartner;
  webhooks: PartnerWebhooks;
  serviceLogs: void;
}

interface WorkerFixtures {
  db: DbHelper;
  inspectQueue: QueueHelper;
  transfersQueue: QueueHelper;
  deadLetterQueue: QueueHelper;
}

// Specs import { test, expect } from here instead of @playwright/test, and
// get these fixtures handed to them, already set up and cleaned up.
export const test = base.extend<TestFixtures, WorkerFixtures>({
  // Every request a test sends carries the test's own correlation id, so its
  // lines in the service logs can be found.
  extraHTTPHeaders: async ({ extraHTTPHeaders }, use, testInfo) => {
    await use({
      ...extraHTTPHeaders,
      "x-correlation-id": correlationIdFor(testInfo.testId),
    });
  },

  // Runs around every test. When one fails, the log lines carrying its
  // correlation id are attached to the report, next to the failure.
  serviceLogs: [
    // eslint-disable-next-line no-empty-pattern
    async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
      await use();
      if (testInfo.status !== testInfo.expectedStatus) {
        const lines = logsFor(correlationIdFor(testInfo.testId));
        if (lines.length > 0) {
          await testInfo.attach("service logs", {
            body: lines.join("\n"),
            contentType: "text/plain",
          });
        }
      }
    },
    { auto: true },
  ],

  // A client that sends the normal API key (from playwright.config.ts).
  api: async ({ request }, use) => {
    await use(new LedgerlineClient(request));
  },

  // Call newAccount() for a fresh builder: newAccount().withBalance(500).create()
  newAccount: async ({ api, db }, use) => {
    await use(() => new AccountBuilder(api, db));
  },

  // A client with a different API key, or none, for authentication tests.
  apiWithKey: async ({ playwright, baseURL }, use) => {
    const contexts: APIRequestContext[] = [];
    await use(async (apiKey) => {
      const context = await playwright.request.newContext({
        baseURL,
        extraHTTPHeaders: apiKey ? { "x-api-key": apiKey } : {},
      });
      contexts.push(context);
      return new LedgerlineClient(context);
    });
    // Everything after use() runs when the test finishes: clean up.
    for (const context of contexts) await context.dispose();
  },

  // A client for the second API, the one whose queue doesn't exist.
  brokenQueueApi: async ({ playwright }, use) => {
    const context = await playwright.request.newContext({
      baseURL: BROKEN_QUEUE_API_URL,
      extraHTTPHeaders: { "x-api-key": API_KEY },
    });
    await use(new LedgerlineClient(context));
    await context.dispose();
  },

  // A client for the fourth API, the one whose Redis doesn't exist.
  brokenRiskApi: async ({ playwright }, use) => {
    const context = await playwright.request.newContext({
      baseURL: BROKEN_RISK_API_URL,
      extraHTTPHeaders: { "x-api-key": API_KEY },
    });
    await use(new LedgerlineClient(context));
    await context.dispose();
  },

  // A client for the third API, which publishes to the inspect queue.
  inspectApi: async ({ playwright }, use) => {
    const context = await playwright.request.newContext({
      baseURL: INSPECT_API_URL,
      extraHTTPHeaders: { "x-api-key": API_KEY },
    });
    await use(new LedgerlineClient(context));
    await context.dispose();
  },

  // A fake partner bank with its own counterparty, so its stubs only match
  // this test's payments. Its stubs are removed when the test ends.
  // eslint-disable-next-line no-empty-pattern
  partner: async ({}, use) => {
    const partner = new FakePartner();
    await use(partner);
    await partner.cleanup();
  },

  // Sends signed webhooks, the way the partner bank does.
  webhooks: async ({ api }, use) => {
    await use(new PartnerWebhooks(api));
  },

  // The queues in MiniStack, one helper each per worker.
  inspectQueue: [
    // eslint-disable-next-line no-empty-pattern
    async ({}, use) => {
      await use(new QueueHelper(INSPECT_QUEUE));
    },
    { scope: "worker" },
  ],
  transfersQueue: [
    // eslint-disable-next-line no-empty-pattern
    async ({}, use) => {
      await use(new QueueHelper(TRANSFERS_QUEUE));
    },
    { scope: "worker" },
  ],
  deadLetterQueue: [
    // eslint-disable-next-line no-empty-pattern
    async ({}, use) => {
      await use(new QueueHelper(DEAD_LETTER_QUEUE));
    },
    { scope: "worker" },
  ],

  db: [
    // Playwright requires the {} here even though this fixture needs nothing.
    // eslint-disable-next-line no-empty-pattern
    async ({}, use) => {
      const db = new DbHelper();
      await use(db);
      await db.close();
    },

  ],
});

What the code does

  • The extraHTTPHeaders fixture overrides Playwright's own option for every test, adding x-correlation-id: test-<the test's id> to everything the request fixture sends.
  • The serviceLogs fixture is marked auto: true, so it runs around every test without being asked for. After the test, it checks testInfo.status against testInfo.expectedStatus, and on a failure it attaches the matching log lines with testInfo.attach.
  • "One id follows a payment" finds lines from both the API ("external transfer accepted") and the processor ("payment submitted") using a single id. That's a trace, built from nothing but logs.
  • test.skip(!logFilesExist(), ...) skips that test when you're reusing a npm run dev server that isn't writing log files, instead of failing for a reason that has nothing to do with the product.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 47: Service logs on failure".

In a company

Services don't write log files that people read by hand. Every line is sent to a central tool like Datadog or CloudWatch, where you search by correlation id, build dashboards, and set alerts.

Step 48: The race the repeat run found

About 45 minutes.

The first time I ran the whole suite three times over, the way the nightly job does, one run in 255 failed: "an approved payment goes on to the bank" waited 15 seconds for submitted and saw pending the whole time. Every normal run passed. That's a flaky test, and the policy says to find the cause, not add a retry.

The cause was in the processor, and it had been there since Week 5:

  1. Approving a payment publishes its message inside the transaction, just before COMMIT. New payments do the same.
  2. The processor is fast. Sometimes it received the message, and read the payment's status, before that COMMIT had finished.
  3. It saw in_review (or, for a brand-new payment, no payment at all), decided there was "nothing to do", and deleted the message.
  4. The payment was then committed as pending, with no message left to send it. It would have waited forever.

The fix is in the handler.ts you added in Step 47. When the payment doesn't exist yet, or is still in_review, the processor treats that as "not yet" rather than "never": it leaves the message on the queue and tries again a moment later. A payment that really never arrives still fails its way to the dead-letter queue, where a person sees it.

Prove it with the same run that found it:

npx playwright test --repeat-each 3

  255 passed

Your time will differ; mine took about a minute and a half.

This is the dual-write problem from Week 4, showing its other face. The industry's full answer is the outbox pattern: write the message into a database table inside the same transaction, and have a separate process publish it after COMMIT. The retry fix is simpler, and enough for this project. Being able to explain both is a strong interview answer.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 48: Fix the publish-before-commit race".

Step 49: The quality dashboard

About an hour.

What, why and how: Quality metrics

What it is. Quality metrics are numbers that describe a test suite's health over time: the pass rate, the flake rate (the share of tests that sometimes fail with no code change), how long the suite takes, and which tests are slowest.

Why we use it. "The tests are fine" is an opinion; "2.4% of our tests are flaky, and these two are why" is something a team can act on. Relay's posting lists the numbers its QA engineers are measured by, including flakiness and test duration.

How we use it. The nightly job runs every test three times and saves the results as JUnit XML. scripts/quality-report.ts reads that file and writes a one-page dashboard. A test that passed on some runs and failed on others is counted as flaky.

How it works inside. Flakiness is detected by repetition, never by a single run. The dashboard groups every run of the same test and flags any test that both passed and failed. Pass rate counts runs, while flake rate counts tests, so a suite can pass 99% of its runs and still have 10% of its tests flaky. That's why the dashboard shows both.

The nightly run already repeats every test three times. Now it also turns the results into a one-page dashboard: pass rate, flake rate, run time, which tests were flaky, and the slowest tests.

Create scripts/quality-report.ts:

scripts/quality-report.ts
import { mkdirSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

// Builds a one-page quality dashboard from Playwright's JUnit results. Run it
// on the nightly results, where every test ran several times: a test that
// both passed and failed is flaky.
const file = process.argv[2] ?? "results.xml";
const xml = readFileSync(file, "utf8");

const decode = (text: string) =>
  text
    .replace(/&quot;/g, '"')
    .replace(/&apos;|&#39;/g, "'")
    .replace(/&lt;/g, "<")
    .replace(/&gt;/g, ">")
    .replace(/&amp;/g, "&");
const escapeHtml = (text: string) =>
  text.replace(/&/g, "&amp;").replace(/</g, "&lt;").replace(/>/g, "&gt;");
const attr = (tag: string, name: string) =>
  decode(new RegExp(`\\b${name}="([^"]*)"`).exec(tag)?.[1] ?? "");

const runs = [
  ...xml.matchAll(/<testcase\b([^>]*?)(?:\/>|>([\s\S]*?)<\/testcase>)/g),
]
  .map((match) => ({
    name: attr(match[1], "name"),
    seconds: Number(attr(match[1], "time")),
    failed: /<failure\b/.test(match[2] ?? ""),
    skipped: /<skipped\b/.test(match[2] ?? ""),
  }))
  .filter((run) => !run.skipped);

// Group every run by test, to see how each test behaved across repeats.
const byTest = new Map<string, typeof runs>();
for (const run of runs)
  byTest.set(run.name, [...(byTest.get(run.name) ?? []), run]);
const tests = [...byTest.entries()].map(([name, results]) => ({
  name,
  runs: results.length,
  failures: results.filter((r) => r.failed).length,
  averageSeconds:
    results.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.seconds, 0) / results.length,
}));

const flaky = tests.filter((t) => t.failures > 0 && t.failures < t.runs);
const broken = tests.filter((t) => t.failures === t.runs);
const failedRuns = runs.filter((r) => r.failed).length;
const passRate = runs.length
  ? ((runs.length - failedRuns) / runs.length) * 100
  : 0;
const flakeRate = tests.length ? (flaky.length / tests.length) * 100 : 0;
const minutes =
  Number(attr(/<testsuites\b[^>]*>/.exec(xml)?.[0] ?? "", "time")) / 60;
const slowest = [...tests]
  .sort((a, b) => b.averageSeconds - a.averageSeconds)
  .slice(0, 10);

const list = (items: typeof tests, empty: string) =>
  items.length
    ? `<ul>${items.map((t) => `<li>${escapeHtml(t.name)}: failed ${t.failures} of ${t.runs} runs</li>`).join("")}</ul>`
    : `<p>${empty}</p>`;

const html = `<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>Ledgerline quality</title>
<style>
body{font:16px/1.5 system-ui,sans-serif;max-width:46rem;margin:2rem auto;padding:0 1rem;color:#13233A}
.stats{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(9rem,1fr));gap:.75rem;margin:1rem 0 2rem}
.stat{border:1px solid #CFD9D3;border-radius:8px;padding:.75rem}
.stat b{display:block;font-size:1.6rem}
table{border-collapse:collapse;width:100%}td,th{text-align:left;padding:.35rem .5rem;border-bottom:1px solid #CFD9D3}
td:last-child,th:last-child{text-align:right}
</style></head><body>
<h1>Ledgerline quality</h1>
<p>From ${escapeHtml(file)}, built ${new Date().toISOString()}.</p>
<div class="stats">
<div class="stat"><b>${tests.length}</b>tests</div>
<div class="stat"><b>${passRate.toFixed(1)}%</b>of runs passed</div>
<div class="stat"><b>${flakeRate.toFixed(1)}%</b>of tests flaky</div>
<div class="stat"><b>${minutes.toFixed(1)} min</b>total run time</div>
</div>
<h2>Flaky tests</h2>${list(flaky, "None: every test behaved the same on every run.")}
<h2>Failing every time</h2>${list(broken, "None.")}
<h2>Slowest tests, on average</h2>
<table><tr><th>Test</th><th>Seconds</th></tr>
${slowest.map((t) => `<tr><td>${escapeHtml(t.name)}</td><td>${t.averageSeconds.toFixed(1)}</td></tr>`).join("\n")}
</table></body></html>
`;

mkdirSync("quality", { recursive: true });
writeFileSync("quality/index.html", html);
console.log(
  `${tests.length} tests, ${passRate.toFixed(1)}% of runs passed, ${flaky.length} flaky. Written to quality/index.html`,
);
