.github/workflows/nightly.yml
name: Nightly flaky-test hunt

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *" # every day at 06:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch: # and whenever you press "Run workflow"

jobs:
  repeat:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_DB: ledgerline
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U ledgerline -d ledgerline"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10
      ministack:
        image: ministackorg/ministack:latest
        ports:
          - 4566:4566
      redis:
        image: redis:7
        ports:
          - 6379:6379

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Start the fake partner bank
        run: |
          docker run -d --name wiremock -p 8080:8080 -v "$PWD/infra/wiremock:/home/wiremock" wiremock/wiremock:3.13.2
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -sf http://localhost:8080/__admin/mappings > /dev/null && break; sleep 1; done
      - run: npm run db:migrate
      - run: npm run aws:setup

      # Every test three times. A test that fails even once here is flaky.
      - name: Run the suite three times
        run: npx playwright test --repeat-each 3 --reporter=list,junit
        env:
          PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME: results.xml

      - name: Write the summary
        if: always()
        run: npm run --silent ci:summary -- results.xml >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

      - name: Build the quality dashboard
        if: always()
        run: npm run quality:report -- results.xml

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: quality-dashboard
          path: quality/
          retention-days: 30

Replace README.md:

README.md
# Ledgerline

A small business-banking backend, and the automated test framework around it.
Built to practise how fintech teams test money movement: ledgers, contracts,
concurrency and CI.

## Run it

You need Docker Desktop and Node 24.

```bash
npm install
npm run setup        # start Postgres, MiniStack, WireMock and Redis, then create
                     # the tables, queues, table and bucket they need
npm run check        # everything CI checks: types, lint, formatting and tests
```

Start a new test file with `npm run new:test -- "feature name"`. When a test
flakes, follow [docs/flaky-tests.md](docs/flaky-tests.md).

Run the API on its own with `npm run dev`, then try `curl localhost:3000/health`.

## How the tests are organised

```
tests/
  unit/        Vitest. Pure functions, no network or database.
  api/         Playwright specs. Each file covers one feature.
  framework/   The plumbing specs are built on:
    fixtures.ts           api, newAccount, apiWithKey, db
    ledgerline-client.ts  one method per endpoint
    contract.ts           checks every response against openapi.yaml
    account-builder.ts    newAccount().withBalance(5000).create()
    db-helper.ts          ledger integrity queries
    queue-helper.ts       reads and writes queues in MiniStack
    fake-partner.ts       programs WireMock to act as the partner bank
    partner-webhooks.ts   sends signed webhooks, as the partner bank would
    settlement-files.ts   drops the bank's settlement files into S3
    service-logs.ts       finds a test's lines in the service logs
    assertions.ts         expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds")
bruno/         Bruno collection for exploring the API by hand
infra/wiremock/  the fake partner bank's default stubs
src/processor/   the Lambda that sends payments to the partner bank
openapi.yaml   The API contract
```

## Add a test

1. Pick the spec file for the feature, or create `tests/api/<feature>.spec.ts`.
2. Import `{ test, expect }` from `../framework/fixtures`.
3. Set up data with `newAccount()`, act with `api`, assert on the result.

```ts
test("rejects a transfer over the balance", async ({ api, newAccount }) => {
  const from = await newAccount().withBalance(1_000).create();
  const to = await newAccount().create();

  const result = await api.createTransfer({
    fromAccountId: from.id,
    toAccountId: to.id,
    amountCents: 1_001,
  });

  expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds");
});
```

Every test creates its own accounts, so tests run in parallel and in any order.

npm run quality:report -- results.xml

Week 10 wrap-up

  • Teach it back. Present the dashboard in three minutes to an imaginary VP of Engineering: what each number means, and what you'd do about the slowest tests.
  • Dev log. Write up the race: the symptom, how the repeat run exposed it, the cause, the fix, and the outbox pattern. It's the best debugging story in the project.
  • The interview line. "I added correlation ids that follow a payment through the API, the queue and the processor, attached each failing test's service logs to its report automatically, and built a flake-rate dashboard from nightly repeat runs, which caught a publish-before-commit race that single runs never showed."

Phase 5 starts with Week 11: keeping the fake bank honest, load testing, and AI.

Week 11: Honest fakes, load, and AI

Phase 5 is about keeping a suite trustworthy for months, not just today. This week you'll prove the fake bank still matches the real one, measure how the API behaves under load, and set up a way to use AI without trusting it blindly.

Step 50: Keep the fake bank honest

About 90 minutes.

What, why and how: Stub drift and provider contracts

What it is. Stub drift is when a fake stops matching the real system it stands in for. The tests keep passing, but against a fiction. A provider contract is the real system's own description of its API. Checking every stub against it keeps the fake honest.

Why we use it. Every Ledgerline test that involves the bank talks to WireMock, never to the real bank. If the stubs are wrong, all of those tests prove the wrong thing, and nothing tells you. A contract check catches drift cheaply, in a unit test that runs in milliseconds.

How we use it. contracts/partner-bank.yaml describes the bank's /ach/originate endpoint, written from the bank's documentation. A unit test checks every stub file and every FakePartner reply against it, and an API test checks what the processor actually sends. Tools like Pact go a step further: the provider's own CI checks what each consumer expects. That needs the bank's cooperation, so this project checks against its published contract instead.

How it works inside. A drift check is ordinary validation turned around. Instead of checking your own responses against your own contract, it checks your fake's answers against somebody else's contract, using the same Ajv validator. The API-level test covers the remaining direction: that what your code sends is something the provider will accept.

Every test that touches the bank talks to WireMock. If WireMock answers differently from the real bank, those tests prove the wrong thing. You'll write the bank's contract, from its documentation, and check every fake answer against it.

Create contracts/partner-bank.yaml:

contracts/partner-bank.yaml
openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: Partner bank ACH API, the parts Ledgerline uses
  version: 1.0.0
  description: >
    Written from the partner bank's documentation. The WireMock stubs that
    stand in for this API are checked against it, so they can't quietly drift
    away from what the real bank does.

paths:
  /ach/originate:
    post:
      summary: Send an ACH payment
      parameters:
        - name: idempotency-key
          in: header
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: "#/components/schemas/PaymentRequest"
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Accepted
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Accepted"
        "400":
          description: Refused. Sending it again won't help.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Rejected"
        "429":
          description: Too many requests. Try again later.
        "500":
          description: The bank had a problem. Try again later.

components:
  schemas:
    PaymentRequest:
      type: object
      required: [transferId, amountCents, counterparty]
      additionalProperties: false
      properties:
        transferId:
          type: string
          format: uuid
        amountCents:
          type: integer
          minimum: 1
        counterparty:
          type: object
          required: [name, routingNumber, accountNumber]
          additionalProperties: false
          properties:
            name:
              type: string
              minLength: 1
            routingNumber:
              type: string
              pattern: "^[0-9]{9}$"
            accountNumber:
              type: string
              pattern: "^[0-9]{4,17}$"

    Accepted:
      type: object
      required: [status, reference]
      additionalProperties: false
      properties:
        status:
          const: accepted
        reference:
          type: string
          minLength: 1

    Rejected:
      type: object
      required: [error]
      additionalProperties: false
      properties:
        error:
          enum: [invalid_account, account_closed, limit_exceeded]

Create tests/framework/partner-contract.ts:

tests/framework/partner-contract.ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";
import Ajv2020 from "ajv/dist/2020";
import addFormats from "ajv-formats";
import { parse } from "yaml";

// The partner bank's contract, written from its documentation. The fake bank
// must never answer in a way the real one can't, and the processor must never
// send something the real one would refuse.
const spec = parse(
  readFileSync(path.resolve("contracts/partner-bank.yaml"), "utf8"),
);
const ajv = new Ajv2020({ allErrors: true, strict: false });
addFormats(ajv);
ajv.addSchema(spec, "partner");

export type PartnerSchema = "PaymentRequest" | "Accepted" | "Rejected";

/** Everything wrong with a body, measured against the partner's contract. */
export function partnerContractErrors(
  schema: PartnerSchema,
  body: unknown,
): string[] {
  const validate = ajv.getSchema(`partner#/components/schemas/${schema}`);
  if (!validate) throw new Error(`partner-bank.yaml has no schema ${schema}`);
  if (validate(body)) return [];
  return (validate.errors ?? []).map(
    (error) => `${error.instancePath || "body"} ${error.message}`,
  );
}

/** The schema a response with this status must match, if it has a body. */
export function schemaForStatus(status: number): PartnerSchema | null {
  if (status === 200) return "Accepted";
  if (status === 400) return "Rejected";
  return null;
}

Replace tests/framework/fake-partner.ts. Its replies now live in one exported object, PARTNER_REPLIES, so they can be checked:

tests/framework/fake-partner.ts
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const WIREMOCK_URL = process.env.WIREMOCK_URL ?? "http://localhost:8080";

export interface Reply {
  status: number;
  jsonBody?: unknown;
}

// Everything the fake bank can say, in one place, so the drift check in
// tests/unit/stub-drift.test.ts can hold it to the real bank's contract.
export const PARTNER_REPLIES = {
  accepted: {
    status: 200,
    jsonBody: { status: "accepted", reference: "ACH-7F3A2B" },
  },
  acceptedOnRetry: {
    status: 200,
    jsonBody: { status: "accepted", reference: "ACH-SECOND-TRY" },
  },
  rejected: (error: string): Reply => ({ status: 400, jsonBody: { error } }),
  serverError: (status: number): Reply => ({ status }),
};

export interface PartnerRequest {
  body: Record<string, unknown>;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
}

// Programs WireMock to behave like the partner bank, for one test's payments.
// Every stub matches this partner's unique counterparty name, so tests
// running in parallel never see each other's stubs.
export class FakePartner {
  readonly counterparty = {
    name: `Supplier ${randomUUID().slice(0, 8)}`,
    routingNumber: "021000021",
    accountNumber: "123456789",
  };
  private readonly stubIds: string[] = [];

  /** The partner accepts every payment. */
  accepts() {
    return this.stub(PARTNER_REPLIES.accepted);
  }

  /** The partner refuses: a 400 that's not worth retrying. */
  rejects(error = "invalid_account") {
    return this.stub(PARTNER_REPLIES.rejected(error));
  }

  /** The partner answers with a server error every time. */
  failsWith(status = 500) {
    return this.stub(PARTNER_REPLIES.serverError(status));
  }

  /** The first call fails with a 500; every call after that works. */
  async failsOnceThenAccepts() {
    const scenarioName = `flaky ${this.counterparty.name}`;
    await this.stub(PARTNER_REPLIES.serverError(500), {
      scenarioName,
      requiredScenarioState: "Started",
      newScenarioState: "recovered",
    });
    await this.stub(PARTNER_REPLIES.acceptedOnRetry, {
      scenarioName,
      requiredScenarioState: "recovered",
    });
  }

  /** Every request the partner received for this test's payments. */
  async requests(): Promise<PartnerRequest[]> {
    const response = await fetch(`${WIREMOCK_URL}/__admin/requests/find`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ ...this.matcher() }),
    });
    const { requests } = (await response.json()) as {
      requests: { body: string; headers: Record<string, string> }[];
    };
    return requests.map((r) => ({
      body: JSON.parse(r.body),
      headers: Object.fromEntries(
        Object.entries(r.headers).map(([k, v]) => [k.toLowerCase(), v]),
      ),
    }));
  }

  async cleanup() {
    await Promise.all(
      this.stubIds.map((id) =>
        fetch(`${WIREMOCK_URL}/__admin/mappings/${id}`, { method: "DELETE" }),
      ),
    );
  }

  private matcher() {
    return {
      method: "POST",
      urlPath: "/ach/originate",
      bodyPatterns: [
        {
          matchesJsonPath: `$.counterparty[?(@.name == '${this.counterparty.name}')]`,
        },
      ],
    };
  }

  private async stub(response: Reply, extra: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
    const result = await fetch(`${WIREMOCK_URL}/__admin/mappings`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        priority: 1,
        ...extra,
        request: this.matcher(),
        response: {
          headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
          ...response,
        },
      }),
    });
    const { id } = (await result.json()) as { id: string };
    this.stubIds.push(id);
  }
}

Create tests/unit/stub-drift.test.ts:

tests/unit/stub-drift.test.ts
import { readdirSync, readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import path from "node:path";
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { PARTNER_REPLIES, type Reply } from "../framework/fake-partner";
import {
  partnerContractErrors,
  schemaForStatus,
} from "../framework/partner-contract";

const MAPPINGS = "infra/wiremock/mappings";

// Every answer the fake bank can give: the stub files WireMock loads at
// start-up, and the replies FakePartner programs during tests.
const replies: [string, Reply][] = [
  ...readdirSync(MAPPINGS).map((file): [string, Reply] => [
    `${MAPPINGS}/${file}`,
    JSON.parse(readFileSync(path.join(MAPPINGS, file), "utf8")).response,
  ]),
  ["FakePartner.accepts()", PARTNER_REPLIES.accepted],
  ["FakePartner.failsOnceThenAccepts()", PARTNER_REPLIES.acceptedOnRetry],
  ["FakePartner.rejects()", PARTNER_REPLIES.rejected("invalid_account")],
  ["FakePartner.failsWith()", PARTNER_REPLIES.serverError(500)],
];

describe("the fake bank only says what the real bank can say", () => {
  it.each(replies)("%s", (_, reply) => {
    const schema = schemaForStatus(reply.status);
    if (!schema) return; // 429 and 5xx answers have no body to check
    expect(partnerContractErrors(schema, reply.jsonBody)).toEqual([]);
  });
});

Create tests/api/partner-contract.spec.ts, which checks the other direction, what the processor sends:

tests/api/partner-contract.spec.ts
import { expect, test } from "../framework/fixtures";
import { partnerContractErrors } from "../framework/partner-contract";

test("what the processor sends matches the bank's contract", async ({
  api,
  newAccount,
  partner,
}) => {
  await partner.accepts();
  const from = await newAccount().withBalance(10_000).create();

  const { body } = await api.createExternalTransfer({
    fromAccountId: from.id,
    amountCents: 2_500,
    counterparty: partner.counterparty,
  });
  await expect
    .poll(async () => (await api.getTransfer(body.id)).body.status)
    .toBe("submitted");

  const [sent] = await partner.requests();
  expect(partnerContractErrors("PaymentRequest", sent.body)).toEqual([]);
  expect(sent.headers["idempotency-key"]).toBe(body.id);
});

npm run format
npm run typecheck
npm run test:unit
npm run test:api

44 unit tests and 86 API tests pass.

Found while testing this guide

The first time I ran the drift check, it failed:

 × FakePartner.accepts()
 × FakePartner.failsOnceThenAccepts()
+   "body must have required property 'status'",

The fake bank had been answering {"reference": "ACH-7F3A2B"} since Week 5. The real bank's contract says every acceptance also includes "status": "accepted". The processor only reads reference, so no test had ever noticed. That's exactly what drift looks like: nothing fails, and the fake quietly stops describing reality. The PARTNER_REPLIES above include the fix.

What the code does

  • The bank's contract covers only the parts Ledgerline uses. Writing it from the bank's documentation, not from your own stubs, is the whole point.
  • The drift check runs every stub file in infra/wiremock/mappings and every PARTNER_REPLIES entry through the contract. Answers without a body, like 500 or 429, have nothing to check.
  • The API test checks the other direction: that what the processor really sends is something the real bank would accept.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 50: Stub drift check".

Step 51: Load testing with k6

About 90 minutes.

What, why and how: Load testing and k6

What it is. A load test sends many requests at once, for a while, and measures how the system copes: how quickly it answers, how many requests fail, and how much it can handle. k6 is an open-source load-testing tool. You describe the load in a JavaScript file, and it reports the results against thresholds you set.

Why we use it. A payment API that's correct for one user can fall over, or crawl, for fifty. Performance testing is part of the plan for this role, and "p95 latency" is a phrase interviewers expect you to know.

How we use it. load/transfers.js runs 10 virtual users, or VUs, for about 30 seconds, each sending transfers. p95 is the time within which 95% of requests answered. It describes what nearly every user experiences, where an average hides slow outliers. Thresholds make the run fail if p95 goes over 300 ms or more than 1% of requests fail. The nightly CI run includes it.

How it works inside. Each virtual user is a small independent loop inside k6, running your default function over and over as fast as the API answers. That's called a closed model: a slower API means fewer requests per second, because every user waits for its answer before sending the next request. k6 records every request's duration, and p95 is found by sorting them and taking the value 95% of the way up the list. A handful of very slow requests barely moves the average, but shows up plainly in p95 and p99.

Install k6. On a Mac:

brew install k6

On Ubuntu or WSL, download it from k6's GitHub releases:

K6=v2.3.0
curl -sL -o k6.tgz "https://github.com/grafana/k6/releases/download/$K6/k6-$K6-linux-amd64.tar.gz"
tar xzf k6.tgz && sudo mv k6-$K6-linux-amd64/k6 /usr/local/bin/ && rm -r k6.tgz k6-$K6-linux-amd64
k6 version

Create load/transfers.js:

load/transfers.js
import { check } from "k6";
import http from "k6/http";

// A short load test: 10 virtual users sending transfers for about 30 seconds.
// Run it while the API is running: npm run test:load
const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || "http://localhost:3000";
const HEADERS = {
  "content-type": "application/json",
  "x-api-key": __ENV.API_KEY || "local-dev-key",
};
const USERS = 10;
// HOT=1 sends every transfer from the same account, to see the row lock work.
const HOT = __ENV.HOT === "1";

export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: "5s", target: USERS }, // ramp up
    { duration: "20s", target: USERS }, // hold
    { duration: "5s", target: 0 }, // ramp down
  ],
  // The test fails if any of these are broken.
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"], // fewer than 1% of requests fail
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"], // 95% answer within 300 ms
    checks: ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

function post(path, body) {
  return http.post(`${BASE_URL}${path}`, JSON.stringify(body), {
    headers: HEADERS,
  });
}

// Runs once, before the load: a funded pair of accounts for each user, so
// users don't queue behind each other's row locks.
export function setup() {
  const pairs = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < USERS; i++) {
    const from = post("/accounts", { name: `Load sender ${i}` }).json("id");
    const to = post("/accounts", { name: `Load receiver ${i}` }).json("id");
    post(`/accounts/${from}/deposits`, { amountCents: 100_000_000 });
    pairs.push({ from, to });
  }
  return { pairs };
}

// Runs over and over, by every user, for the whole test.
export default function (data) {
  const pair = HOT ? data.pairs[0] : data.pairs[(__VU - 1) % USERS];
  const response = http.post(
    `${BASE_URL}/transfers`,
    JSON.stringify({
      fromAccountId: pair.from,
      toAccountId: pair.to,
      amountCents: 1,
    }),
    {
      headers: {
        ...HEADERS,
        "idempotency-key": `load-${__VU}-${__ITER}-${Date.now()}`,
      },
      tags: { name: "POST /transfers" },
    },
  );
  check(response, { "transfer created": (r) => r.status === 201 });
}

k6 scripts use a few globals, like __ENV, that ESLint doesn't know. Replace eslint.config.mjs to tell it:

eslint.config.mjs
import eslint from "@eslint/js";
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";
import prettier from "eslint-config-prettier";
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";

export default defineConfig(
  {
    ignores: ["node_modules/", "playwright-report/", "test-results/", "dist/"],
  },
  eslint.configs.recommended,
  tseslint.configs.recommended,
  // k6 scripts run inside k6, which provides these globals.
  {
    files: ["load/**/*.js"],
    languageOptions: {
      globals: { __ENV: "readonly", __VU: "readonly", __ITER: "readonly" },
    },
  },
  prettier,
);

npm pkg set scripts.test:load="k6 run load/transfers.js"

Start the API with npm run start in one terminal, then run the load test in another: 

npm run test:load

The end of the report shows the thresholds. Mine:

  █ THRESHOLDS
    checks
    ✓ 'rate>0.99' rate=100.00%
    http_req_duration
    ✓ 'p(95)<300' p(95)=56.46ms
    http_req_failed
    ✓ 'rate<0.01' rate=0.00%

That was 6,425 transfers in 30 seconds, about 213 a second. Your numbers will differ with your machine.

What the script does

  • options.stages ramps up to 10 virtual users over 5 seconds, holds for 20, and ramps down.
  • thresholds turn the numbers into a pass or fail, so the run can gate a pipeline.
  • setup runs once first and makes a funded pair of accounts for each user, so users don't queue behind each other's row locks.
  • The default function runs over and over for every user. Each transfer carries its own idempotency key, so the DynamoDB path is loaded too.
  • check records whether each response was a 201, separately from the timing.

Try this

Make every user send from the same account, so they all need the same row lock: 

HOT=1 npm run test:load

When I ran it, throughput dropped from about 213 transfers a second to about 183, and p95 only moved from 56 ms to 60 ms. Each transaction holds the lock for a millisecond or two, so the queue stays short. Keeping transactions short is exactly what keeps locks cheap, and it's why the processor calls the bank outside any database transaction. A bank call inside a transaction would hold the lock for the whole round trip.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 51: Load test".

Step 52: Using AI without trusting it blindly

About an hour.

What, why and how: AI in your testing

What it is. AI assistants like Claude and Cursor can write tests, explain failures and suggest cases you missed. They can also write tests that pass without checking anything, that assert whatever the code happens to do today, or that skip the negative cases.

Why we use it. Relay's posting asks for engineers who use AI every day and can critique what it produces. Generating tests is the easy part; knowing where AI-written tests go wrong is the skill.

How we use it. Use AI freely for scaffolding and ideas. Review every AI-written test against docs/ai-review-checklist.md before it's merged. And keep docs/ai-log.md: each time the AI got something wrong, write down what it was and how you caught it.

Create docs/ai-review-checklist.md:

docs/ai-review-checklist.md
# Reviewing a test an AI wrote

AI assistants write tests quickly, and some of those tests check nothing at
all. Before merging one, go through this list.

## Does it test behaviour?

- Would it fail if the feature broke? Break the code on purpose and run it.
- Does it check what a client can see, like a status, a body or a balance,
  rather than internal details?
- Were the expected values worked out on their own, or copied from whatever
  the code happens to return today?

## Does it cover the edges?

- Is there a negative case: bad input, not enough money, the wrong key?
- Are limits tested on the edge and one step past it?
- After a refusal, does it check that nothing changed?

## Is it reliable?

- No fixed sleeps. Anything asynchronous waits with `expect.poll`.
- It creates its own data and shares nothing with other tests.
- It passes no matter which order the tests run in.

## Does it fit the framework?

- It uses the fixtures, builders and client, never raw URLs.
- Its name says what should happen, in plain words.

## Keep an AI log

In `docs/ai-log.md`, write down each time an AI's output was wrong, and how you
caught it. Three good entries are a ready answer to "How do you use AI in your
testing?"

Then try it for real:

  1. Ask Claude or Cursor to write a Playwright test that checks GET /transfers/:id returns 404 for an unknown transfer, pointing it at your tests/framework folder.
  2. Before running it, go through the checklist. Does it use the fixtures and client? Does it check the error code, not just the status? Would it fail if the route returned 500?
  3. Fix what's wrong, run it, and break the route on purpose to see it fail.
  4. Create docs/ai-log.md and write down what you had to fix.

If you'd like a stretch after Week 12: connect an AI assistant to your test results through an MCP server, so it can answer "which tests are slowest?" from real data. Or try Pact, which lets a provider's own CI check what its consumers expect from it.

Step 53: The load test in the nightly run

About 20 minutes.

Replace .github/workflows/nightly.yml, which ends with a load test:

.github/workflows/nightly.yml
name: Nightly flaky-test hunt

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *" # every day at 06:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch: # and whenever you press "Run workflow"

jobs:
  repeat:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ledgerline
          POSTGRES_DB: ledgerline
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U ledgerline -d ledgerline"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10
      ministack:
        image: ministackorg/ministack:latest
        ports:
          - 4566:4566
      redis:
        image: redis:7
        ports:
          - 6379:6379

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Start the fake partner bank
        run: |
          docker run -d --name wiremock -p 8080:8080 -v "$PWD/infra/wiremock:/home/wiremock" wiremock/wiremock:3.13.2
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -sf http://localhost:8080/__admin/mappings > /dev/null && break; sleep 1; done
      - run: npm run db:migrate
      - run: npm run aws:setup

      # Every test three times. A test that fails even once here is flaky.
      - name: Run the suite three times
        run: npx playwright test --repeat-each 3 --reporter=list,junit
        env:
          PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME: results.xml

      - name: Write the summary
        if: always()
        run: npm run --silent ci:summary -- results.xml >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

      - name: Build the quality dashboard
        if: always()
        run: npm run quality:report -- results.xml

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: quality-dashboard
          path: quality/
          retention-days: 30

      # A short load test, while the machine has nothing else to do.
      - name: Load test
        if: always()
        run: |
          npm run start &
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do curl -sf http://localhost:3000/health && break; sleep 1; done
          docker run --rm --network host -v "$PWD/load:/load" grafana/k6 run /load/transfers.js

Replace README.md:

README.md
# Ledgerline

A small business-banking backend, and the automated test framework around it.
Built to practise how fintech teams test money movement: ledgers, contracts,
concurrency and CI.

## Run it

You need Docker Desktop and Node 24.

```bash
npm install
npm run setup        # start Postgres, MiniStack, WireMock and Redis, then create
                     # the tables, queues, table and bucket they need
npm run check        # everything CI checks: types, lint, formatting and tests
```

Start a new test file with `npm run new:test -- "feature name"`. When a test
flakes, follow [docs/flaky-tests.md](docs/flaky-tests.md). With the API running,
`npm run test:load` runs a 30-second load test. Before merging a test an AI
wrote, go through [docs/ai-review-checklist.md](docs/ai-review-checklist.md).

Run the API on its own with `npm run dev`, then try `curl localhost:3000/health`.

## How the tests are organised

```
tests/
  unit/        Vitest. Pure functions, no network or database.
  api/         Playwright specs. Each file covers one feature.
  framework/   The plumbing specs are built on:
    fixtures.ts           api, newAccount, apiWithKey, db
    ledgerline-client.ts  one method per endpoint
    contract.ts           checks every response against openapi.yaml
    account-builder.ts    newAccount().withBalance(5000).create()
    db-helper.ts          ledger integrity queries
    queue-helper.ts       reads and writes queues in MiniStack
    fake-partner.ts       programs WireMock to act as the partner bank
    partner-webhooks.ts   sends signed webhooks, as the partner bank would
    settlement-files.ts   drops the bank's settlement files into S3
    service-logs.ts       finds a test's lines in the service logs
    assertions.ts         expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds")
bruno/         Bruno collection for exploring the API by hand
infra/wiremock/  the fake partner bank's default stubs
src/processor/   the Lambda that sends payments to the partner bank
openapi.yaml   The API contract
contracts/     the partner bank's contract, for the stub drift check
load/          the k6 load test
```

## Add a test

1. Pick the spec file for the feature, or create `tests/api/<feature>.spec.ts`.
2. Import `{ test, expect }` from `../framework/fixtures`.
3. Set up data with `newAccount()`, act with `api`, assert on the result.

```ts
test("rejects a transfer over the balance", async ({ api, newAccount }) => {
  const from = await newAccount().withBalance(1_000).create();
  const to = await newAccount().create();

  const result = await api.createTransfer({
    fromAccountId: from.id,
    toAccountId: to.id,
    amountCents: 1_001,
  });

  expectApiError(result, 422, "insufficient_funds");
});
```

Every test creates its own accounts, so tests run in parallel and in any order.

Fail: the load test step can't connect. --network host lets the k6 container reach the API on localhost, which works on GitHub's Linux machines. Check the API started: the step's log should show the curl loop ending without errors before k6 begins.

  • The interview line. "I checked every WireMock stub against the partner bank's contract, which caught a drift the tests had missed for weeks, and added a nightly k6 load test with p95 and error-rate thresholds."

Step 54: The test strategy

About 90 minutes.

A test strategy says what each kind of test is for, where it runs, what's faked, and what isn't covered. It's the document a QA lead writes, and "walk me through your test strategy" is a standard question for senior roles.

Before you copy the file below, try writing your own version from memory, with the same headings. Wherever you get stuck is something you'd struggle to explain in an interview.

Create docs/test-strategy.md:

docs/test-strategy.md
# Test strategy

Ledgerline moves money, so the tests aim at the ways money goes wrong: moving
twice, moving without a trace, moving past a limit, or disagreeing with the
bank. This page says what each kind of test is for, where it runs, and what it
deliberately doesn't cover.

## Layers

| Layer       | Tool       | What it proves                                                                                                       |   How many |
| ----------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------: |
| Unit        | Vitest     | Pure rules: money parsing, risk decisions, reconciliation, the fake bank's contract                                  |         44 |
| API         | Playwright | The running system over HTTP, with Postgres, MiniStack, Redis and WireMock                                           |         86 |
| Contract    | Ajv        | Every API response matches `openapi.yaml`, on every call                                                             | every call |
| Integrity   | SQL        | Rules for all data at once: every transfer's entries sum to zero, the ledger sums to zero, no customer goes negative |          3 |
| Exploratory | Bruno      | A collection for trying the API by hand, also run in CI                                                              | 6 requests |
| Load        | k6         | 10 users for 30 seconds: p95 under 300 ms and under 1% errors                                                        |    nightly |

## Where each runs

- **On your machine:** `npm run check` runs everything a push runs.
- **On every push:** types, lint, formatting and unit tests first, then the API
  suite split across two machines, then a merged report and a summary.
- **Every night:** the whole API suite three times over, a quality dashboard
  with the flake rate, and the load test.

## What's faked, and why

- **AWS** (SQS, Lambda, DynamoDB, S3) runs in MiniStack: free, offline, and
  the same on every machine.
- **The partner bank** is WireMock. Its stubs are checked against
  `contracts/partner-bank.yaml`, so the fake can't drift from the real bank.
- **Time** isn't faked. Tests that need an old account or a particular day set
  that up in the database directly, through the framework, never by waiting.

## What we focus on

- **Duplicates:** idempotency keys, duplicate queue messages, resent webhooks.
- **Concurrency:** parallel transfers, parallel payments against a daily limit,
  and a race between publishing and committing.
- **Failure paths:** queue outages, Redis outages, a bank that errors, times
  out, refuses or never answers.
- **"And nothing changed":** every refusal checks that no money moved.

## What this doesn't cover

- A user interface, so no browser or mobile end-to-end tests.
- Real AWS permissions (IAM), which MiniStack doesn't enforce.
- A real bank. The contract is written from documentation, and a real
  integration would need a sandbox from the bank.
- Security testing beyond authentication, signatures and input validation.

The most senior section is the last one. Saying plainly what your tests don't cover shows judgment; pretending they cover everything shows the opposite.

Commit with git add -A && git commit -m "Step 54: Test strategy".

Step 55: Decision records

About an hour.

An architecture decision record, or ADR, is a short note with four parts: the situation, the decision, and its consequences, good and bad, plus a status. Teams keep them so nobody has to guess later why things are the way they are. Four decisions in this project deserve one. 

mkdir -p docs/decisions

Create docs/decisions/0001-ministack-for-aws.md:

docs/decisions/0001-ministack-for-aws.md
# 1. Run AWS locally with MiniStack

**Status:** accepted

## Context

The system uses SQS, Lambda, DynamoDB and S3. Tests against real AWS need an
account, cost money, need a network, and can be disturbed by anyone else using
the same account.

## Decision

Run every AWS service in MiniStack, locally and in CI. The code reads its
endpoint from `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`, so pointing it at real AWS needs no changes.

## Consequences

- Tests are free, fast, offline and repeatable.
- MiniStack doesn't enforce IAM permissions, so permission mistakes won't show
  up in tests.
- MiniStack in Docker can behave slightly differently from MiniStack installed
  directly, so setup steps that depend on it have a verification step.

Create docs/decisions/0002-poll-dont-sleep.md:

docs/decisions/0002-poll-dont-sleep.md
# 2. Wait for conditions, never for time

**Status:** accepted

## Context

Payments finish asynchronously: through a queue, a processor and a fake bank.
A test that sleeps for a fixed time is slow when the system is fast, and flaky
when it's slow.

## Decision

Every asynchronous check uses `expect.poll`, which retries until the condition
holds or a timeout passes. The timeout is 15 seconds, because on a busy run a
payment can wait in the queue behind many others.

## Consequences

- Tests finish as soon as the system is ready.
- A timeout that's too tight still causes flakes under load, which the nightly
  repeat run is there to catch.

Create docs/decisions/0003-fail-closed-on-risk.md:

docs/decisions/0003-fail-closed-on-risk.md 
# 3. When the risk check can't run, hold the payment

**Status:** accepted

## Context

Daily limits depend on a counter in Redis. If Redis is unreachable, the API can
either send payments unchecked (fail open) or hold them for a person to review
(fail closed).

## Decision

Fail closed. A payment that couldn't be checked is saved as `in_review` with
the reason `risk_check_unavailable`, and a person decides.

## Consequences

- An outage delays payments instead of letting unchecked money leave.
- Reviewers get more work during an outage.
- A test runs a copy of the API with no Redis, to prove the rule holds.

Create docs/decisions/0004-retry-until-the-payment-exists.md:

docs/decisions/0004-retry-until-the-payment-exists.md 
# 4. Publish before commit, and retry until the payment exists

**Status:** accepted

## Context

A payment is saved in Postgres and announced on a queue. Those can't happen as
one atomic step. Publishing before `COMMIT` means a queue outage rolls the
payment back cleanly, but the processor can receive the message before the
payment has been committed. The nightly repeat run caught exactly that race:
the processor saw no payment, dropped the message, and the payment waited
forever.

## Decision

Keep publishing before `COMMIT`. When the processor can't find the payment
yet, or finds it still `in_review`, it retries a few seconds later instead of
dropping the message. A payment that never appears ends in the dead-letter
queue.

## Consequences

- No payment waits forever for a message that was thrown away.
- A few extra retries happen on busy days.
- The complete fix is the outbox pattern: write the message to a table in the
  same transaction, and publish it after `COMMIT`. That's the next step if the
  retries ever become a problem.

Each one names its downsides. A decision record with no downsides isn't being honest, and interviewers notice. The fourth tells the Week 10 race in twenty lines, which makes it a good link to send with an application.

# Ledgerline

![CI](https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/ledgerline/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)

A small business-banking backend, and the test framework around it. It moves
money the way a fintech does, through a double-entry ledger, a queue, an AWS
Lambda and a partner bank, and the tests go after the ways money goes wrong:
twice, silently, past a limit, or out of step with the bank.

## What it shows

- **A layered test framework:** a typed client, fixtures, builders, and a
  contract check on every response.
- **Payments testing:** idempotency keys, duplicate messages, signed webhooks,
  ACH returns, daily reconciliation against the bank's files.
- **Concurrency:** row locks and atomic counters proven with parallel tests,
  and a publish-before-commit race found by nightly repeat runs.
- **Infrastructure:** AWS in MiniStack, a fake bank in WireMock whose stubs are
  checked against the bank's contract, and Redis for risk limits.
- **CI people trust:** fast checks first, sharded API tests, a merged report,
  a nightly flaky-test hunt with a quality dashboard, and a load test.

Step 57: Demo, resume and interviews

A few hours, spread over the week.

Record a three to five minute demo

A short screen recording lets someone see the project work without installing anything. On a Mac, open QuickTime Player and choose File, then New Screen Recording. Follow this order:

  1. The README and the diagram, in about 30 seconds: what Ledgerline is and what it shows.
  2. A green run: npm run check, or a CI run's page with its summary table.
  3. Break something on purpose: delete FOR UPDATE in src/ledger.ts and run npx playwright test -g "parallel transfers". It goes red.
  4. Show the report: npx playwright show-report, the failure, and the service logs attached under it.
  5. Fix it, and show the test green again.
  6. End on the dashboard, with the race from Step 48 told in one sentence.

Resume bullets

Adjust the numbers if yours differ, and describe it plainly as a personal project. Implying production experience you don't have is the fastest way to lose an interviewer's trust.

  • Built a TypeScript and Playwright API test framework for a double-entry payments backend: a typed client, fixtures, builders, and OpenAPI contract checks on every response (86 API tests, 44 unit tests).
  • Tested asynchronous payments end to end across SQS, Lambda, DynamoDB and S3 (in MiniStack) with a WireMock partner bank: retries, dead-letter queues, idempotency keys, signed webhooks and ACH returns.
  • Designed GitHub Actions CI with staged checks, sharded API tests, merged reports, and nightly repeat runs feeding a flake-rate dashboard, which caught a publish-before-commit race condition.
  • Added stub-drift checks against the partner bank's contract, k6 load tests with p95 thresholds, and Redis-backed risk limits proven under parallel load.

Five stories to have ready

Each one is a problem found, a cause worked out, and a fix proved, which is the shape interviewers look for.

  • The crash nobody tested for (Step 4): stopping the database crashed the whole API, until one error listener fixed it.
  • The friendly defaults (Step 11): Fastify quietly accepted "2500" as a number and threw away unknown fields.
  • The race condition (Step 14): without a row lock, parallel transfers overdrew accounts on every run; with it, never.
  • The race the dashboard found (Step 48): one run in 255 failed, and the cause was a message arriving before its payment existed.
  • The drift (Step 50): the fake bank had been answering in a way the real one never would, since Week 5.

The case study

The most likely technical exercise is "design a test strategy for a new kind of payment". Practise with international wires, out loud, in 45 minutes. Start with what makes them different: they're generally irreversible once sent, they travel over SWIFT, they involve currency conversion, they need sanctions screening (in the US, against OFAC lists), and they have strict cutoff times. Then walk through the same headings as your docs/test-strategy.md: the risks, the layers, what you'd fake and how, what you'd automate first, and what you'd measure. Compare your answer with your strategy document afterwards.

Three lengths of pitch

Practise describing Ledgerline in 30 seconds (what it is, and one hard bug), in 2 minutes (add the framework and CI), and in 10 minutes (walk through the README, the framework, and one story in depth).

The whole project

In twelve weeks, you've built:

  • A payments backend with a double-entry ledger, payments to other banks through a queue and a Lambda, idempotency keys, signed webhooks, ACH returns, risk limits, and daily reconciliation.
  • A test framework with a typed client, fixtures, builders, contract checks on every response, a fake bank checked against the real bank's contract, and service logs attached to failures.
  • CI people trust, with staged and sharded runs, merged reports, a nightly flaky-test hunt with a quality dashboard, and a load test.

  • The documents that explain it all: a test strategy, decision records, a flaky-test policy and an AI review checklist.

  • Teach it back. Give the 10-minute walk-through to someone, a friend or a mirror, and note where you hesitated.

  • Dev log. Read it from the beginning. Your best interview answers are already in there.

Concepts by topic

Every "What, why and how" box in the handbook, grouped by subject. Each link opens the box inside the step where it appears.

Setup and tools

  • The terminal Step 1.

    The terminal is a window where you control the computer by typing commands instead of clicking.

  • Node.js, npm and nvm Step 1. With a demo.

    JavaScript was born in web browsers.

  • Git and GitHub Step 1.

    Git records snapshots of your project, called commits, so you can see what changed, when and why, and return to any earlier state.

  • Docker and containers Step 1.

    Docker runs programs in containers: isolated boxes holding a program and everything it needs.

  • Docker Compose Step 4. With a demo.

    Docker Compose starts several containers from one file, docker-compose.yml.

  • TypeScript Step 2. With a demo.

    TypeScript is JavaScript plus types: labels saying what shape each value must have.

  • Linters and formatters Step 7.

    A linter, ESLint here, reads code and flags patterns that are usually mistakes, like a variable that's never used.

Building the API

  • APIs, servers and Fastify Step 3. With a demo.

    An API is a set of URLs that a program answers, so that other programs can use it.

  • JSON Schema and request validation Step 11.

    JSON Schema is a standard way to describe what valid JSON looks like: which fields are required, what type each one is, and which values are allowed.

  • Authentication and API keys Step 15.

    Authentication answers the question "who is calling?".

  • OpenAPI Step 16.

    OpenAPI is a standard file format, written in YAML or JSON, that describes a REST API: every endpoint, what it accepts and what it returns, with data shapes written in JSON Schema.

  • The SQL you'll meet Step 9.

    SQL is the language for talking to a relational database.

  • Databases and PostgreSQL Step 4. With a demo.

    A database stores data so it survives restarts, and so that many users can safely read and write it at once.

  • curl and jq Step 12.

    curl sends HTTP requests from the terminal.

Money and payments

  • The ACH lifecycle and returns Step 31. With a demo.

    ACH is the US network most business payments travel on.

  • Idempotency Step 27. With a demo.

    An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.

  • Webhooks Step 31.

    A webhook is a partner calling your API when something happens on their side, so you don't have to keep asking them.

  • Signatures with HMAC Step 31. With a demo.

    An HMAC is a fingerprint of a message, made with a secret key.

  • State machines Step 31.

    A state machine lists the states something can be in, and the moves allowed between them.

  • Risk rules and decision tables Step 34.

    Risk rules decide whether a payment goes ahead on its own or waits for a person to look at it.

  • Reconciliation Step 38. With a demo.

    Reconciliation compares your records with someone else's, line by line, and flags every difference.

AWS and infrastructure

  • Cloud computing and AWS Step 22.

    Cloud computing means renting computing instead of owning servers.

  • Regions, credentials and permissions Step 22.

    Every AWS call involves three ideas: - A region is a place where AWS runs its services, like us-east-1 in Virginia.

  • The AWS SDK for JavaScript Step 22.

    The SDK, short for software development kit, is Amazon's library for calling AWS from code.

  • MiniStack Step 22.

    MiniStack is an emulator: a program that pretends to be AWS.

  • Amazon SQS Step 22. With a demo.

    Simple Queue Service, or SQS, holds messages until a program takes them.

  • AWS Lambda Step 27. With a demo.

    Lambda runs your code without you managing a server.

  • DynamoDB Step 30.

    DynamoDB is AWS's key-value database.

  • Amazon S3 Step 39.

    S3, the Simple Storage Service, stores files, called objects, inside containers called buckets.

  • Redis Step 35. With a demo.

    Redis is an in-memory data store: it keeps keys and values, like counters, in memory, so reading and writing them is extremely fast.

  • WireMock Step 26. With a demo.

    WireMock is a fake HTTP server you program.

  • Retries, backoff and dead-letter queues Step 27.

    A retry repeats an operation that failed for a temporary reason.

  • Bundling and deployment packages Step 29.

    A bundler, esbuild here, follows every import from one starting file and combines that code, and every package it uses, into a single JavaScript file.

Testing

  • Unit tests and Vitest Step 5. With a demo.

    A unit test checks one small piece of logic on its own: call a function with an input, and assert on its output.

  • API testing with Playwright Step 6.

    You know Playwright for driving browsers.

  • Fixtures and builders Step 18. With a demo.

    A fixture is something Playwright prepares for a test and cleans up afterwards, like an API client, a database connection or a fake bank.

  • Ajv, the validator Step 17. With a demo.

    Ajv is a JavaScript library that takes a JSON Schema and checks data against it, listing every rule the data breaks.

  • Bruno Step 20.

    Bruno is an API client like Postman: you build requests, send them and read the responses.

  • Test data shortcuts Step 36.

    A test data shortcut sets up a test's starting state directly in the database, instead of through the API.

  • Stub drift and provider contracts Step 50.

    Stub drift is when a fake stops matching the real system it stands in for.

  • Load testing and k6 Step 51.

    A load test sends many requests at once, for a while, and measures how the system copes: how quickly it answers, how many requests fail, and how much it can handle.

  • AI in your testing Step 52.

    AI assistants like Claude and Cursor can write tests, explain failures and suggest cases you missed.

CI, quality and observability

  • CI and GitHub Actions Step 7. With a demo.

    Continuous integration, or CI, means every push is checked automatically on a fresh machine.

  • Jobs, matrices and sharding Step 44. With a demo.

    A GitHub Actions workflow can hold several jobs, each running on its own fresh machine.

  • Flaky tests Step 43.

    A flaky test passes and fails without any change to the code.

  • Quality metrics Step 49.

    Quality metrics are numbers that describe a test suite's health over time: the pass rate, the flake rate (the share of tests that sometimes fail with no code change), how long the suite takes, and which tests are slowest.

  • Logs, traces and correlation ids Step 46. With a demo.

    Observability is being able to tell what a running system is doing from the outside.

When you get stuck

Send me:

  • the step number;
  • the command you ran;
  • the full error text, or a screenshot of the terminal;
  • anything you changed from the handbook.

Most problems land in a few buckets: Docker or Postgres isn't running (check with docker compose ps), a file was saved in the wrong folder (compare its path with the one in the step), or a paste lost its indentation, especially in YAML. git diff shows everything you've changed since your last commit, which often points straight at the problem.
